editorialDecl.p: The commentary prints 794 Zu βαρυστόνως. The corresponding Greek word occurs at line 793 in the installed Blass Greek XML and Smyth reference. revisionDesc.change: Converted the supplied HathiTrust OCR into an aligned, citation-aware CTS TEI commentary.

Reviewed missed Greek lemma openings and line-numbered comments against the source OCR. Added mentioned markup and paragraph divisions; split explicit line comments with Blass-to-Smyth corresp and card milestones. Preserved source wording and existing bibliographic/quotation markup.

Second Blass lemma review: separated Greek-first numbered notes and German-prefaced lemma comments, preserving printed word order including In before atieton. Assigned verified Blass verse anchors with Smyth corresp and card milestones. Commentary wording and existing citations unchanged.

Reviewed sentence-boundary Greek lemma candidates against the corresponding Blass Greek passage, including inflected dictionary forms and numbered openings. Fourth Blass review: recovered numbered comments after dashes, number plus Zu plus Greek, and V. plus number. Created commline divisions with card milestones, marking verified Greek openings as mentioned and leaving lemma-free comments as prose. Original wording preserved. Printed 794 versus Greek XML 793 is explicitly documented.

Tagged 47 previously unmarked bibliographic citations using reusable citation-family regular expressions; normalized inherited Pausanias passages, Apollonius and Aristophanes ranges, and Dindorf/Nauck fragment identifiers in @n without altering the displayed transcription.

Page-image review resolved 327 commentary divisions and added 838 Gemini-assisted OCR corrections as choice/sic/corr. Resolved low-certainty flags were retired; ambiguous readings and the diplomatic OCR text were preserved.

p.seg: πρῶτον μὲν θεῶν πρεσβεύω τὴν πρωτόμαντιν Γαῖαν First among the gods I honor Gaia, the first prophet; since πρῶτον first and πρωτόμ first are related (Weckl.), one should not, with others, seek the apodosis only in ἔπειτα then V. 29.
Πρεσβεύειν to honor first = προτιμᾶν to honor above all (Hesych.) as at 21. Ch. 488 (with πρῶτον first as here). 631. Ag. 1300. —

ἐκ δὲ τῆς and from her as at (7.) 784 ἐκ δὲ τοῦ and from him; further 693 ἐν δὲ τῶι and in him. 137. 174. 338 etc., Dindorf Lex. 233ᵇ. Themis is here, as in Hesiod, distinguished from Gaia and appears as her daughter (Theog. 135), while in the Prom. 209f. A. likes to mix them: ἐμοὶ δὲ μήτηρ and my mother . . Θέμις καὶ Γαῖα Themis and Gaia, πολλῶν ὀνομάτων μορφὴ μία one form of many names; but Themis-Gaia is also prophetic there, cf. Homer π p 403 Διὸς μεγάλοιο θέμιστες the ordinances of great Zeus, i.e. oracles, Pind. P. 4, 54 Φοῖβος ἀμνάσει θέμισσιν Phoebus will remind with ordinances (likewise); νημερτέα βουλὴν πᾶσι θεμιστεύοιμι I would give unerring counsel to all (Apollo speaks) Hom. Hymn. Ap. Pyth. 74f.; Harpocration θεμιστεύειν to give oracles = χρησμωιδεῖν to prophesy, attested from Lysias (GHerm.); see also on 32. So from the beginning of things there have been oracles at this site, and the deity has manifested itself ever more clearly, through ordinances and utterances that it announced to humans.
This tradition gives Pausanias X, 5, 6 from a poem bearing the name of Musaeus, Eumolpia, at any rate a product of the Pisistratid period, like other such things; cf. Euripides I. T. 1249 ff.

Ἥ δὴ who indeed as at Prom. 922 ὃς δὴ who indeed. Hik. 265 τὰ δὴ the things indeed etc.; ὡς λόγος τις as some story says points to the variation in the tradition among different sources, of which Pausanias also speaks there, § 5.

Phoebe as holder only here; she too, like Themis, is one of the Hesiodic children of Uranus and Gaia, Theog. 136, and provides a particularly simple transition to the last holder Φοῖβος Phoebus. Λάχος lot (= κλῆρος lot Schol.) is a word especially frequent in the Eumenides: 310. 334. 347. 386. 400 (otherwise only Ch. 361).

Θελούσης willing: everything has taken place in a calm manner, as is fitting among gods; even the so-called Musaeus let Apollo receive the oracle from Themis as a gift. Τιτανὶς παῖς Χθονός Titaness, child of Earth as at Prom. 205 Τιτᾶνας Οὐρανοῦ τε καὶ Χθονὸς τέκνα Titans, children of Uranus and Earth; naturally Χθών Earth is also one of the "many names" of Gaia, there 210, above on 2.

δ᾽ ἣ and she: as at V. 2; one need not, with Porson, emend to δίδωσιν ἢ gives or. Verses 7 and 8 are parallel in punctuation and sentence structure (Weil): Φοίβῃ to Phoebe· δίδωσιν gives (so M.) | δ᾽ ἣ γενέθλιον δόσιν and she, a birthday gift | Φοίβῳ to Phoebus· | τὸ Φοίβης the name of Phoebe | δ᾽ ὄνομ᾽ ἔχει παρώνυμον has a derived name (- -, - -, ICI (1). Phoebe now, according to Hesiod Th. 404 ff., is mother of Leto; therefore γενέθλιον δόσιν birthday gift = συγγενικήν kindred, as the Schol.?

Γενέθλιος Genethlios (of birth) means a parentibus proficiscens Ch. 912 according to Ddf., more generally gentilis Sept. 639. But since certainly no listener knew of this kinship, one must now, for the sake of clarity, write with Weil τήθης of the grandmother for Φοίβης of Phoebe. In the scholiast, however, another explanation is mixed in with this one, which points to the giving of gifts at the ὀπτήρια optēria (gifts for seeing a newborn) of the child; cf. passages such as Eurip. Ion 1127, where Xuthos sacrifices ὀπτήρια optēria (gifts for seeing a newborn) for the seeing of his son, and especially Kallimachos Artem. 72 ff.: ἔτι τριέτηρος ἐοῦσα still being three years old, εὖτ᾽ ἔμολεν Λητώ σε μετ᾿ ἀγκαλίδεσσι φέρουσα when Leto came carrying you in her arms, Ἡφαίστου καλέοντος of Hephaestus calling, ὅπως ὀπτήρια δοίη so that he might give optēria. Certainly the scholiast read Φοίβης of Phoebe; otherwise he would not make Ph. and Leto out to be sisters. Since elsewhere (Plat. Symp. 203 C; Eur. Ion 653 θῦσαί θ᾽ ἅ σου πρὶν γενέθλι᾽ οὐκ ἐθύσαμεν and to sacrifice the birthday offerings which we did not sacrifice to you before; thus γενέθλια birthday offerings = ὀπτήρια optēria (gifts for seeing a newborn) 1127) τὰ γενέθλια the birthday offerings is the birthday festival (cf. below 293 γενεθλίου πόρου of the birth passage), one can also understand γενέθλιος of birth in this way, and then a closer determination of the kinship is unnecessary, even if for τήθης of the grandmother Apollonios Lex. Hom. can be cited: Φοίβος Phoebus . . ὁ μὲν the one A. ἀπὸ Φοίβης from Phoebe, τῆς μητρὸς Λητοῦς of his mother Leto (GHerm.). — Παρώνυμος paronymous (derived name) is usually understood as "derived name", after Aristot. Kateg. 1 ὁ γραμματικὸς παρώνυμος ἀπὸ τῆς γραμματικῆς the grammarian is paronymous from grammar; Plat. Soph. 265 C from the σοφιστής sophist: μιμητὴς ὢν τοῦ σοφοῦ δῆλον ὅτι παρωνύμιον αὐτοῦ τι λήψεται being an imitator of the wise man, he will clearly take some paronym of his; thus Apollo ἔχει τὸ Φοίβης παρώνυμον ὄνομα he has the paronymous name of Phoebe. But παρ par. also means epithet, see Arist. Πολ. Αθ. 17, 3 Ἡγησίστρατος ὧι παρωνύμιον ἦν Θετταλός Hegesistratus, whose paronym was Thessalos, and Φοίβος Phoebus is in fact only an epithet (ἐπίθετον Ἀπόλλωνος epithet of Apollo Apollonios Lex. Hom.); so I prefer to understand it thus (παρώνυμον paronym namely ὄνομα name "as epithet"). - A. has therefore, as the scholiast also notes, silently eliminated all the tales of the dragon Python, the earth-born monster which Apollo slew, and of the wrath of Gaia, and of the blood-atonement to which the god then submitted as a model. In this, however, Alkaios was already a predecessor, Frg. 2f., Preller-Robert Myth. 240, 1. Cf. also the paean of Aristonoos (Weil Mélanges de litt. et de rythm. gr. 49 ff.) 21 ff.: πείσας Γαῖαν ἀνθοτρόφον Θέμιν τ᾽ εὐπλόκαμον θεὰν αἰὲν εὐλιβάνους ἕδρας ἔχεις ὦ Ἰεπαιάν having persuaded Gaia, the flower-nurturing, and Themis of the lovely hair, the goddess, you ever hold seats rich in incense, O Iepaian.

9ff. λίμνην Δηλίαν τε χ the Delian lake and. = Δηλίαν λ Delian. καὶ χ and., as at Ag. 589 ἅλωσιν Ἰλίου τ᾽ ἀνάστασιν the capture of Ilium and its destruction, and often. The τροχοειδὴς λίμνη circular lake on Delos, where Apollo was born, is mentioned Theognis 5. Hdt. II, 170 and elsewhere; in χοιράδα rocky islet (the cliffs and rocks, naturally not Mount Cynthus) lies, as a scholiast correctly observes, also the reason why Apollo exchanged Delos for Delphi. (Δήλιαί τε χοιράδες the Delian rocky islets Eur. Tro. 89, Weckl.). On line 10 the scholiast emphasizes that Aeschylus, as an Athenian, makes Apollo take this route, whereas the Boeotian Pindar has him go via Tanagra (in whose territory Delium lay; hardly correct, O. Müller Orchom. p. 147 Τεγύρας Tegyra). But sea traffic (cf. ναυπόρους sea-faring) went from the Cyclades far more to Attica than to the Boeotian coast. Also in the paean of Aristonous, where the purification in Tempe is mentioned, it says (19f.): ἐπεὶ Παλλὰς ἔπεμψε Πυθῶδε when Pallas sent him to Pytho (19f.); deliberately therefore here ἀκτὰς τὰς Παλλάδος the shores of Pallas, and cf. 21. — 11.
Παρνησοῦ Parnassus on Ch. 563;
ἕδρας seats cf. 805 ἕδρας τε καὶ κευθμῶνας ἐνδίκου χθονός seats and hiding places of the just land.

In passing, a service of Athens to civilization is highlighted: the Athenians, who first learned the arts from Hephaestus and Athena (Plat. Menex. 238 B), also first made a road through the wilderness. This is the sacred road for the sacred embassies to Delphi (Ephoros b. Strab. IX, 422), on which (Schol.) people still went ahead with axes, ὡς διημερώσοντες τὴν γῆν as if they would tame the land.
Παῖδες Ἡφαίστου Children of Hephaestus are the Athenians as sons of Erichthonius, at the same time also with reference to the forged axes.
τιμαλφεῖν to honor also 626, 807. Agam. 922 (τιμαλφής honored Frg. 53); besides Pindar N. 9, 54.

On Δελφός Delphos (the eponymous hero of Delphi) the scholiast on line 2 supplies the mythological background: a son of Poseidon and Melaina, who was a granddaughter of Deucalion. — Πρυμνήτην χθονός the stern of the land also at 765, hardly a normal word, but coined after the model of κυβερνήτης helmsman to match πρωιράτης prow officer. Ἐν πρύμνηι πόλεως οἴακα νωμῶν holding the helm at the stern of the city of the ruler, Sept. 2.

Τέχναισιν ἐνθέοις with inspired arts of the art of prophecy Ag. 1209; here constructed differently (ἔνθεος inspired as at ἔμπειρος experienced) and with some harshness, in that the god ἔνθεος inspired, possessed by a god. On κτίζω I found, establish with double accusative see on Ch. 441; here there is additionally a double object, νιν him, her, it (accusative singular) — φρένα mind, heart (accusative singular), as at 88 μὴ φόβος σε νικάτω φρένας let not fear overcome your mind (Minckwitz). Τόνδε this man (accusative singular) (manuscript) can be understood of the present holder; however τοῖσδε to these (dative plural) (Kirchhoff) is highly recommended, especially by line 3 τόδ᾽ ἕζετο μαντεῖον this oracle seat was established. In line 19 a main thought is expressed, which recurs at 616ff., 713; see also Frg. 82 (Ἱέρειαι priestesses): ταῦτα γὰρ πατὴρ Ζεὺς ἐγκαθίει Λοξίαι θεσπίσματα for these prophecies father Zeus instilled in Loxias, and cf. (Weckl.) Hom. Hymn. Ap. Del. 132 χρήσω δ᾽ ἀνθρώποισι Διὸς νημερτέα βουλήν I shall proclaim to mortals the unerring will of Zeus, Hymn. Herm. 471, Verg. Aen. III, 251. Thus as the Pythia stands to Apollo, so he stands to Zeus: a proclaimer, nothing more.

Λοξίας Loxias is also often used by Aeschylus for Apollo, yet always in some relation to his oracles, the λοξοὶ χρησμοί oblique oracles, Preller-Robert Myth. 286. On δέ and, but (postpositive particle) in third position (also at 21) to Ch. 425.

Verse 20 I have, as Weil earlier, transposed after 26, for which an external indication brought forward by W. lies in the fact that the scholiast on 28 καλοῦσα calling upon (nominative singular feminine participle) supplements the φροιμιάζομαι I make a prelude from 20; with the transmitted order that would be incomprehensible. But also the sequence of thought is considerably improved by the transposition. Φροιμιάζεσθαι to make a prelude (to make a proem) stands Ag. 1354 intransitively, here = προοιμιαζομένη καλῶ making a prelude I call upon transitively. Now according to the transmitted position the invocation of the gods of the oracle would be the proem to the invocation of the other gods; by contrast, after the transposition the entire invocation is the proem to the business of the prophetess, and this is surely the only natural thing. See further below. — In the weak and unclear ἐν λόγοις in words 21 GHermann correctly found the Aeschylean εὐλόγως reasonably, with good reason: Sept. 508. Hik. 47. 252. 591, Frg. 5; thus εὐλόγως πρεσβεύεται with good reason she is honored first = δικαίως προτιμᾶται τῶν λοιπῶν justly she is preferred above the rest, namely already as the nearest, and also because of her service to Apollo, 10. 12 ff.

Προνᾴα Pronaia (Athena of the fore-temple) the same Hermann, since the a is long; thus Ionic (Herodot 8, 37) τὸ ἱρὸν τῆς Προνήιης Ἀθηναίης the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia (cf. 1, 92). The temple is described by Pausanias X, 8, 6, who calls the goddess Πρόνοια Pronoia (Forethought), according to the misunderstanding already found in Demosth. 25, 34: καὶ παρὰ τῶι Ἀπόλλωνι τῶι ἐν Δελφοῖς κάλλιστος καὶ μέγιστος νεὼς and by Apollo at Delphi the fairest and greatest temple (scil. Προνοίας Ἀθηνᾶς of Athena Pronoia) εὐθὺς εἰσιόντι εἰς τὸ ἱερόν immediately upon entering the sanctuary. The goddess is also mentioned in Aischines 3, 108. 110f. (according to the tradition likewise as Πρόνοια Pronoia (Forethought)), and indeed in Delphic formulae connected with Apollo, Artemis, Leto, whereby the πρεσβεύεται she is honored first is even better explained. The Delphic inscriptions have Ἀθάνα Προνάια Athena Pronaia, Dial.-Inschr. 2503, 12. 2513, 13. 2514, 5. The present indicative denotes the habit of the Pythia, just as καλοῦσα calling upon (nominative singular feminine participle) and καθιζάνω I sit down, take my seat 28f., see there; thus also σέβω I revere, worship 22 and εὐχαῖς φροιμιάζομαι with prayers I make a prelude 20, while εὐχῆι τῆιδε πρεσβεύω with this prayer I give first honor 1 denotes the present prayer.

22f. The Κωρύκιον ἄντρον Corycian cave, situated high on the ascent to the summit of Parnassus, is described in detail by Pausanias X, 32, 2 ff., according to whom this cave was the largest of all known to him; at the end he says: ἱερὸν δ᾽ αὐτὸ οἱ περὶ τὸν Παρνασὸν Κωρυκίων εἶναι Νυμφῶν καὶ Πανὸς μάλιστα ἥγηνται and the people around Parnassus consider it sacred especially to the Corycian Nymphs and to Pan. See also Strabon IX, 417; Herodot 8, 36; Κωρύκιαι νύμφαι Βακχίδες Corycian Bacchic nymphs Soph. Antig. 1128, etc. — With the brachylogy Νύμφας ἔνθα where the Nymphs . . (the Nymphs who dwell where . .) Weckl. compares 689 σκηνάς tents (ἵν᾽ ἐσκηνοῦντο where they encamped) ὅτ᾽ ἦλθον when they came.
Φίλορνις bird-loving as is natural, since caves are suitable for nesting;

δαιμόνων of the deities (of the Nymphs and of Pan) ἀναστρ return., as δωμάτων ἐπιστροφάς visitations of the house Sept. 648 Eum. 547, βούνομοί τ᾽ ἐπιστροφαί and pastoral visitations Frg. 243, Σύρων ἐπιστροφαί visitations of the Syrians 264, according to which ἀναστροφαί returns, like the other manuscripts except M, is highly recommended in comparison with the ἀναστροφή return of the scholiast (M ἀναστροφά returns).

Ἀναστρέφεσθαι to turn about, to stay = ἐπιστρ turn. "to stay" already in Homer ν n 326; therefore ἀναστροφαί places of stay "place of stay" (wrongly explained by Dindorf as deverticulum). Cf. the grotto in Ithaca Hom. v 103ff., which is likewise sacred to the Nymphs. Aristonoos (on 7f. 10) says V. 33 ff.: δωροῦνται δέ σ᾽ ἀθάνατοι the immortals grant you, Ποσειδῶν ἁγνοῖς δαπέδοις Poseidon on the holy ground, Νύμφαι Κορυκίοισιν ἄντροις the Nymphs in the Corycian caves, ἰήιε Παιάν Hail, Healer, τριετέσιν φαναῖς Βρόμιος Bromius with triennial torchlight etc.

Dionysus (Βρόμιος Bromius as often in the poets, Eur. Bacch. 87 etc.) had great veneration in Delphi (Preller-Robert Mythol. 686); in particular the heights of Parnassus were sacred to him, where he celebrated his dances with his Bacchae by torchlight, Soph. Ant. 1126 etc.; so also Pausan. X, 32, 7 of the peaks of P.: καὶ αἱ Θυιάδες ἐπὶ τούτοις τῶι Διονύσωι καὶ τῶι Ἀπόλλωνι μαίνονται and the Thyiades rave for Dionysus and Apollo on these occasions. Therefore Dionysus also had to be mentioned by the Pythia: οὐδ᾽ ἀμνημονῶ nor do I forget ("nor must I forget Bacchus" Paley). The lesser manuscripts have against M Βρόμιος δ but Bromius', which anapest would be somewhat covered by ὕπατός τε and the highest Ag. 509 and ἑκατὸν δὶς twice a hundred Pers. 343; but some compulsion is always the reason for this foot, and here there was no compulsion.

Ἐξ οὗτε from which like Pers. 762 (Dindorf Lex. ὅστε so that); στρατηγεῖν τινι to be general for someone like ἡγεῖσθαι to lead, Eur. Tro. 926. Hdt. 6, 72, Kühner-Gerth I 409 f. That Pentheus according to this passage must have been torn to pieces on Parnassus, whereas according to Aeschylus' Xantriai the scene was Cithaeron, is an erroneous assumption of the scholiast. Rather (Weckl.): on his victorious march, after overcoming Pentheus, Dionysus also took Parnassus.

In καταρράψας having stitched together (Diod. Sic. 17, 45, to stitch together) we have the metaphor common since Homer (τοῦδε τοῦ φόνου ῥαφεύς the stitcher of this murder Ag. 1604, μηχανορραφῶ I contrive by stitching Ch. 221). The comparison with the hare, according to the scholiast, points to the complete lack of resistance; or “like dogs tearing a hare to pieces.” The verse may be deliberately without caesura, because of μίμησις imitation, as in Pers. 465 and elsewhere; something like Ch. 150. 493. 883 is excluded here. 20. 27 f. After the transposition there is no longer any reason for the change μὲν εὐχαῖς with prayers 20 (Blaydes). The river-god Pleistos, Poseidon, and Zeus now appear, after this transposition, as being named only in an appendix to the prayer; but this is also appropriate. The Pleistos flowed, according to Pausan. X, 8, 8, about 3 stades from Delphi and emptied into the sea at Kirrha; Apollonios Rhod. II, 713 Κωρύκιαι νύμφαι Πλείστοιο θύγατρες Corycian nymphs, daughters of Pleistos. The local pronunciation was Πλειστός Pleistos; nevertheless Herodian, E. M. 676, 5 (Dindorf Lex. 290 f.), made it barytone. Poseidon was the former possessor of Delphi, which he had exchanged for Kalaureia, Callimachus in the scholia, Pausan. X, 5, 6. 24, 4, Aristonoos in the paean, see on 22 f. at the end; therefore (Paus. 24) there was an altar of Poseidon in the sanctuary of Apollo.

Κράτος Power periphrastic as in σόν your, Κλυταιμήστρα Clytemnestra, κράτος power Ag. 258; on this and on τέλειον Δία Zeus the fulfiller cf. especially τελέων τελειότατον κράτος ὄλβιε Ζεῦ of fulfillers the most fulfilling power, blessed Zeus Hik. 525 (Ζεῦ τέλειε (Zeus the fulfillerAg. 973). Zeus in third and last place as in Ch. 244 f. (Weil).

Καλοῦσα . . καθιζάνω Calling . . I sit down describes what the Pythia habitually does (on 21); in the contrast καὶ νῦν and now . . τῶν πρὶν εἰσόδων than my former entrances this emerges quite clearly.
Ἔπειτα Then 29 picks up the participle καλοῦσα calling again (Dindorf Lex. 124 b); cf. on 1.
The θρόνος throne is the same as in 18, in that the Pythia represents the god; thus the tripod, Eurip. Ion 91 θάσσει δὲ γυνὴ τρίποδα ζάθεον κτὲ and a woman sits on the holy tripod, etc..

The transmitted construction: δοῖέν με τυχεῖν ἄριστα τῶν πρίν may they grant me to obtain the best things than before, is at least not clear, since the object ἄριστα best things has the appearance of an adverb; also τυγχάνειν to obtain with accusative is not sufficiently secured for Aeschylus either by the corrupt verse Ch. 711 or by Ag. 1230 τεύξεται he will prepare (“will prepare,” = τεύξει he will prepare). On the other hand, with μοι for me instead of με me, ἄριστα best things becomes an unambiguous subject, and cf. Ch. 785 δὸς τύχας grant fortunes, τυχεῖν δέ μοι to obtain for me (Turn. for μου of me) κυρίως τὰ σώφροσιν μαιομένοις ἰδεῖν properly, for the chaste to see when they seek. Τῶν πρὶν ἄριστα the best of those before like ἀξιολογώτατος τῶν προγεγενημένων most worthy of account of those who came before Thuc. 1, 1, 1 etc.; but what motivates the wish? On this day of oracle-giving there is nothing special that would cause one to expect or wish for special good fortune. So this too may be a formula, in which the wish is intensified as much as possible: each time she enters the temple, she prays thus.

In 31 παρ᾿ Ἑλλήνων τινές some of the Greeks (this is the traditional spelling) the absence of the verb is offensive (sc. πάρεισιν they are present Dindorf), but also the παρ from', which would have to mean "sent from," whereas the thought requires the simple partitive. Thus GHermann and Abresch write πάρ from', which can stand for πάρεισι they are present, see Eur. Med. 443. Ar. Ach. 962. 1091, though it is not readily elided (any more than ἔπι upon, μέτα with). The change κεἴ τις Ἑλλ and if any Greek. πάρα from (Burges, Weckl.) makes things worse, not only because the plural follows, but also because the singular is unmotivated. According to Plut. Qu. gr. 9, oracles were given only once a month, so each time a larger number of consultants had to gather. Thus πάρ from' has the least objection. On Ἑλλήνων of the Greeks there is no further emphasis, as if barbarians in general were also thought of (cf. Eurip. Ion 92, see below); they were not usually present. Among the consultants there was a drawing of lots for the order (unless a state had the προμαντεία priority in consulting the oracle); hence ὀμφὸν κληροῦν to assign the oracle by lot by Apollo Eurip. Ion 908 (Paley). According to Simplicius in Ar. Phys. p. 333, 16 Diels, the drawing of lots was preceded by the question: ὦ τύχη καὶ Λοξία O Fortune and Loxias, τῶνδε of these (Weckl. for τῶιδε to this one) τίνι θεμιστεύεις to whom do you give oracles?; This is, as Schütz rightly saw, the guidance of the god, of which V. 33 speaks; therefore one should not write μαντεύσομαι I will prophesy (Kirchhoff), however easy the change is. For it is motivated by custom and practice, and that is better than an explanation of what the P. now intends to do.
Ἴτων let them go (only here) is formed from ἴτω let him go as ἔστων let them be from ἔστω let him be, without the internal ν n, alongside ἰόντων of those going and ὄντων of those being.

The Pythia comes out again in terror and announces the cause. Although no one in what follows is addressed or even indicated as a listener, the oracle consultants of V. 31 can easily be understood as listeners, since the matter concerns them too; for no oracles will be given for the time being. The scholiast in the summary of V. 1 rejects the opinion that this is a Euripidean prologue for the spectators (τὰ ὑπὸ τὴν σκηνήν the things under the stage in the scholion is "that behind the stage," as ὑπὸ τὴν θύρην under the door Hdt. 1, 12 "behind the door"); in fact, the speech must be thought of as addressed, as at the beginning to the invoked gods, so now to specific people, as δεινὰ λέξαι terrible to say immediately shows: I can scarcely tell you, just as I scarcely endured the sight. (On the anaphora to Ch. 628.)
πάλιν ἔπεμψε sent back as στέλλει πάλιν he sends back Prom. 387.

On μήτε σωκεῖν μήτε μ᾿ ἀκταίνειν neither to be strong nor to be able to move, where the common με me is attached only to the second member, cf. Prom. 156 ὡς μήτε θεῶν μήτε τις ἀνδρῶν so that neither of the gods nor any of men.

Σωκεῖν to be strong (Soph. El. 119, otherwise unattested) ἰσχύειν to be strong Hesych.; on ἀκταίνειν to move the scholiast notes: κουφίζειν to lift up· σημαίνει δὲ καὶ τὸ γαυριᾶν καὶ ἀτάκτως πηδᾶν it also means to exult and to leap disorderly, cf. Timaeus, Lexicon Platonicum: ἀκταίνειν to move· γαυριᾶν καὶ ἀτάκτως πηδᾶν to exult and to leap disorderly. Here there is serious confusion: at Platon Ges. II, 672 C it is said of young children and young animals that at first they μαίνεταί τε καὶ βοᾶι ἀτάκτως he rages and shouts disorderly, then ὅταν ἀκταινώσηι ἑαυτὸ τάχιστα whenever he moves himself most quickly, ἀτάκτως αὖ πηδᾶι again he leaps disorderly. The scholion on that passage again agrees with ours, but clearly ἀκταινῶσαι to move = ὑψῶσαι to raise, μετεωρίσαι to lift up, to stand upright, Phrynich. Bk. An. 23, and so this one continues: Αἰσχύλος Aeschylus “οὐκέτ᾽ ἀκταίνω I no longer move” φησὶ βαρυτόνως he says with barytone accent (not ἀκταινῶ I move), οἷον οὐκέτι δύναμαι ὀρθοῦν ἐμαυτήν as if I am no longer able to raise myself. Is this, as Ruhnken (Tim. p. 21) thinks, our passage? A woman was speaking (ἐμαυτήν myself), but the quotation would be very inaccurate, and so this is listed as a separate fragment, 416 Ddf. Ruhnken collects further material from the lexicographers; there were still more attestations for this word family, and so also in Odyssey ψ psi 3 (πόδες δ᾽ ὑπερικταίνοντο and their feet moved excessively) the old and probably correct reading was ὑπερακταίνοντο they moved excessively or ὑποακταίνοντο they moved under. Fortunately the meaning is beyond doubt.

According to the scholion, the Pythia comes out τετραποδηδόν on all fours (like the blinded Polymestor Eur. Hek. 1058, Stanl.), which modern scholars are unwilling to believe; they even explain it as propping her hands on a staff. The words admit no explanation other than that of the scholion, except that one can understand them as narrative (as at ἕρπω I crawl); in particular ἀντίπαις childlike points to this: she crawled like a small child, ὃ μήπω ἠκταίνωσεν ἑαυτό who has not yet raised himself. Cf. the riddle of the Sphinx: the child is actually four-footed, the old man only three-footed. So also ἀντίπαις childlike (here = ἰσόπαις equal to a child Ag. 75, cf. ἀντίδουλος instead of a slave Ch. 135) is a certain intensification (μὲν οὖν indeed, Ch. 999. Ag. 1396 etc.) of οὐδέν nothing, and the very fine conjecture of Herwerden ἀντίπαις childlike, οὐδὲν μὲν οὖν nothing indeed is not needed; cf. also (Paley) Hik. 749 γυνὴ μονωθεῖσ᾽ οὐδέν· οὐκ ἔνεστ᾽ Ἄρης a woman left alone is nothing; there is no Ares in her.

Τρέχω I run (and ποδωκείαι swiftness of foot), because she is trying to flee as quickly as possible; with ποδωκείαι swiftness of foot (Homer B 792) σκελῶν of legs Weckl. compares 915 ἀστύνικον πόλιν city that conquers the city, Sept. 221 ἀστυδρομουμέναν πόλιν city running through the city, 729 κτεάνων χρηματοδαίτας distributor of possessions.

On γραῦς old woman it should be noted that according to Diodorus XVI, 26, originally virgins prophesied at Delphi; but when one had once been abducted, from then on women over 50 years of age were taken, though still in maiden's dress.
Ἕρπειν to go: simply = βαδίζειν to walk as at Prom. 810. 1024 (Soph. Eur. etc.);

μυχός innermost sanctuary penetralia as at 170. 180. Ch. 954; with πολυστεφής much-wreathed one compares Eur. Ion 222 μέσον ὀμφαλόν . . στέμμασί γ᾽ ἐνδυτόν the central navel-stone . . clothed with fillets, Ar. Plut. 39 τί δῆτα Φοῖβος ἔλακεν ἐκ τῶν στεμμάτων why then did Phoebus cry out from the fillets; that woolen fillets are meant is shown by Strab. IX p. 419f. ὀμφαλὸς τεταινιωμένος the navel-stone bound with fillets. The ὀμφαλός navel-stone, of white marble, is also mentioned by Paus. X, 16, 3.
V. 40 θεομυσής hated by the gods (only here) as murderer; the resolution in the 5th foot is rare, but not unheard of (δεσμὰ περιβαλεῖν to cast bonds around Pr. 52, Weckl.).

Προστρόπαιος suppliant see Ch. 287 (here 234. 237. 445, and προστραπέσθαι to turn to as suppliant 205, προστροπή supplication 718; everywhere of the seeking of purification; the sense is different at 176). Here it is connected with ἕδραν seat (Wieseler), which is why ἕδραν seat (M) is more elegant than ἕδρας seats (f g h), which forces everything to be referred to ἄνδρα man. The blood is naturally not that of the mother, but that of the expiatory victim slaughtered by Apollo, V. 282 f.; see the description of the rite Apollon. Rhod. Argon. IV, 698 ff. (αἵματι χεῖρας hands with blood [of Jason] τέγγεν was wetting [Circe], ἐπιτμήγουσα δέρην cutting the throat [of the piglet]). So this has happened recently; Orestes, however, is still waiting for Apollo's reappearance and further instructions. The Pythia, however, can know nothing of this purification, but must think of murder and blood. Also with νεοσπαδὲς ξίφος newly drawn sword compare Apoll. V. 694: Jason has seated himself at the hearth μέγα φάσγανον ἐν χθονὶ πήξας having fixed his great sword in the ground.

Νεοσπαδές newly drawn (only here) is naturally said not from visual inspection, but from an obvious inference (see Schütz): this sword must, since the hand still drips, have been drawn recently for murder. The conjecture νεοσταγές newly dripping (Burges) is plausible, but the word is after αἵματι στ with blood. χ hand. somewhat tautological, and seems besides to presuppose a purification also of the sword, of which nothing else is known.

ὑψιγέννητος high-born only here. Λῆνος Linus also has Apollon. 4, 173. 177 (λήνεα woolen fillets, of the golden fleece) and Nikandros Al. 453; it must have been a rare, sacral word, and for that very reason, as the scholiast also notes, in need of the explanation given in 45 (Weil). Then, however, μεγίστωι greatest will refer not to the size of the fillets, but to their significance in the ritual ("mighty").
Σωφρόνως chastely "in a chaste manner";
τρανῶς (εἰδέναι) Ag. 1371. Vgl. über die Bezugnahme auf Hörer zu V. 34; man vergleicht Sept. 489 ἅλω δὲ πολλήν, ἀσπίδος κύκλον λέγω.
πρόσθεν, also näher dem Eingange.

Λόχος „Schar" wie 1026. Sept. 112. Frg. 407. Mit den Gorgonen sind die Erinyen schon Ch. 1048 verglichen, wegen der dunklen Kleidung und der Schlangen im Haar, δρακοντόμαλλοι Γοργόνες βροτοστυγεῖς Prom. 799. V. 49

Γόργειος = Γοργόνειος (Prom. 793), jenes schon Homer λ 633 Γοργείην κεφαλήν. Τύποι Bildung, Form, wie Ἱππομέδοντος σχῆμα καὶ μέγας τύπος Sept. 488, Hik. 282 ἐν γυναικείοις τύποις (wo der König ähnlich wie hier die Pythias die fremden Gestalten mit diesen und jenen, die er etwa kennt, vergleicht, Wellauer).
Εἰκάζω schreibt Wecklein, doch ist in εἰκάσω „ich will vergleichen" kein Anstoſs.

V. 50 haben für εἶδόν ποτ᾽ ἤδη (M) die geringeren Hdschr. εἶδόν ποτ᾽ εἶδον, und auch in M selbst stand erst εἶδόν ποτ' ηδο[ν]. Vgl. αὐχῶ γὰρ αὐχῶ Prom. 338; aber in unsrer Stelle scheint die Epanalepsis zu starke Emphase zu geben, und die Verschreibung ηδον (idon) statt ἤδη ergab sich nach εἶδον leicht. Anders und passend οἶδ᾽ οἶδα Ar. Βάτρ. 580. 584; ἤδη ποτ᾽ εἶδον steht Soph. Aias 1142 (Weil). Nach γεγραμμένας fehlt nichts (Dindorf nimmt Lücke an); denn das Femininum -νας ist alles was gesagt werden kann, nachdem γυναῖκας negiert ist, und der Name Ἅρπυιαι war nach Φινέως entbehrlich und tat nichts zur Sache. Die Harpyien sind eine Steigerung an Abscheulichkeit und Hässlichkeit auch den Gorgonen gegenüber; Aischylos hatte sie im Φινεύς (aufgeführt 472 mit den Persern), wenn nicht auf die Bühne gebracht, so doch beschrieben. Die triefenden Augen (54, schon Ch. 1058) sind den Gorgonen fremd, auch die dunkle Hautfarbe, die 52 doch als Ähnlichkeit mit den Harpyien hervorgehoben wird; aber die Flügellosigkeit unterscheidet auch von diesen. (Γε μήν Prom. 871. Sept. 1062. Ag. 1378). Euripides giebt den Erinyen auch Flügel (Or. 317 δρομάδες ὦ πτεροφόροι ποτνιάδες θεαί), mit denen sie indes den Flüchtling auf alle Weise einholen müſsten, was sie doch nicht sollen. Die schwarze Farbe hebt auch Eur. hervor: μελάγχρωτες Or. 321, νυκτὶ προσφερεῖς κόρας 408, χρῶτα κελαιναί El. 1345). Die Krallen der Harpyien (Apoll. Rh. II, 188) darf man den Erinyen des A. nicht beilegen; nirgends spricht er vom Erfassen und Zerfleischen.

Βδελύκτροποι abominable-turners the scholiast seems to derive from βδελύσσεσθαι to feel disgust and ἐκτρέπεσθαι to turn away; more correctly one takes βδελυκτο-τροποι abominable-turners as the base (ἀβδέλυκτος not abominable Frg. 130), with the usual elision of one of the similar syllables and with deliberate accumulation of consonants.
Ἐς τὸ πᾶν to the whole Ch. 684, below at 83 etc. differently than here, where ἐς to expresses only the relation, as in ἐς τὰ πάνθ᾽ ὁμῶς βίαιος to all things equally violent Prom. 736.

Λίβα libation at 54 is an excellent conjecture, cf. εὐκταίαν λίβα prayed-for libation Frg. 52, ἀφθονεστέραν λίβα more abundant libation 68; φιλοσπόνδου λιβός libation-loving Ch. 292. It may very well be thought of as the libation in contrast (Hik. 981 θύειν τε λείβειν τε to sacrifice and to pour), cf. the following verse. Ch. 1058 κἀξ ὀμμάτων στάζουσιν αἷμα δυσφιλές and from their eyes they drip hateful blood. –

Κόσμος adornment refers to the clothing, cf. Hik. 246 εἴρηκας ἀμφὶ κόσμον ἀψευδῆ λόγον you have spoken a true word about the adornment, after the king has spoken of the clothing at 234 ff. The clothing of the Erinyes (imitated by the Cynic Menedemus) was according to Diog. VI, 102: χιτών φαιὸς dark tunic (Choeph. 1049) ποδήρης reaching to the feet, περὶ αὐτῶι ζώνη φοινικῆ around him a crimson belt, πίλος Ἀρκαδικὸς ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς an Arcadian cap on his head — —, ἐμβάται τραγικοί tragic boots, – ῥάβδος ἐν τῆι χειρὶ μειλίνη a staff of ash in his hand; cf. Strabon III, 175 of the inhabitants of the Καττιτερίδες Tin Islands: ἄνθρωποι μελάγχλαινοι people with black cloaks, ποδήρεις ἐνδεδυκότες χιτῶνας wearing tunics reaching to the feet, ἐζωσμένοι περὶ τὰ στέρνα girded around their chests, μετὰ ῥάβδων περιπατοῦντες ὅμοιοι ταῖς τραγικαῖς Ποιναῖς walking with staffs like the tragic Furies (Schütz). The ῥάβδοι staffs, however, occur in A. as little as the burning torches which, according to Aischines 1, 190, the tragic Ποιναί Furies carry. — On φέρειν to carry (not φέρεσθαι to be carried) cf. Kühner-Gerth II, 15 Anm. 13.
Ὄπωπα I have seen (epic) the tragedians always have instead of ἑόρακα I have seen, A. moreover only here. The Attic perfect contained an anapest.
Ὁμιλία company concretely company (σύστημα assembly Schol.) also at 406, 711, 1030, always so with ἦδε this.
58 is easily supplemented from ὄπωπα I have seen with a οἶδα I know. Aἶα earth serves the tragedians as well as Homer for metrical need instead of γαῖα earth, Dindorf Lex. 9 b.

Ἀνατεί without end (so correctly the manuscripts), since it must bring crop failure and all ruin, 780 ff. (Paley). Arnaldus' πόνον toil for πόνων toils of the manuscripts is also supported by the scholion: τὸ the⟨ν n⟩ τῆς ἀνατροφῆς of the rearing (cf. Sept. 16 ff.).
Ἐντεῦθεν from there cf. Sept. 457;
Λοξίᾱι μεγασθενεῖ to Loxias of great strength like Ch. 259 Λοξίου μεγασθενής χρησμός the oracle of Loxias of great strength.
᾿Ιατρόμαντις healer-prophet is Apollo, like his son Apis Hik. 263, who cleansed the Argive land of monsters (separated ἰατρὸς ὢν καὶ μάντις being a healer and prophet from Ap. Ar. Plut. 11, Weckl.);

τερασκόπος (Ch. 551) he is the interpreter of the signs, and the appearance of these women is, and they themselves are, a τέρας (cf. Ch. 548 τέρας the dragon of the dream; Hik. 570). After the Pythia has departed, the doors of the temple open for the spectator, and the interior becomes visible to him, just as the Pythia described it; yet beside Orestes now stands also Apollo, and beside him Hermes. The machinery employed was surely the same as Ch. 973 (Ag. 1372), although the scholiast on the Choephori speaks of the ekkyklema, here of στραφέντα μηχανήματα (cf. Introduction p. 15), and certainly here too the picture displayed was an extremely effective one. G. Hermann, to be sure, placed the ekkyklema before v. 94, so that the Erinyes, as they became visible, would not draw all the attention of the audience to themselves; as long, however, as they sleep and rest, this is by no means the case. I also do not think (cf. below) that Orestes still sits in the background, but rather that Apollo has already led him past the Erinyes into the foreground, whereby these were to some extent concealed (cf. v. Wilamowitz, Translation p. 52). Then Orestes no longer needs to walk past them. According to Kirchhoff, the words of Orestes to Apollo, 85-87, must stand here first. As transmitted, one must presuppose that such a request of Orestes has already taken place; for otherwise Apollo could not begin as he does. Worse is that Orestes' words now sound as if the god had not yet promised any care at all, and again, in what he says further, he in no way refers to the request with a new promise, but rather the first verse: μὴ φόβος σε νικάτω φρένας emphasizes what he himself said last. So what Orestes says is now nothing but a useless and ineffective interruption. But if one transposes, the person of Orestes, already indicated to the spectators, properly introduces the person of Apollo, not yet indicated as present: ἄναξ Ἄπολλον, and one must presuppose that Apollo has made him stand up and led him to the entrance, so that he may now continue his journey, after the purpose of his coming, the purification, has been fulfilled. Naturally Orestes is afraid: he acknowledges that Apollo has performed what he promised and has purified him, but his further care is still necessary. Thus the device of transposition, as already at v. 20 and in the Choephori several times, is again required here, and the cause of the disorder must be, as Ch. 631 ff., the wandering of the eye from one paragraphos to another. The scholiast (see on 64) seems already to have had the wrong order. In Athens, in accounts, one distinguished between ἀδικίου and ἀμελίου (Hesychius); Orestes feels secure with the god with regard to the former, also according to what he himself has experienced; but the god must first prove his care. The words contain no reproach; but they also do not sound, as Weil says, modest. "Since the one thing is so easy for you, you can do something extra and learn the other as well." Orestes is ἱκέτης of the god; this gives him, in relation to the latter, a certain dignity, see v. 233 f. Μὴ ἀδικεῖν and μὴ ἀμελεῖν with the vowel combination frequent in μή (συνίζησις attributed in f h; in M corr. there is aphaeresis of the ἁ-; according to Dindorf crasis to μᾱ-), see Kühner-Blass I, 242. ᾿Επίστᾱι (also 581) beside ἐπίστασαι Prom. 374, 982, see ibid. II, 68, 4 (also Pindar both, Pyth. 3, 80, 8, 7). Φερέγγυος Sept. 396 (with inf.) and often in the same play.

Οὔτοι προδώσω: wie Ch. 269 οὔτοι προδώσει Λοξίου . . . χρησμός. Ἐγγὺς παρ. κτἑ. kann nicht sein cum praesens tum vero absens (Weil), sondern διὰ τέλους σοι φύλαξ ἐγγὺς π. gehört eng zusammen: tatsächlich werde ich dir immer behütend nahe sein, wenn auch weit entfernt; denn κλύει δὲ καὶ πρόσωθεν ὢν θεός (297). Also = ἐγγὺς παρεστήξω· καὶ πρόσω δ' (wie Ch. 879) ἀποστατῶν ἐγγὺς παρεστήξω (das 2. Partizip dem 1. untergeordnet), wenn nicht mit Blomfield πρόσω γ' zu schreiben ist.
Ἐχθροῖσι: jedem der dir etwas antun will; speziell diesen hier (67).

Πέπων = μαλθακός oder μείλιχος, Frg. 259 von Hektor ἀνὴρ δ᾽ ἐκεῖνος ἦν πεπαίτερος μόρων, nach dem homerischen ὦ πέπον; von einer Sache Ag. 1365. Eine falsche Variante war πρέπων (Schol.) = ὅμοιος (Hik. 301), was der Schol. auf das Schlafen der Erinyen deutet.

Die analog gebauten Verse 67, 68 scheinen nicht zu ändern: καὶ νῦν | ἁλούσας | τᾶσδε τὰς μάργους | ὁρᾶις | ὕπνωι | πεσοῦσαι | δ᾽ αἱ κατάπτυστοι | κόραι; denn es lässt sich auch leicht aus ὁρᾶις etwas wie ὁρῶνται ergänzen. 'Ὕπνωι ist nicht = εἰς ὕπνον, sondern ,,durch Schlaf dahingesunken", wie öfters πίπτω so absolut gebraucht wird (Sept. 794 u. s. w.). Vor Bothe wurde nach ὕπνωι interpungiert; aber δέ an 3. Stelle stand schon 19. 21.

Κατάπτυστος (Ch. 632) ist der erste der starken Ausdrücke des Abscheus, die der Lichtgott gegen die Höllengeister gebraucht. Das überlieferte γραῖαι παλαιαὶ παῖδες (Νυκτὸς π. π. Valckenaer) nimmt Weil gut in Schutz: παῖδες ist puellae, nicht filiae (wie Ag. 277. Prom. 865), und die Häufung κόραι παῖδες, γραῖαι παλαιαί ist ganz in Aischylos' Art, zumal da dies mit παῖδες in Contrast tritt (Schol.); auf die Abkunft käme es bei einer Vorstellung an, wie 416, oder bei einer Ehrung wie 1034 Νυκτὸς παῖδες ἄπαιδες. Αἷς οὐ μείγνυται κτἑ. nach Homer ζ 288 (von Kalypso) οὐδέ τις αὐτῆι μίσγεται οὔτε θεῶν οὔτε θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων, hier noch gesteigert durch οὐδὲ θήρ. Ιn γραῖαι παλαιαὶ παῖδες αἷς οὐ μείγνυται wiegt αἰ auffällig und gewiſs absichtlich vor.
71 f. sind besonders malerisch im Klange: κακῶν δ᾽ ἕκατι κἀγένοντ᾽ ἐπεὶ κακόν / σκότον, und mit vorwiegendem τ: σκότον νέμονται Τάρταρόν θ᾽ ὑπὸ χθονός.

Κακῶν of evils: they exist entirely for ruin (125); therefore they have no intercourse, and Tartarus is their dwelling-place, the opposite of bright Olympus. Tartarus is, as in Hesiod, the actual black hell, beneath Hades, Prom. 152 νέρθεν θ᾽ Ἅιδου τοῦ νεκροδέγμονος εἰς ἀπέραντον Τάρταρον beneath Hades, receiver of the dead, into boundless Tartarus, although one should not expect too precise a topography of the afterlife in Aeschylus (as, for example, in Plato, Gorg. 524 A, Phaid. 113 E, Rep. X, 616 A). Μισήματα objects of hatred like Sept. 186 σωφρόνων μισήματα objects of hatred to the temperate.
74 ff. φεύγε 74 ff. flee (present imperative) "flee further".

V. 75 καὶ and cannot be connected with τε and 77; therefore καὶ even is "even", but ἤπειρος continent, as little as elsewhere in Aeschylus (Prom. 735. 790. Pers. 718. 737), means "dry land" (χέρσος dry land 240) in contrast to water, but rather continent (Asia and Europe in those passages), thus: "indeed through a whole long-stretched continent." To this attaches ὑπέρ τε πόντον over the sea 77 ("and also") exactly as at 250 ὑπέρ τε πόντον κτέ over the sea, etc..

In V. 76 I write with G. Hermann ἀν up' αἰεὶ ever, for which he refers to Plat. Leg. VIII 832 c σὺν ἀεί τινι βίᾶι with ever some force; but then one must also carry through the similarity and write τινα πλανοστιβῆ χθόνα some wander-trodden land (for the resolution cf. Pers. 296 τίνα δὲ καὶ πενθήσομεν) whom then shall we mourn?. Ἀνά up with accusative is very much in Aeschylus's manner, e.g. Prom. 574 πλανᾶι τε νῆστιν ἀνὰ τὰν παραλίαν ψάμμαν and he wanders fasting along the shore sand. Thus γῆν πρὸ γῆς ἐλαύνεται land after land he is driven, through one land of the continent after another. Βεβῶντα walking (-όντα being) finally must be βεβῶτα having walked or βιβῶντα striding: the former means "standing firm", the latter indeed "going", but is not attested from the tragedians; since, however, besides Homer, Pindar (Ol. 14, 16) also has it, one must prefer it with G. Hermann.

Πόλεις cities "dwelling-places" of islands, like Eur. Ion 294 πόλις city Euboea, Ar. Εἰρ Eir. 251 of Sicily; the scholiast on Ar. traces this back to Homer, Ξ 230 Λῆμνον Lemnos . . πόλιν θείοιο Θόαντος the city of divine Thoas.
Περιρρύτας sea-girt like περικλύστα νᾶσος sea-washed island Pers. 596, νήσωι ἐν ἀμφιρύτηι on a sea-girt island Homer α a 50.

One expects rather προκάμῃς you should grow weary beforehand, like Eur. ῾Ηρακλ. μ. 119 μὴ πόδα προκάμητε do not weary your foot beforehand: but the sense is: do not become slack anywhere before the time (i.e., from the repeated occasions for it); but when you come to Athens, then etc. Paley correctly compares 88 μὴ φόβος σε νικάτω φρένας let not fear overcome your mind. Βουκολεῖσθαι to be tended as cattle like αἰπολεῖσθαι to be tended as goats 196, passive (wrongly περιέπων tending Schol.); the driving Erinyes are the βουκόλος herdsman, as in the case of Io the οἶστρος gadfly, Hik. 557, in the case of ships the storm wind, Ag. 657; the accusative as τοὺς the.. δρόμους γυμνάζεται he exercises his courses Prom. 591.
79 πτόλιν city also frequent in trimeters, like Sept. 6;
ποτί toward only here in trimeter.
80 ἵζου sit (imperative) exactly like ἵζεσθε sit (plural imperative) Hik. 224, rather "sit" than "sit down", which would be ἑζοῦ sit down (imperative).
Ἄγκαθεν λαβών taking in his arms = ἀγκὰς ἑλεῖν to take in one's arms Homer.

The παλαιὸν βρέτας ancient image is the one described by Pausanias I, 26, 6 as being in the temple of Polias on the acropolis, according to legend fallen from heaven. In 81 f. there again seems to be letter-painting, but through soft letters, aspirates (see Dionysius π p. συνθ synth. p. 85) and μ m: θελκτηρίους μύθους ἔχοντες μηχανὰς εὑρήσομεν having soothing words we shall find devices.
Ἐς τὸ πᾶν for the whole 83 here as at Ch. 684. Eum. 291. 670 (complete ἐς τὸ π for the p. χρόνου of time) etc. (differently above 52).

Δέμας body in periphrasis frequent in Sophocles and Euripides, in Aeschylus only here (Dindorf), unless one adduces passages like Prom. 1018 κρύψει δέμας τὸ σόν will hide your body. Sept. 522; the word itself Aeschylus also uses often.

Μέμνησο remember: that you must finally reach Athens; may you preserve this in all your fear. Not by the straight path, for from it the pursuers soon divert him, but by a thousand detours yet finally. Μὴ φόβος σε κτέ let not fear seize you. like Empedokles 23, 9 Diels μή σ᾽ ἀπάτη φρένα καινίτω let not deceit overcome your mind (= νικάτω let it prevail).
89 αὐτάδελφον αἷμα kindred blood like Sept. 718 (αὐτάδ kindred. Soph. Ant. 1);
αἷμα blood= γένος race, συγγένεια kinship since Homer (below 606. 608).
Κοινοῦ πατρός of a common father stands parallel to the adjective. –

90 ἐπώνυμος eponymous like Sept. 8 f. ὧν Ζεὺς ἀλεξητήριος ἐπώνυμος γένοιτο Καδμείων πόλει of whom Zeus the averter of evil may be named for the city of the Cadmeans, Ch. 190 etc. Ἑρμῆς πομπαῖος Hermes the guide, πομπός escort is preferably the chthonic one (Preller-Robert 407, 1), yet nothing stood in the way of turning the word differently.

V. 90 ποιμαίνων shepherding counterpart to βουκολούμενος tending 78. Difficulties have been made by the ending, but Hermann, Dindorf, Weil simply follow the transmitted text and the scholiast's explanation: τὸ τῶν ἱκετῶν the suppliants' (= ἐκνόμων of the lawless, exlex) σέβισμα καὶ δέημα reverence and entreaty (? this not fitting) οὐ μόνον τιμᾶι ὁ Ζεύς not only does Zeus honor, ἀλλὰ καὶ σέβει but also reveres, ὁρῶν αὐτὸ ὁρμώμενον προσηκούσηι seeing it setting out with fitting (?) τύχηι fortune.
Ἐκνόμως lawlessly Ag. 1473 (Triclinius for ἐνν enn.) indeed means as much as παρανόμως unlawfully, and other evidence for ἔκνομος lawless exlex is lacking; however the word is understandable, and

ἔκδημος abroad = ἀπόδημος away from home, and ἀπόπολις exiled from the city Ag. 1410 (Seidler for ἄπολις cityless), ἀπόπτολις banished from the city Soph. OR. 1000. OC. 208 the one who has departed from the state. Thus the awe and consideration that we grant to the outcast and to those who take refuge with us gods is something honored by Zeus himself (cf. his behavior toward Ixion at 717 f., and τὸν ἱκέταν σέβων honoring the suppliant the chorus against Apollo at 151; below on 233 f.), and with εὔπομπος τύχη favorable fortune for the journey Hermes now sets out as escort of Orestes. Apollo also departs, unclear to where; in the following scene he is certainly not present. Now there appears before the sleeping Erinyes, raised up by the ἀναπίεσμα stage machine for raising ghosts (Pollux 4, 132), the ghost of Clytemnestra, according to 116 ὄναρ dream, 155 ὀνειράτων of dreams the sensory embodiment of a dream that the sleepers are having; between dream and actual ghostly apparition it is mediated by the fact that in sleep the heart is clairvoyant, 104 f. Cf. in Homer the Ὄνειρος Dream (personified), who takes the form of Nestor, B 20 ff., and the dream vision of Penelope δ δ 795 ff., an εἴδωλον phantom in the form of her sister. Yet from Homer the appearance of the soul of Patroclus Ψ 65 ff. compares even more closely, where Achilles sleeps, while there is no talk of a dream, but only of the actual soul; what it says is very similar to the words of Clytemnestra here: εὕδεις you sleep, αὐτὰρ ἐμεῖο λελασμένος ἔπλευ Ἀχιλλεῦ κτἑ but you have forgotten me, Achilles, etc.. (see also on 98); B 23 the dream god likewise: εὕδεις you sleep, Ἀτρέος υἱέ son of Atreus; Clytemnestra's speech (94--116) is passionately wild; hence anacolutha as in the speech of the nurse Ch. 734 ff. - 94

εὕδοιτ᾽ ἂν you would sleep = imperative εὕδετε sleep, Ch. 105 λέγοις ἄν you might say; so 118 μύζοιτ᾽ ἄν you would moan; but the summons is ironic both times, as is shown in the address ὠή oh!. Cf. Eurip. Ion 907 ὠή, τὸν Λατοῦς αἰδῶ oh, the reverence due to Leto's son; Xen. Kyneg. 6, 19 ἦ κατεῖδες ὠὴ did you see, oh! (you there) τὰς κύνας the dogs;

95 ἀπητιμασμένη dishonored cf. ἀπητίμησεν he dishonored (better -μασσεν to dishonor Nauck) Homer N 113. It belonged to ἐγὼ I . . νεκροῖσιν to the dead V. 98 αἰσχρῶς ἀλῶμαι I wander in disgrace; but anacoluthically there is inserted what she has to endure in the way of reproaches because of her own deed, which is after all far from being as bad as that of Orestes against her. The picture of the underworld here corresponds to the usual ones, where all the shades are united; there is no hint that Clytemnestra has now been condemned by the judges of Hades and must suffer torment. V. 96 ὧν whom Aeschylus. μὲν ἔκτανον whom I killed (Tyrwhitt, Wakefield) is written instead of ὡς μ so that I. ἔττ still. because of the scholion: ὑπὲρ ὧν ἐφόνευσα Ἀγαμέμνονα ἀπώσασθε καὶ οἱ ἐμὲ φονεύσαντες οὐκ ἀτιμάζονται on whose account I killed Agamemnon, you reject me, and those who killed me are not dishonored, which scholion, however, is very imprecisely formulated and rather attaches itself to 99, where for κείνων ὕπο by them Weil has written κείνων ὕπερ on their behalf (see below). This seems commendable, but for that ὡς as 96 is now to be left as it is: cf. numerous passages with this ὡς as, Ag. 1465. 1505. Ch. 691. 988. 1011 etc. Also ὧν ἔκτανον ὄνειδος reproach of those I killed is by no means unambiguous.
Ἐκλείπεται is left out passive, is not omitted;
ἐν φθιτοῖσιν among the dead (Pers. 220. 523) takes up the ἐν νεκροῖσιν among the corpses again.

Ἀλῶμαι I wander: cast out from their company (Weckl.); cf. Homer Ψ 74 (Paley), where the soul of Patroclus says: ἀλλ᾿ αὔτως ἀλάλημαι ἀν᾿ εὐρυπυλὲς Ἄϊδος δῶ but I wander vainly through the wide-gated house of Hades. Δέ but after αἰσχρ disgrace. corresponds to the negation. Her wrath at this unequal treatment makes her repeat it once more, προυννέπω I proclaim (852) δ᾽ ὑμῖν ὅτι ὕπερ to you that on behalf of; for ὕπερ on behalf of is in any case to be adopted, with reference of κείνων of those to Agamemnon (= οὓς ἔκτανον whom I killed), opposite ὑπέρ μου on my behalf 101, while with ὕπο by the pronoun would have to refer to the φθιτοί the dead and κείνων ὕπο by them would be rather meaningless. In this assessment of Clytemnestra, her deed and her suffering, the general voice shows itself. Paley compares Plat. Phaid. 108B: τὴν ἀκάθαρτον the impure – ἢ φόνων ἀδίκων ἡμμένην or one who has laid hold of unjust murders (ψυχήν soul) – ταύτην μὲν ἅπας φεύγει τε καὶ ὑπεκτρέπεται this one everyone flees and avoids, καὶ οὔτε ξυνέμπορος οὔθ᾽ ἡγεμὼν ἐθέλει γίγνεσθαι and neither companion nor guide is willing to be· αὐτὴ δὲ πλανᾶται ἐν πάσηι ἐχομένη ἀπορίαι but she herself wanders in total perplexity.

Παθοῦσα having suffered: again anacoluthic, but this is the usual anacoluthon, see on Ch. 520. In the repetition of the thought, which is likewise (see on 98f.) expressed twice, there is a connection to the construction of 101.

Φιλτάτων of the dearest exactly like φιλτάτους the dearest Ch. 234, to the nearest. Μηνίεται he is angry 101 is very striking, first because of the middle voice, which is found nowhere, and then because of the ī, with which only Hom. B 769 ὄφρ᾽ Ἀχιλεὺς μήνιεν so that Achilles was angry can be compared, while otherwise ι i is short (also probably Eur. Hippol. 1146, at any rate Rhes. 494). I therefore write μηνίσεται he will be angry, since in the future the middle is far more common; at the same time the connection with 103 becomes better, in that the angry question contains a demand (as at 124).

The address to the chorus in the singular is so common that no offense should be taken; similar change at 118 μύζοιτε you (pl.) moan. 124 ὤιζεις you were crying, and then further in the singular; 180 χωρεῖτε go (pl.), 181 λαβοῦσα having taken, etc. The heart is τερασκόπος observer of portents also Ag. 977, and the φρήν mind (in the literal sense) adjacent. Hermann's change καρδίας ὅθεν from where the heart (where they come from) is completely wrong; it also conflicts with 592. The summons ὅρα κτἑ see etc.. is then justified by εὕδουσα γὰρ κτἑ for sleeping etc.., as Pindar Frg. 131 of the immortal part of man: εὕδει δὲ πρασσόντων μελέων but it sleeps while the limbs are active· ἀτὰρ εὑδόντεσσιν ἐν πολλοῖς ὀνείροις δείκνυσι τερπνῶν ἐφέρποισαν χαλεπῶν τε κρίσιν but to those sleeping in many dreams it shows the judgment of pleasant and grievous things creeping upon them, and the whole chapter περὶ τῆς καθ᾽ ὕπνον μαντικῆς about divination in sleep, especially also (Stanley) Aelian V. h. 3, 11 according to "Peripatetics": — — νύκτωρ δὲ διαλυθεῖσαν and at night, having been dissolved (τὴν ψυχὴν the soul) τῆς περὶ τοῦτο of the service concerning this (i.e. τὸ σῶμα the body) λειτουργίας καὶ σφαιρωθεῖσαν ἐν τῶι περὶ τὸν θώρακα τόπωι μαντικωτέραν γένεσθαι and having been made spherical in the region around the chest, it becomes more prophetic, ἐξ ὧν τὰ ἐνύπνια from which dreams. To ὄμμασιν λαμπρύνεται are brightened in the eyes Blaydes compares Ar. Plut. 636 ἐξωμμάτωται καὶ λελάμπρυνται κόρας it has been given eyes and the pupils have been brightened, from Sophocles' Phineus according to the schol.; see also Ch. 854 φρέν᾽ ὠμματωμένην mind furnished with eyes. But what is the point of the contrast at 105, which has no application to this situation, in which it is day? Moreover, βροτῶν of mortals is unsuitable for this, and if one writes ἡ τῆς φρενὸς μοῖρα οὐ προορᾶι ἐν ἡμέρᾱι the portion of the mind does not foresee in the day according to the scholion: φρενῶν of the mind, the repetition is disturbing, and it is always idle philosophizing.

With μοῖρα fate one can compare 476 αὗται δ᾽ ἔχουσι μοῖραν οὐκ εὐπέμπελον but these have a fate not easy to send away, i.e. their nature and kind given by fate; but with βροτῶν of mortals, it seems to me, one should think of Clytemnestra's own experience, since she foresaw nothing and let herself be caught, despite having thought so much about this case in advance and having tried to win over the Erinyes, 106 ff. And her spirit too had been clairvoyant in a dream, Ch. 32 ff. 523 ff.
Μέν on the one hand contrast 110 καὶ πάντα κτὲ and all things etc.., so again anacoluthic; πολλά δή many things indeed as at 144. Ch. 897.
Ἐλείξατε you licked, like thirsty dogs (Paley), cf. 131. Ch. 924. Χοάς τε and libations corresponding to καὶ δεῖπνα and meals, but this receives a new finite verb with ἔθυον they sacrificed.

Ἄοινοι wineless the scholiast explains: οἶνος γὰρ οὐ σπένδεται Ἐρινύσιν for wine is not poured to the Erinyes, and better still Soph. OC. 100. 469 ff. (only water and honey; 481 μηδὲ προσφέρειν μέθυ nor to offer wine); see also the scholia on this.
Μειλίγματα soothing offerings Ch. 15;

νηφάλια wineless offerings with the final syllables as a resolved arsis, like μαρτύρια παρῆν witnesses were present 797, Ch. 1 Ἑρμῆ χθόνιε πατρῶι᾿ κτἑ. Hermes of the underworld, ancestral, etc.. (other examples in Paley on V. 797).
108 νυκτίσεμνος night-revered is surely one word, like νυκτίπλαγκτος νυκτίφοιτος νυκτιφρούρητος night-wandering, night-roaming, night-watched.

Ἐσχάρα hearth can and will be a separate altar here (ἐσχάρα Φοίβου hearth of Phoebus Pers. 205; see also Eum. 806), which could easily be set up for the purpose; but the special thing is the hour (Schol. ἐν τῶι μεσονυκτίωι μόναις Ἐρινύσιν ἀπάρχονται at midnight they begin the offerings to the Erinyes alone).

Ὥραν hour (and ἀωρίαν untimely hour) in the time expression always thus in the accusative, Eurip. Bacch. 723 τὴν τεταγμένην ὥραν the appointed hour, Aristot. Πολ Pol.. ᾿Αθ Ath.. 30 end τὴν ὥραν τὴν προρρηθεῖσαν the hour that had been announced, Gramm. of New Testament Greek § 34, 8 p. 97² (= εἰς ὥραν at the hour, at the hour).

Λὰξ πατούμενα trampled underfoot: Cho. 642, καὶ ταῦτα and these things 112 as at 627.904? Prom. 949? (Kühner-Gerth I, 68 note, II, 247); according to ordinary usage ὀρούσας having rushed should follow.
Ἀρκύστατον net-setter Ag. 1375 (Pers. 99 M.). Soph. El. 1476; cf. ἀρκυ-στασία net-setting Xen. Kyneg. 6, 6.

Ἐγκατιλλώψας having cast a sidelong glance Schol. χλευάσας having mocked, ἐγγελάσας having laughed at; Hesych. ἐγκατιλλῶψαι ἐγκαταμυκτηρίσαι to cast a sidelong glance, to mock, from ἰλλός ἰλλώπτω squinting, to squint (ἰλλωπέω to squint), to make distorted eyes; also Frg. 225 Ddf. 226 N., where εὖ κατιλλώψας having cast a sidelong glance well is transmitted.

Ὡς as: is ambiguous: "as" and "while", "since", like Ch. 660 and often; the latter seems preferable. Τῆς ἐμῆς περὶ ψυχῆς of my life like Homer περὶ ψυχῆς θέον running for life (Χ 161), ὥστε περὶ ψυχῆς as for life (ι i 422), and Soph. El. 1492 with ἀγών contest, etc. (see Paley), everywhere "for life", which does not exactly fit here; also Kl. is a mere ψυχή life. But the sense is similarly strong.
Φρονήσατε take thought "understand, take to heart", cf. γιγνώσκω φρονέω I know, I think Hom. π 136 etc.
Ὄναρ dream see above p. 81; Κλυταιμνήστρα Clytemnestra with the false ν n is also in M. here. The name is meant to bring to consciousness.

Distichomythia on the part of Kl.; the chorus likewise symmetrically first twice μῦ mu, then twice ὤ oh, finally, what Hermann calls epodic, μῦ μῦ mu mu and after that λαβέ take etc. The interjections are indicated by παρεπιγραφή stage direction (Schol.); such a thing occurs (Weckl.) among the tragedians now only here, in Aristophanes more often. Μῦ μῦ Mu mu Arist. Ἱππ Hipp.. 10. Thesm. 231 (sound of pain; in the Th. follows τί μύζεις why do you moan?, cf. μύζουσιν they moan likewise Eum. 189).

119 is meaningless in the manuscripts and only apparently healed by Hermann's ἐμοί to me instead of ἐμοῖς to my; for then φίλοις friends refers to Orestes, and προσίκτορες suppliants (441) means protector, for which one cites Ζεὺς ἀφίκτωρ Zeus of suppliants Hik. 1. Correctly Weil φίλοι γάρ εἰσιν οὐκ ἐμοῖς προσεικότες for they are friends, not resembling my own (cf. εἰκώς resembling Ch. 561).

121 κατοικτίζει he pities (or -ῃ ēi) is not necessary, since οἰκτίζειν to pity and -εσθαι esthai occur side by side. The γ g’ after ἄγαν too much is to be adopted without hesitation from f g h (just as it is also to be retained at Ag. 1241); cf. Ag. 1254. Prom. 696 (πρώι γε early at least) etc. On the naming of the name see on 116.

ὤιγμός wailing, if 124 ὤιζεις you wailed is correct M; cf. ὤιμοι alas, which according to Reisig is the correct spelling for Soph. OC. 820; see on this Ellendt in the Lexicon Soph. p. 798, Dindorf Lex. Aesch. p. 239, Rabe, Rh. Mus. XLVII, 413 (ὤιμοι alas mostly the Laur. of A. and Soph., likewise Ven. A of the Iliad).

125 πέπρακται has been done is by no means covered by Eurip. Med. 1064 πάντως πέπρακται ταῦτα κοὐκ ἐκφεύξεται In any case these things have been done, and he will not escape; for there πέπρωται has been fated is a variant, which Bentley here demanded by conjecture; cf. Prom. 519 τί γὰρ πέπρωται Ζηνὶ πλὴν ἀεὶ κρατεῖν For what is fated for Zeus except to rule forever?; the corruption here was especially easy through πρᾶγμα deed; πέπρωται has been fated however (cf. 334 ff.) is both closer to the letter-forms and stronger than τέτακται has been ordained (Wakefield, προστεταγμένον ordained 208), cf. Schütz. On κακά evils cf. 71. –

ὕπνος πόνος τε sleep and toil cf. Homer ζ z 2 ὕπνωι καὶ καμάτωι ἀρημένος overcome by sleep and weariness; to be sure, this is not exactly coordinated, but the sleep is actually (even if Kl. does not know this) brought about by Apollo, and with it the exhaustion joins to the same end.
Συνωμόται fellow conspirators cf. Ag. 650, and on Ch. 74;

κύριοι masters in control of their power. Δράκαινα she-dragon ironic; ἐκκηραίνω I destroy utterly only here, but Hesych. ἐξεκήραινεν ἐξέφθειρε he destroyed utterly, he corrupted, and κηραίνουσι they destroy Hik. 999 (κήρ doom, death).

O. Müller introduces meter by placing φράζου take heed at the beginning and bringing λαβέ take seven times instead of four; differently Dindorf under the text: A λαβοῦ λαβοῦ take, take. B λαβοῦ λαβοῦ take, take. C φράζου λαβοῦ take heed, take. The shouts occur as in the hunt (as explained at line 131), to dogs or hunters among themselves ("pay attention").

Against the transmitted κλαγγαίνεις you cry out, even if it is attested only here, there is no well-founded objection to be raised; see G. Hermann (-άνεις you cry out Wakefield, for which a few other attestations exist; cf. ἀλιταίνω I sin, ὀσφραίνομαι I smell). The analogy of the construction with 133 seems to argue against the change: ὄναρ dream | διώκεις you pursue | θῆρα beast | κλαγγαίνεις you cry out | δ᾽ ἅπερ but just as — τί δρᾶις what are you doing? | ἀνίστω arise | μή σε lest you | νικάτω let it overcome | πόνος toil, and the same form is also found in 132, especially if one writes μερίμνας cares and ἐκλείπων leaving off: κύων dog | μερίμνας cares | οὔποτ᾽ never | ἐκλείπων leaving off | πόνου toil, with an echo of πόνου toil in πόνος toil 133. Ἐκλείπων leaving off (Blomfield) seems in fact to be better; in the case of ει ei — ι i the manuscript evidence is indifferent. On the matter (Paley) Arist. Ζώιων ἱστ History of Animals. 4, 10 p. 536b, 27: ἐνυπνιάζειν φαίνονται οὐ μόνον ἄνθρωποι not only humans appear to dream, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἵπποι καὶ κύνες καὶ βόες but also horses and dogs and cattle, ἔτι δὲ πρόβατα and further sheep — — · δηλοῦσι δ᾽ οἱ κύνες τῶι ὑλαγμῶι and dogs show it by barking, and (Schütz) Lucr. IV, 992: venantumque canes in molli saepe quiete iactant crura tamen subito, vocesque repente mittunt, et crebras redducunt naribus auras, ut vestigia si teneant inventa ferarum.

133 μή σε νικάτω πόνος let not toil overcome you here (cf. 88) "do not let weariness overcome you any further (as it has so far)"; then μηδ nor' ἀγνοήσηις you may fail to recognize of what has newly happened (πῆμα calamity the escape of Orestes), which is to be recognized.

135 ff. The first verses again parallel: ἄλγησον ἦπαρ grieve the liver | ἐνδίκοις ὀνείδεσιν with just reproaches | τοῖς σώφροσιν γὰρ for to the prudent | ἀντίκεντρα γίγνεται they become goads; likewise 137 f. σὺ δ᾽ αἱματηρὸν πνεῦμ but you, a bloody breath(α a) | ἐπουρίσασα τῶι having sent a fair wind upon him | ἀτμῶι κατισχναίνουσα wasting him away with your vapor | νηδύος πυρί with the fire of your belly, and 139 f. (pure iambs, mimetic) ἕπου follow | μάραινε waste away | δευτέροις with a second | διώγμασιν pursuit | ἔγειρ᾽ ἔγειρε rouse, rouse | καὶ σὺ τῆνδ᾽ and you this one | ἐγὼ δὲ σέ and I you. The explanation of 135 is given by V. 155 ff.; in agreement (also in τοῖς σώφροσιν to the prudent) is Demosth. Olynth. I, 17 καὶ πρόσεσθ᾽ ἡ ὕβρις καὶ ἔτ᾽ ἡ τῶν πραγμάτων αἰσχύνη and moreover insolence and the shame of the deeds, οὐδεμιᾶς ἐλάττων ζημία τοῖς γε σώφροσιν is a penalty no less than any other to the prudent; further cf. Plat. Leg. XI, 926 D ψόγος καὶ ὄνειδος κείσθω let blame and reproach be laid, πολλῶν χρημάτων νοῦν κεκτημένωι ζημία βαρυτέρα to one who has sense, a heavier penalty than much wealth.
On ἦπαρ liver cf. Ch. 272. Ag. 432 (below 158 λοβόν lobe; the ὀνείδη reproaches are those of the Furies;

ἀντίκεντρα goads (after 466) = ἀντὶ κέντρου instead of a goad, cf. ἀντίδουλος slave instead of Ch. 135. After the general statement, the return to these persons occurs with σὺ δέ but you (in which, therefore, there is not, as Paley thinks, a change of address to different Erinyes). —
ἐπουρίσασα having sent a fair wind with a certain irony, at the same time fitting the ambiguous πνεῦμα breath;
τῶι to the as at Sept. 385. 912. 1065, below 174 etc., see on 2. After the last words the ghost disappears again into the depths.

Three introductory trimeters by the chorus leader (1 and 3 pure iambs, in any case also recited at a rapid tempo); then three strophic pairs, in which there was undoubtedly solo delivery or divided delivery of the individual pieces; but how, is quite impossible to determine. G. Hermann distributed among 15 choreuts (including the 3 trimeters at the beginning), dividing Str. α a Ant. α a fivefold, among four each, Str. β b Ant. β b twofold among two each, Str. γ c Ant. γ c but undivided, giving one Erinys each. Rossbach, Kirchhoff, Wecklein distribute among half-choruses; with them too the splitting of Str. Ant. α a is fourfold, of Str. Ant. β b only single; Str. Ant. γ c remain units and are even given by Rossbach to the whole chorus. The scholiast notes only: κομματικῶς in a commatic manner (as a detached piece, not part of a period) ἕκαστον προενεκτέον each piece must be delivered separately · αἱ γὰρ διακοπαὶ for the interruptions (interruptions of the construction) πρόσφοροι τοῖς πάθεσιν appropriate to the emotions; so no division was transmitted to him either. One must imagine that the Erinyes, waking one after another, sprang up, looked around, ran back and forth, but finally forward, i.e. down from the ekkyklema into the orchestra, where it was possible to group themselves and perform regular movements; therefore for Str. Ant. a the division into half-choruses seems to me excluded, for β b (γ c) on the other hand permissible. According to the poet's fiction (179) they are nevertheless still inside the temple. That the excitement is strongest at first, then subsides somewhat, is natural. Of rhythms the dochmiacs dominate, to which, however, as elsewhere, recited trimeters are mixed, α a 2. 4, β b 1, γ c 1, with not many spondees, finally however (Ant. γ c) even with three. Cf. on these trimeters at Ch. 423 ff.; in the second parodos and in the strophe 778 ff. the same mixture occurs. The dochmiacs correspond exactly except at 157, 164, where one emends, and 143, 149. Besides: Str. α a 6~-~--~- - ~ -, cf. β b5 (ICICI-CIICI, but probably iambs with suppressed resolutions (Ch. 940); on the other hand resolved iambs β b, 6000 / U U U / ~ ~ ~ / ~-; dochmiac and iambic dipody (cf. at Ch. 68, p. 86) β b, 2 and in reversed position (CI, CIICI) γ c 4; dochmiac and κατὰ βακχεῖον according to a bacchius ۔۔۔۔۔۔۔γ c, 2 (cf. strophe endings like 793 Sept. 688. 701). Very unclear is Str. Ant. 2, 4: ὑπὸ φρένας under the diaphragm, ὑπὸ λοβόν under the lobe — περὶ πόδα around the foot, περὶ κάρα around the head, paeons without synapheia? catalectic trochaic dipodies likewise? Cf. 328 etc. Or iambic tripody? Then the anaphora would be somewhat blurred.

The first wakes the second and has her wake the third, and meanwhile herself wakes a fourth who is addressed (ἐγὼ δὲ σέ but I you); for that this should mean "as I you" is hardly credible. The first ἔγειρε awake can be understood as "awake"; for this must precede the waking of another; so Eurip. I. A. 624, namely σαυτόν yourself or σαυτήν yourself (feminine), cf. παῦε stop "stop". At εὕδεις you are sleeping a change of speaker is possible; Paley compares Homer B 23 (cf. above p. 81) εὕδεις you are sleeping, Ἀτρέος υἱέ son of Atreus; Ἀπολακτίζειν to kick away (Prom. 651) a strong word; from the singular there is a transition to the plural as in Ar. "Ὄρν Birds. 203 (Weckl.) ἀνεγείρας τὴν ἐμὴν ἀηδόνα καλοῦμεν αὐτούς having woken my nightingale we call them.
Φροίμιον prelude is the dream, as Ag. 1354 (φροιμιάζονται they prelude) is the death-cry and its cause;
ματᾶν to be vain (μάταιον εἶναι to be vain or γίγνεσθαι to become) also Prom. 57. Sept. 37.
Ἰοὺ ἰού Alas, alas: as Ch. 881. Ag. 1214;
πίπαξ pipax cf. πύππαξ puppax Plat. Euthyd. 303 A, from which ὑπερπυππάζειν to cry puppax Arist. 'Ἱππ Hipp.. 680 is derived. Yet this is an exclamation of astonishment;
πόπαξ popax here rather σχετλιαστικόν expressing indignation, as πόποι alas 146; accordingly πόπαξ popax Aldina Ddf.
— The πάθος suffering is the escape of the fugitive, who is really gone; the πολλὰ παθεῖν to suffer much, and indeed μάτην in vain, are the many vain toils of the pursuit.
Δυσαχής ill-sounding only here;

ἄφερτος unbearable (Ch. 442. 469, below 479, five times in Ag.) likewise only in A. and indeed in this trilogy (in prose ἀφόρητος unbearable). The hiatus after the interjection does not yet compel one to assume that the synaphea is interrupted before ἄφερτον κακόν unbearable evil and τοκεῦσιν πικρόν bitter to parents.

πέπτωκεν ἐξ ἀρκύων he has fallen out of the nets: as Ag. 1245 ἐκ δρόμου πεσών having fallen out of the race, got out; πέπτωκεν ἔξω τῶν κακῶν he has fallen out of the evils Arist. Βάτρ Frogs. 970 (before ἢν κακοῖς που περιπέσηι if he falls into evils). Then οἴχεταί θ he is gone' (Abresch) instead of δ d''; here the connection is too close for δέ de to be tolerated.

Ἰὼ παῖ Διός Alas, child of Zeus: agrees little with the strophe (◡ — ◡ — ◡ —) and has a striking syllaba anceps at the end of a first dochmius of the dimeter, as Soph. Ant. 1322 ἄγετέ μ᾿ ὅτι τάχος (τάχιστ' lead me as quickly as possible is emended) / ἄγετέ μ᾽ ἐκποδών lead me out of the way. Here one must let the transmitted text stand; also in the strophes 778ff. and 837ff. similar things occur.
Ἐπίκλοπος deceitful as Hom. (λ l 364 etc.);
πέληι you may be middle as 199. Ag. 255 etc. (more often active).

- 150 very similar to 731 ἐπεὶ καθιππάζηι με πρεσβύτιν νέος since you ride me down, an old woman, young as you are; also 778=808 θεοὶ νεώτεροι younger gods, παλαιοὺς νόμους καθιππάσασθε you have ridden down the old laws; the verb stands in its literal sense Hdt. 9, 14 ἡ ἵππος κατιππάσατο χώρην τὴν Μεγαρίδα the horse rode down the Megarian land (devastated).
- 151 σέβων revering cf. ἐκνόμων σέβας reverence for the lawless 92; this is precisely a piece of the new world order, Introduction p. 9.
Ἄθεος godless also at 540 (Pers. 808, cf. δύσθεος hated by the gods Ch. 46 etc.).

Τοκεῦσιν to parents i.e. of the mother, as at τῶν τεκομένων of those who gave birth Ch. 419; for such plurals cf. the examples from the tragedians in P. Menge, De poet. scaen. graecorum sermone (Göttingen 1905) 25 ff.;
πικρόν bitter hostile, like Ch. 234.

Μητραλοίας mother-beater (210) properly means one who strikes his mother (ἀλοᾶν to strike), and still has this milder meaning in Plato, Phaedo 114 A (afterwards there ὕβρισαν they committed outrage of the same wrongdoers).
Ὢν θεός being a god in contrast to ἄθεον godless (Schütz). Τί τῶνδε κτἑ What of these things, etc.. cf. (Weckl.) Ag. 211. Ch. 338.

In this strophe and the antistrophe there are numerous assonances, partly between strophe and antistrophe (μεσολαβεῖ seizes in the middle – φονολιβῆ dripping with blood, διφρηλάτου of the charioteer – δίκας justice, πάρεστι is present – πάρεστι is present, κρύος ἔχειν to have cold – ἄγος ἔχειν to have pollution), partly within a single verse: 155 ὄνειδος reproach – ὀνειράτων of dreams, 156 δίκαν διφρηλάτου justice of the charioteer, 160 δαΐου δαμίου of the hostile, of the public, 161 βαρύ περίβαρυ heavy, very heavy; but especially, with corresponding formation in strophe and antistrophe, yet without assonance between them, 159 ὑπὸ φρένας ὑπὸ λοβόν beneath the mind, beneath the lobe and 165 περὶ πόδα περὶ κάρα around the foot, around the head. Cf. W. Kühne, De vocum sonorumque in strophicis A. canticis aequabilitate (Halle 1905) p. 5 f. The beginning repeats (intentionally) Clytemnestra's words at 135 f., with a vigorous development of the image.
Μεσολαβής seizing in the middle only here (thus the blow is stronger),

λοβός lobe = ἧπαρ liver 135, therefore ὑπὸ λ beneath the l. = ὑφ᾽ ἦπαρ beneath the liver Ch. 272. But the last verses of the strophe add another image, that of the public torturer and scourger and his blows.
Κρύος cold like Sept. 834 (cf. κρυερός icy);

περίβαρυ very heavy only here (on the formation Lobeck, Phryn. 539; ὑπερβαρὴς exceedingly heavy Ag. 1175 M, ὑπερβαρὺς exceedingly heavy h). Instead of the unsuitable article, with Wakefield one should write τι something, as the verse from the Septem shows: κακόν τι καρδίαν με περιπίτνει κρύος some evil cold falls upon my heart, i.e. a shudder as (Schol.) under the blows of the executioner.

The contrast with the younger race of gods (already in the antistrophe α a) now emerges even more sharply. There is parallelism and variation: strophe α a and strophe β b are related, likewise the two antistrophes (Weil).

Κρατοῦντες ruling is to be connected with θρόνον throne, Hik. 254f. αἶαν κρατῶ I rule the land, Soph. OC. 1380 τοὺς σοὺς θρόνους κρατοῦσιν they hold your thrones, only that θρόνους thrones, for which a spondee stands in the strophe, is probably an explanation: θᾶκον seat Rauchenstein, θρᾶνον bench H. L. Ahrens, possible would also be φονολιβαῖς ἕδρας seats dripping with blood, as at Prom. 389 τῶι νέον θακοῦντι παγκρατεῖς ἕδρας for the newly enthroned, all-powerful seats.
Τὸ πᾶν the whole "in general", with Ch. 331;

δίκας πλέον more than justice = πέρᾶι δίκης beyond justice Prom. 30, which Heimsoeth also demands here, especially since Hesychius explains πέρᾶι beyond by πλέον more; yet πλέον more can be adverbial, Ch. 902 etc. The φονολιβὴς περὶ πόδα blood-dripping around the foot must have a broader sense than what the following verses, dealing with Apollo's deed, say: Zeus too received the murderer Ixion and defiled his own throne, cf. 717 ff. - V.

168 ἀρόμενον winning like ἄροισθε κῦδος win glory Sept. 316, "to win", to ἄρνυμαι I win and not to ἀείρω αἴρω to lift, Kühner-Blass II, 350; with it the epexegetic infinitive ἔχειν to have, Kühner-Gerth II, 576.
Βλοσυρός grim A. has only here, in the sense of "terrible", like Γοργὼ βλοσυρῶπις grim-eyed Gorgon Hom. Λ 36.

If ἐχρανατ᾿ he defiled i.e. ἐχράνατο he defiled is correct (against which there can be no objection, since the middle corresponds to the sense), then Apollo is no more addressed than in the antistrophe (ἐκλύσεται he will release 174), and now also μαντισωι prophetic in μάντις ὤν being a prophet (Schütz; cf. below ποτιτρόπαιος ὤν being a suppliant 177) is to be emended; for with μαντικὸν prophetic (Stanley, like μαντικῶν μυχῶν prophetic recesses 180) one misses the subject far too much.

Αὐτόσσυτον self-impelled = αὐτοκέλευστον self-commanded Hesychius quotes from Sophocles' Σκύριαι Skyriai; this verb here preserves the doubling of the initial consonant, as in Homer; but in ἐπισύμενος rushing upon below 786 it has been lost.
Αὐτόκλητος self-summoned "of one's own accord" Soph. Tr. 392, Plato Ep. VII 391 B; the scholiast explains αὐτὸς αὐτὸν καλέσας having called himself, thus actively.

Βρότεος mortal instead of -ειος eios in the tragedians only here (Ddf.), but in Pindar always, as also (according to Didymus) in Aristotle's Paean V. 1. In 173 one writes (except Weil and already Schütz in the commentary) very wrongly Μοίρας Fates, as if it could be a matter of destroying the Fates; A. explains himself in V. 727, where the Erinyes say to Apollo: σύ τοι παλαιὰς διανομὰς καταφθίσας you, having destroyed the ancient allotments, thus the ancient separation between gods and men, by rescuing a man from death. Cf. on μοῖρα fate Eum. 105. 476 (plural, because referring to gods and men); on παλαιγενεῖς ancient-born Sept. 742 παλαιγενῆ παρβασίαν ancient transgression; on this reproach Introduction p. 9.

Antistr. γ g, 174–178. "He makes himself hateful to me, and yet he will not achieve his purpose"; thus as Zeus says to Hera, Homer A 562: πρῆξαι δ᾽ ἔμπης οὔτι δυνήσεαι but you will not be able to accomplish it, ἀλλ᾽ ἀπὸ θυμοῦ μᾶλλον ἐμοὶ ἔσεαι but you will be more hateful to my heart.
Ἐκλύσεται he will release middle like Prom. 235 (λύσασθε release Ch. 804).
Ἐλευθεροῦται he is freed is the prophetic present, Kühner-Gerth I, 138.
Ποτιτρόπαιος suppliant is here (as at 237) the guilt-laden one;

μιάστωρ pollution, defilement (or the polluted one), however, is the blood-avenger, while Ch. 944 is the criminal; so it fluctuates as with ἀλάστωρ avenging spirit, curse, ἀλειτήριος sinner, guilty one; also προστρόπαιος suppliant, one who turns to the gods for purification itself, as Antiphon Tetr. 3 α a 4 δεινοὺς ἀλειτηρίους ἕξομεν τοὺς τῶν ἀποθανόντων προστροπαίους we shall have terrible avenging spirits, the suppliant ghosts of the dead says.

Πάσεται he will acquire = κτήσεται he will possess as πεπαμένος having acquired = κεκτημένος having possessed Ch. 191. Ag. 835. The corrupt ἐκείνου of that one Weil has excellently emended to εἶσιν οὗ he will go where: EK(E)INOΥ = ΕΙ EICΙΝΟΥ INOU, with the well-known interchange of K and IC, from which the fine corruption СКΥΦΟΣ YPHOS instead of CICYΦOC (Ephorus in Athen. XI, 500 BC) arose. Ἔστιν οὗ there is where or ἔστιν ὃν there is whom already G. Hermann, with a mysterious hint, which however also lies in εἶσιν οὗ he will go where. For the sense cf. 273 f. First episode, 179-(243) 306. While Orestes flees, Apollo appears again and drives the Erinyes out of his temple. A first conflict between the contending deities is presented here, as it were a prelude to the one in Athens; thus partly to prepare for this, partly to gloss over the long time of Orestes' flight, which could not be done here by a choral ode. The young god behaves hostilely and imperiously (like a young lord, as has been said), the old goddesses with dignity and restraint, as also later; from 213 onward, however, Apollo's tone is equally dignified.

Apollo 179—197. V. 181. The metaphor ὄφις serpent is explained by the scholiast from the poison, more correctly from the bite; πτερόεντες winged are the arrows already in Homer (cf. A. Myrmid. Frg. 129, Paley); the myth also knows winged serpents, Hdt. 2, 75 f.

Ἀργηστής bright, white (ἀφρός foam Sept. 60) is probably to be understood as brightly shining, μέλας ἀφρός black foam 183 forms a contrast, precisely that between the god of light and the powers of darkness. The figurative language is at the same time suited to the threat.
182 χρυσήλατος gold-wrought is the bowstring (θῶμιγξ cord, string, also Pers. 461 so), as everything belonging to the gods is golden or silver (ἀργυρότοξος with silver bow of Apollo Homer A 37).
183 f. The Erinyes are bloodsuckers also according to their own song 264 ff.

The punishing goddesses take pleasure in punishment, and the more barbaric and savage it is, the more so. A. had seen and heard enough of Persian penal justice. Immediately for καρανιστῆρες δίκαι decapitating justices one compares Pers. 371; gouging out of eyes occurs Xenoph. Anab. 1, 9, 13 alongside other mutilations; castration of boys Hdt. 6, 9; stoning and a kind of crucifixion carried out on a Persian and his son by Xanthippos there 9, 120, ἀνασκολοπισμός impalement (189 f.) on 3000 Babylonians after the capture of Babylon 3, 159. In contrast to this, the Athenian, for whom only κώνειον hemlock and ἀποτυμπανισμός cudgeling to death were the punishments, had to feel humane and civilized. Δίκαι καρανιστῆρες Justices that behead like τύχη σωτήρ saving fortune Ag. 664; the word like ὀφθαλμωρύχος eye-gouger only here, but καρανιστής μόρος beheading doom in Rhesos 817 (κάρανα δαίξας having torn off heads Ch. 396). Both adjectives belong to δίκαι justices; standing by itself is σφαγαί slaughterings slaughterings, such as indeed also occurred in Hellas; then σπέρματος τ᾿ ἀποφθοραὶ destructions of seed (manuscript) παίδων of children (boys) clearly for the thing; then κακοῦ τε and of evil (as one must now write with Dindorf) χλοῦνις ἠδ᾽ ἀκρωνία castration and mutilation.
