These too must be substantives, connected by ἠδέ and, cf. 414 (also often elsewhere in A., though not in dialogue); the scholiast, who explains with ἡ ἀκμαία the prime (χλοῦνις castration) ἀποκοπή cutting off (ἀκρωνία mutilation), strangely ignores the conjunction. From Herodian, however, in the scholia σύστημα καὶ ἄθροισμα collection and gathering is cited as an explanation for ἀκρωνία mutilation; better Bk. An. 372, 2 ἀκρωνία τὰ ἀθροίσματα mutilations, the gatherings, καὶ ἡ ἀκρότης and the extremity, καὶ ἡ ἀκμή and the prime, καὶ τὸ ἐπίλεκτον σύστημα and the chosen body (Et. M. 53, 41; Hesych., s. Ddf. Lex.). These meanings fit excellently and can be easily attached (except for ἄθροισμα gathering) to ἄκρος topmost, even if the manner of formation with -ωνία onia remains unclear. If, however, one accents -ωνιά onia, then κρινωνιά lily-bed, ῥοδωνιά rose-bed are analogous, and the meaning is "where the extreme of evils is together." We are less well informed about χλοῦνις castration, only that this word is grouped with βοῦνις hill (Hik. 117 Ἀπίαν βοῦνιν) Apian hill) (Lenz Herod. 95, 9). The scholiast mixes in the Homeric (I 539) χλούνης σῦς ἄγριος wild boar, which posed a great problem; after all, χλοῦνις castration does look like a feminine to χλούνης wild boar (πολίτης citizen – πολῖτις citizeness), and were it not for the ἠδέ and, one could understand it with the scholia as an adjective (= ἀκμαία prime) to ἀκρωνιά mutilation.

Χλούνης Chlounes (a wild boar epithet, perhaps 'couching in the green') itself was found in A. in the Ἠδωνοί Edonians (Frg. 63): μακροσκελὴς μέν long-legged indeed. ἆρα μὴ χλούνης τις ἦν was he not some chlounes? (Herm. for ἦ or), where it apparently meant a locust. See Ddf. Lex. (after GHermann Opusc. V, 10 ff.). All this helps not in the least, and as transmitted, one must, with Dindorf, explain χλοῦνις chlounis as viridis seges and connect it (at least in A.'s sense) with χλόη young green shoot, verdure. Hermann, following Fritzsche, wrote παίδων τε χλοῦνις and a chlounis of children, ἠδ᾽ ἀκρωνία κακοῦ and the topmost branch of evil; thus χλοῦνις chlounis becomes castration, as χλούνης chlounes in Homer was often explained as ἐκτομίας castrated; hence also the scholia at our passage.
In V. 189, λευσμόν stoning contains either -ός os or -οί oi;
μύζουσιν they moan, mutter already at 118.

Οἰκτισμός lamentation according to Ammonios p. 102 (Ddf. Lex.) is ὁ λόγος τοῦ οἰκτιζομένου the speech of the one lamenting, whereas οἶκτος pity, compassion is pity; apparently in A. οἶκτος pity, compassion also has the former meaning, 515; but see there.

190 ὑπὸ ῥάχιν under the ridge in scriptio continua is ὑπορράχιν under the ridge, and so the manuscripts; cf. Prom. 1023 μέγᾱ ῥάκος (μέγαρράκος) a great rag; more numerous examples, however, are for shortness of the preceding vowel, as 232 τὸν ἱκέτην τὲ ῥύσομαι I will protect the suppliant (τὲ and would be against Porson's law); Prom. 992 πρὸς ταῦτᾱ ῥιπτέσθω μὲν, in response to this let it be thrown,, Sept. 105. Ch. 315. Eum. 789 τί ῥέξεις (-ας, -ω) what will you do?Prom. 713 χρίμπτουσᾰ ῥαχίαισιν touching the rocky shores. In Old Comedy, as is well known, lengthening is the rule, in tragedy not.
190 ff. Ἑορτῆς 190 ff. of the feast: with bitter irony; with ἀπόπτυστοι spat upon, abominable cf. above κατάπτυστοι spat upon, abominable 68;

στέργηθρον love-charm, affection Ch. 241. ῾Υφηγεῖσθαι to lead the way, guide "to guide" = to teach, show; Weckl. compares Catull. 64, 193: Eumenides quibus anguino redimita capillo frons expirantes praeportat pectoris iras. — 194.

χρηστηρίοις oracular hardly a substantive = oracle-site, but adjectival as at 241. Ag. 1270; an oracle-saying is called χρηστήριον oracle Ag. 964. Sept. 748, oracle-sacrifice Hik. 450. The substantive, then, is to be sought in πλησίοισ nearby(ι i), for which nothing lies closer than κληισίοισι enclosures i.e. κλεισίοισι enclosures (Wieseler). Τὸ κλεισίον τὸ Λυκομιδῶν the enclosure of the Lycomidae Pausan. 4, 1, 7; on the spelling and derivation (from κλήιω to shut, enclose) see Meisterhans-Schwyzer p. 51. Τρίβεσθαι ἐν to rub in like ἐντρίβεσθαι to rub in, προστρίβεσθαι to rub against, inflict upon; the latter stands in Antiphon 4β b 8 ὑμῖν τὸ μήνιμα τῶν ἀλειτηρίων προστρίψομαι I will inflict upon you the wrath of the sinners, the former now only in later authors, ἐντρίβεσθαί τινι κακόν to rub evil into someone Lukian D. D. 20, 2.
Μύσος defilement, pollution pollution as at 445.
196 f. To Orestes Apollo has given Hermes as escort ("shepherd", see ποιμαίνων shepherding 91); the Erinyes he sends away without escort.
In αἰπολούμεναι being shepherded like goats (cf. βουκολούμενος being herded like cattle 78) lies the comparison with a herd of goats;
εὐφιλής loving, friendly here active (passive Ag. 34).
Stichomythia 198–212, introduced with 3 verses of the chorus (cf. on Ch. 106 ff.), as also at 415, 585.
Ἀντάκουσον hear in turn namely ὀνείδη reproaches: after you have reviled us, let our reproaches also be spoken to you.
Πέληι to Peleus as at 149.
201 ff. πῶς δὴ 201 ff. how then: as at 431, 601, Ag. 543.

Τοσοῦτον so much for -το the Dindorf, since the general usage of the scenic poets prefers the forms with ν n, Ddf. Lex. 361 b. “So much you may say as far as I am concerned,” so repugnant is the conversation with you to me.
202 ὥστε so that pleonastic as after δεχοίμην I would receive 228, Kühner-Gerth II, 8 ff.

– 203 πέμψαι ποινάς to send punishments, of Orestes, could be defended with Pers. 624 πέμπε χοάς send libations i.e. pour out, or τόξευμ᾽ ἔπεμψεν he sent an arrow Hik. 1005; however, Heath's conjecture πέμψας having sent fits better also with regard to the aorist, which thus connects to ἔχρησα I proclaimed.

Τί μήν what then? Ag. 672 n. Linwood (τί μή what not? transmitted, as also here f), Soph. Ai. 668, “what else then?” The expression, especially where it stands as an answer equivalent to an affirmation, seems to be Doric and to have become familiar to Aeschylus, as later to Plato in Sicily; Sophocles, however, shows many points of contact with the Oresteia precisely in the Ajax. Dittenberger Hermes XVI, 334 (who, regarding the passages in Aeschylus and Sophocles, doubts whether τί μήν what then? or τί μή what not? is correct).

Ὑπέστης you promised (you undertook) δέκτωρ receiver as τοῦ λόγου διάδοχον ὑποστάντα having undertaken as successor of the word Plat. Phileb. 19 A (Paley). Apollo confirms this by indicating the manner more precisely (through the imperfect).

— 206 Schol. ἠθικεύσαντο τὰς διωκτρίας προπομποὺς εἰποῦσαι they spoke in character, calling the pursuers escorts, i.e. they speak in (grim) humor, Rutherford Scholia Aristophanica III 130 n. 11, who compares ἐν ἤθει in character in Diogen. VI, 10.
Δῆτα then indeed as often in questions (Ch. 218. 916 etc.) connecting to what precedes, “for,” “then.”
— 207 πρόσφορος suitable Ch. 714; for πρόσφορον suitable Stanley's πρόσφοροι suitable is naturally equally possible.
208 προστεταγμένον assigned “assigned by fate,” as the following verse shows; not “commanded.”

Τιμὴ honor as τιμάς honors 419 (γέρας privilege 394), and the explanation there similar to here: βροτοκτονοῦντας ἐκ δόμων ἐλαύνομεν we drive those who kill mortals from their homes, only that here it is specialized with allusion to Orestes.

— 211 τί γάρ why indeed? see Ddf. Lex. 65 ab; on the genitive with it see Kühner-Gerth I, 363 (Plat. Πολιτεία 470 A τί δὲ γῆς τμήσεως what of the cutting of the earth?, namely πέρι about, and do you think, do you say).

Νοσφίζειν to deprive = to kill Ch. 438. 491. In the answer it becomes clear that the Erinyes restrict their vengeance to the murder of blood relatives (even more clearly at V. 605); thus for them the murder of a husband is also not a φόνος αὐθέντης murder by one's own hand, i.e. αὐτοκτόνος self-murderer (Sept. 681. 734), αὐτοφόνος self-slaughterer (Sept. 850. Ag. 1091), or no αὐτουργία self-deed (336), i.e. committed with one's own hand on one's own blood (θανάτοις αὐθένταισιν by self-inflicted deaths Ag. 1573). This "on one's own blood" is habitually supplied with these words, since this is the worst case of killing with one's own hand; of course αὐθέντης perpetrator (αὐτοέντης self-perpetrator Soph. OR. 107, where, however, the narrower concept shines through), αὐτόχειρ with one's own hand also retain the general meaning.

Apollo 213–224. The corrupt ἠρκέσω I have helped at 213 seems to be curable from the parallel passage 845 f.: ἀπὸ γάρ με τιμᾶν δαναιᾶν θεῶν δυσπάλαμοι παρ᾽ οὐδὲν ἦραν δόλοι For from my honors, the hard-to-fight wiles of the gods have taken me away as nothing. If this means: they have taken me up and carried me off like nothing, away from my honors, then παρ beside' οὐδὲν ἦρκε nothing helped can also be this: has removed like nothing. Αἴρειν to lift so Eur. El. 942 αἴρει κακά lifts up evils, Plat. Πολιτεία ΙΧ Republic IX, 578 E ἄρας ἄνδρα ἐκ τῆς πόλεως θείη εἰς ἐρημίαν having lifted a man out of the city, he would put him into a desert.

On παρ᾽ οὐδέν as nothing cf. Ag. 229, παρ᾿ οὐδέν ἐστι is as nothingSoph. OT. 983. Only a subject is still needed, and this could be restored with ἦρκ᾽ ἔπος the word has helped, in parallelism with 215 τῶιδ᾽ ἀπέρριπται λόγωι has been cast away by this argument; on ἔπος word cf. e.g. 510. 532. 586.

Ἤρκατε you have helped would say the same thing, but Apollo here always speaks in the singular; the same meaning is given by the ἦρκας ὣς you have helped as finally preferred by me, with postponed ὡς as as often, and similar to Soph. Antig. 34 ἄγειν οὐχ ὡς παρ᾿ οὐδέν to lead not as if for nothing; this change is also especially easy.

Κάρτ᾿ ἀτιμα very dishonored now no longer needs to be separated off, but fits into the same construction. — "Ἥρα Hera is τελεία fulfiller (also Frg. 329) precisely in relation to marriage, as Zeus τέλειος fulfiller: Preller-Robert Mythologie 164; Schol. Ar. Thesm. 973 (Paley): Ἥρα τελεία καὶ Ζεὺς τέλειος ἐτιμῶντο ἐν τοῖς γάμοις Hera the fulfiller and Zeus the fulfiller were honored in marriages, ὡς πρυτάνεις ὄντες τῶν γάμων as being the presidents of marriages. τέλος δὲ ὁ γάμος marriage is the fulfillment (on 835).
Πιστώματα pledges cf. Ch. 977.
V. 216 τὰ φίλτατα the dearest things family and children.

217 μόρσιμος destined cf. 961 the Μοῖραι Fates as marriage goddesses. Apollo thus, as the representative of a higher morality, equates the bond of marriage in beautiful and dignified words with the bonds of blood, and one only wonders that later in the legal dispute at Athens this argument is not brought forward again; cf. below.
Τοῖσιν to them= τούτοις to these as at 2 etc.;
τὸ μή the not = ὥστε μή so as not, Ddf. Lex. 236a; for γενέσθαι to become the most obvious correction is τίνεσθαι to pay.
᾿Εποπτεύειν to watch over in this play only here and at 224, frequently in the Choephori.
᾿Ανδρηλατεῖν to banish a man Ag. 1419. 1586 (also Soph. OT. 100. Plat. Πολιτεία Republic VIII 565 E), from ἀνδρηλάτης banisher of a man (Sept. 637) expeller of a man.
V. 222 τὰ μὲν the one is not correct, since only Orestes' fall is spoken of; on the other hand, 223 τὰ δὲ the other agrees with τοῖσιν to them.
῾Ησυχαιτέρᾶι more quietly comparative of ἡσυχῆι quietly slow, calm, Eur. Hipp. 444 ἡσυχῆι μετέρχεται quietly pursues opposite of κάρτα very;
πράσσουσαν pursuing here is not so much "to pursue" as "to avenge", cf. 624 τὸν πατρὸς φόνον πράξαντα the one who avenged his father's murder. Orestes repeats the argument at 604.
225—234. Stichomythia and conclusion, the latter in twice three verses, just as at 198 three verses stood at the beginning.

226 δ᾽ οὖν then different from Ch. 571: the words of the other speaker create the contrast, cf. (Sidgwick) Prom. 935 ὁ δ᾽ οὖν ποιείτω let him do it then ("that is all the same to me, as far as I am concerned"; thus likewise breaking off the discussion). Paley also compares Eurip. 'Ηρ Her.. μ m. 726. Rhes. 868.

227 f.: the Erinyes see a curtailment of their office in it, if all their trouble is to be in vain. Curtail? Apollo replies; I want nothing of your honors. Then they: of course you are great, despite me, under this new regime.

Ἔμπας nevertheless Ch. 389. Prom. 48. 187. Hik. 101. The πὰρ beside transmitted only here in Aeschylus is corrected by Porson to παρὰ beside; it is hard to say whether the aversion to the tribrach was greater or that to the non-Attic form, since ποτί toward (79) is not avoided even in the trimeter. In such matters one does best to follow the tradition. Cf. on 243. Also at 231 apocope seems to be transmitted, if in κἀκκυνηγέτης and the huntress (M) Wellauer's κακκυνηγέτις huntress is concealed; however, this would not be acceptable for several reasons, and κἀκκυνηγετῶ and I hunt (Erfurdt) is likely correct. Ἐκκυνηγετεῖν to hunt out also has Eurip. Ion 1422 (Lykophr. 1025), κατακυνηγετεῖν to hunt down no one; also in its formation κατακυνηγέτις huntress down is somewhat strange. Furthermore, the parallelism with 232 demands a second verb here, and it would be wrong to think that this must be a future because μέτειμι I pursue is one. Rather, this is a real present like πρόσειμι I approach 242 (see below), and denotes what is already happening; for with this verse (consisting of pure iambs) the chorus hurries away. At the end of the verse, however, where writing was often smaller and less clear, something like a misreading of -τω the as THC is possible. Μέτειμι τόνδε δίκας I pursue this man with justice like Eurip. Bakch. 516f. ἄποινα μέτεισι Διόνυσός σε Dionysus will exact recompense from you (similarly there 345, Paley).

the power of the moral law appears as also ruling over the gods, so that the curse of the suppliant ἱκέτης suppliant, betrayed by the god, can harm him; cf. Introduction p. 9. In the transmitted text εἰ προδῶ if I betray nothing needs to be changed except that in the general statement the third person is restored; for τὶς someone can be supplied, see Kühner-Gerth Synt. I, 35 g (Homer N 287 etc.). Εἰ if with subjunctive is found securely also at Hik. 91 (Ddf. Lex. 102 a); Porson writes at our passage ἢν if, Weil ὃς who (προδῶι I betray). Σφε them as singular also Sept. 469. 615 etc., below 610; likewise σφιν them singular Pers. 759 and Soph. OC. 1490 (not otherwise); namely ἑ him and οἱ to him are not used by the tragedians (οἱ to him only Ag. 1147 and Soph. Εl. 196), but νιν him, which they do use, conversely also occurs in the plural (Hik. 729. Prom. 55). With these words Apollo also departs, and now the scenery, while the stage is empty, is changed into the temple of the Polias at Athens (Introduction p. 15). After this not long pause, which is meant to represent a very long time (cf. on 179 ff., p. 90), Orestes appears and seats himself at the image of Athena, i.e. he enters the temple, whose interior was consequently visible. Opened doors suffice for this no more than before; so the previous ekkyklema simply remains, and only the wooden image, which the Athenians knew and from which they immediately inferred the changed scene, takes the place of the tripod. The manipulation could be carried out from below without the stagehands becoming visible.

Orestes, as had also been foretold to him by Apollo at 75 ff., pursued by the Erinyes, has not taken the direct land route from Delphi to Athens, but has made an enormous, indefinitely long detour by land and sea, and has finally found the goal appointed for him.
Ἀθάνα Athena also at 443, 892, always with ἄνασσα queen, evidently for the sake of the verse; otherwise Ἀθηναία Athenaia (old Attic), on 288. Correspondingly the other tragedians.

Ἀλάστωρ avenger is otherwise the avenging spirit, Pers. 354. Ag. 1501 etc.), with the same fluctuation of meaning which we observed in προστρόπαιος suppliant and ἀλειτήριος sinner (on 176); properly ὁ ἄλαστα δρῶν one who does unforgettable deeds (Et. M. p. 57, 29), one who cannot remain hidden and cannot forget, cf. ἄλαστος unforgettable in Homer. Here, however, a sharp distinction is drawn between ἀλ al. and προστρόπαιος suppliant, since Orestes declares himself to be the former, but not the latter; so has Aeschylus not rather thought of ἀλάομαι ἀλαίνω I wander, so that to him

ἀλάστωρ avenger (alastor) = ἀλήτης wanderer is, as Or. Ch. 1042 designates? One has (see Wecklein Einl. p. 19 note, after Blomfield on Pers. 990) derived ἀλάστωρ avenger (alastor) also directly from ἀλαίνω to wander, as belongs to μιαίνω μιάστωρ to stain, polluter, so that it actually denotes the wandering spirit. Another difficulty is the inflection, because in Cramer's Anecd. Oxon. I, 62 it is noted: παρῆκται δ᾽ ἡ εὐθεῖα the nominative is derived (namely ἀλάστορος of alastor) παρὰ τὴν ἀλάστορος γενικήν from the genitive alastoros. Αἰσχύλος Ἰξίονι Aeschylus in Ixion "πρευμενὴς ἀλάστορος kindly alastor" (Frg. 90 Ddf.), and Bk. Anecd. 382, 10 ἀλάστορον ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀλάστορα alastoron instead of alastora, ἀπὸ τῆς εὐθείας ὁ ἀλάστορος from the nominative ho alastoros. Αἰσχύλος Aeschylus "μέγαν ἀλάστορον great alastor". Nauck has brilliantly conjectured that in the original version μέγαν ἀλάστορον great alastor was quoted from the Ixion, 〈δέχου δὲ but receive〉 πρευμενῶς ἀλάστορον kindly alastor but from this passage of the Eumenides, according to which one would have to write thus.
Πρευμενῶς kindly and -ής -es below 922 and often A., also Euripides Hek. 538 etc.; actually Ionic from πρηυμενής kindly.
Ἀφοίβαντος unpolluted only here and Frg. 147; φοιβαίνω to purify has Hesychios.

It seems necessary, in order to bring order into the sentences, with Prien and Paley to write ἀμβλὺς blunt and προστετριμμένος rubbed against; the accusatives are easily explained by assimilation, and other changes are not so easy. (Πρὸς to | ἄλλοισιν οἴκοις other houses, with close binding of the verses, is, as Sidgwick notes, less surprising in Sophocles than in A.; see however on V. 800.) The thought is illustrated by V. 276 ff. and again 445 ff.: the expiation of the fresh blood has long been accomplished, before which act the polluted person was allowed to approach no one and speak to no one, so as not to infect them; now there is no longer any danger, especially since he has since been together with so many, without harm to them (284f.). This therefore must ἀμβλύς blunt mean (θέσφατ᾽ οὐκ ἀμβλύνεται the oracles are not blunted Sept. 844, do not lose their force);

προστετριμμένον rubbed against rubbed on, rubbed off against, so that the edge is, as it were, blunted. Explaining (as so often in this play one passage explains another by repetition) 451f. πάλαι πρὸς ἄλλοις ταῦτ᾽ ἀφιερώμεθα οἴκοισι καὶ βατοῖσι καὶ ῥυτοῖς πόροις long ago we consecrated these things to other houses and passable and flowing paths, therefore πόροις paths = πορεύμασιν journeys here, and this = way (by land as by water). P. Menge (de poetarum scaenicorum gr. dictione p. 66) indeed wants to understand "vehicle" = ship, comparing Eurip. I. A. 299f.; but the land routes then fall out, on which Or. had also met with many, and there follows the epexegesis ὅμοια similar (adverb., as often Hdt. Thukyd.) χέρσον καὶ θάλασσαν ἐκπερῶν crossing land and sea. As in the epexegesis the present ἐκπερῶν crossing is also correct;
σώιζων saving but at 241, since this clause grounds the πρόσειμι I approach.

242 πρόσειμι I approach present tense (on 231), as often in Homer (B 87 etc.), ἴασι they go in the proverb at Plat. Symp. 174B; also at Plat. Phaid. 100B ἔρχομαι ἐπιχειρῶν σοι ἐπιδείξασθαι καὶ εἶμι πάλιν ἐπ᾿ ἐκεῖνα τὰ πολυθρύλητα καὶ ἄρχομαι ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων I come attempting to show you and I go back again to those much-talked-about things and I begin from them, here however relating to ἔρχομαι I come as aorist to imperfect and expressing completion, from which the usual transition to future meaning is close at hand. The period after θεά goddess is to be removed (Weil, van Herwerden), so that βρέτας τὸ σόν your image becomes object of φυλάσσων guarding (cf. 439 βρέτας τόδε ἦσαι φυλάσσων to sit guarding this image); τὸ σὸν θεά your, goddess is easily supplied also for δῶμα house.

Αὐτοῦ there, without moving from the spot; ἀμμενῶ I will remain Dindorf writes, since many examples of the apocope are found with ἀνά up, ἀμπίπτω ἀνδαίω ἀντέλλω ἄγκρισις I fall upon, I kindle, I rise, examination (364) etc., Ddf. Lex. 26 a, also in dialogue. Whether -μένω I remain (M) or -μενῶ I will remain (Stanley), is hardly to be decided.

The second parodos of the chorus takes place, as is natural in the hot pursuit, σποράδην scattered; see in the Life of Aeschylus: φασὶν ἐν τῆι ἐπιδείξει τῶν Εὐμενίδων σποράδην εἰσαγαγόντα τὸν χορὸν τοσοῦτον ἐκπλῆξαι τὸν δῆμον they say that in the performance of the Eumenides, having brought in the chorus scattered, he so astounded the people, ὡς τὰ μὲν νήπια ἐκψύξαι that the infants fainted, τὰ δὲ ἔμβρυα ἐξαμβλωθῆναι and the embryos were aborted, which, if that is to be relied upon, is to be referred first of all to the first parodos; yet the second is no different. So it was delivered by individuals or groups, as in the first parodos, which is also clearly shown; but the distribution is entirely unclear. Hermann gave the first 10 trimeters to the chorus leader; from 254 on he distinguishes 7 pieces, which he assigns to individual Erinyes. Strophic formation cannot occur here at all; moreover, the rhythms and meters (trimeters) are similar to those in the first parodos. Trimeters 261. 264.

269. 272. 273; dochmiacs 255f. (? pure or mixed with cretics, see below). 258f. 263. 265. 270f.? 274 f.; dochmiacs with cretics (which did not occur there in this way) 266. 268; finally iambs similar to those there: ◡ — ◡ —, ◡ — (257, see below) 262. Thus nothing falls outside the rest by being set only once, cf. on Ch. 806 ff. p. 167. The introductory trimeters 244–253 are distinguished by particularly mimetic structure and sound. Corresponding to the rapid course, 244 is already only iambs, without the first foot; but then 246f.: τετραυματισμένον wounded (three feet not interrupted by any word-end, thus especially fluid) γὰρ ὡς κύων νεβρὸν for as a dog [tracks] a fawn | πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σταλαγμὸν ἐκματεύομεν we track by blood and dripping, without spondee, after Dindorf, in accordance with Aeschylus's usage (on Ch. 219), restored -ματεύομεν we track for -μαστ track. The striking hendiadys αἷμα καὶ σταλαγμὸν blood and dripping instead of αἵματος στ of blood can likewise be explained by this: -τος στα dripping- would be a harsh and flow-impeding clash of consonants, cf. what Dionysius π p. συνθ composition. p. 155ff. expounds about hard and soft composition with regard to the meeting of sounds. Then 248f., corresponding to the content, form the full contrast: πολλοῖς δὲ μόχθοις ἀνδροκμῆσι φυσιᾶι with many man-slaying toils he pants | σπλάγχνον entrails· χθονὸς γὰρ πᾶς πεποίμανται τόπος for every place of the earth is pastured. One may not, because of Porson's law, want to write -κμῆσιν slaying (otherwise there would be spondees in all odd positions), but the consonants pile up as much as is at all possible in Greek: σπλάγχνον χθονὸς γὰρ entrails of the earth for contains 13 for only 5 vowels. But over the sea it went unhindered: ὑπέρ τε πόντον ἀπτέροις ποτήμασιν over the sea with wingless flights (Dindorf instead of πωτ flight., since ποτᾶσθαι to fly is the tragedians' form); also again οὐδὲν ὑστέρα νεώς in no way behind a ship.

244 εἶὲν well then (asper over the 2nd syllable in M) Ch. 657. 719, otherwise not in Aeschylus. Suitable for the arrivals, who now stop for a moment and look around. They go by the scent of blood; but one need not dwell with the scholiast on the fact that Orestes' hands are still dripping with his mother's blood, which is supposedly utterly impossible. Also σταλαγμόν dripping 247 arises from the image of the fawn. Ἄφθεγκτος μηνυτήρ voiceless informer of blood is a similar oxymoron to ἄναυδος σαφὴς ἔτυμος ἄγγελος speechless clear true messenger Sept. 82 of dust; cf. Wecklein on Ag. 82. Πρὸς toward 247 "according to, after", like Ag. 332 πρὸς οὐδὲν ἐν μέρει τεκμήριον toward no proof in turn.

V. 248 ἀνδροκμῆσι man-slaying cf. 956. Ch. 889. Hik. 679, either "who can also kill men" or "who want to kill the man (Orestes)"; when the scholiast explains μεγαλοκμῆσι greatly-slaying, he seems to regard ἀνδρο man-- as a similar intensification as ἱππο horse-- or βου ox-- (ἱππόκρημνος horse-steep, βουγάϊος ox-proud). Πεποίμανται has been shepherded "is roamed through, searched", cf. 196f. and especially 78, where of Or. it is said τόνδε βουκολούμενος πόνον tending this toil. Ἀπτέροις ποτήμασιν with wingless flights again oxymoron.

252 καταπτακών having crouched down· καταπτήξας having cowered Hesych. according to Lobeck's emendation for -πλακών having struck -πλήξας having struck. In προσγελᾶι smiles upon the horror of the Erinyes emerges again (likewise several times in what follows): they feast on it. To ὀσμή smell the metaphor does not fit; but here the harshness is not inappropriate.

254 ff. The first sung pieces are clearly distinguished: ὅρα see.. ατίτας avenger and ὅδ᾽ this one.. χερῶν of hands. Ὅρα ὅρα μάλ᾽ αὖ See, see again like Ch. 654 ὦ παῖ παῖ μάλ᾽ αὖθις O child, child, again (cf. there 876, and see on Ch. 869 ff.). Further on in M. there stood first probably λευσσετετον παντα you both look at everything (πάντᾶι everywhere correction), which is λεῦσσέ τε τὸν πάντᾶι look at the one everywhere; since the demonstrative τὸν the is so frequent, there is nothing to object to here, and the μὴ not is to be left with the following verse, from which Hermann removed it to fill out the dochmius: λεῦσσέ τε πάντα μὴ look at everything, lest. So Sophocles OC. 117 ff.: ὅρα see.. λεύσατ᾿ αὐτόν look at him (λεῦσσέ νιν look at him Herm.), προσδέρκου look upon, προσπεύθου πανταχῆι inquire everywhere (Weil). Φύγδα in flight (only here) cf. κρύβδα secretly Ch. 177, κύβδα with head bent down, μίγδα mingled etc. "Whether he has perhaps secretly escaped us". Ἀτίτας avenger the debtor who does not want to pay, a substantive, to which ματροφόνος mother-slayer is an attribute. So Weil; otherwise Ag. 72. 7* Epiparodos.

258 ff. Verse 258 has been turned into a bad trimeter: ὅδ᾽ αὖτέ γ᾽ οὖν ἀλκὰν ἔχων περὶ βρέτει this man again, at any rate, having strength around the image (cf. below, 266); Hermann deleted the inappropriate οὖν then. But one must write ὁ δ᾽ but he, since αὖτε again in Aeschylus is hardly found otherwise than with d' before it, 49 (οὐδ not'). Ch. 415 (at 410 I have, with Wilamowitz, written δαὖτε but again = δὴ αὖτε then again). 980 etc. For χερῶν of hands, χρεῶν of debts (Scaliger, Wakefield) is correct, if above ἀτίτας unavenged is correctly explained. That the scholiast does not unconditionally testify for χρεῶν of debts (ἀνθ᾽ ὧν ἡμῖν χρεωστεῖ πρόσφυξ θέλει γενέσθαι τῆς θεοῦ in return for which he owes us, the suppliant wishes to become the goddess's), Hermann notes, in that, if χρεωστεῖ he owes refers to χρεῶν of debts, ὑπόδικος liable to justice is passed over, and this word is explained by Hesychius with ὑπεύθυνος accountable, χρεώστης debtor, ἔνοχος δίκης liable to judgment. 261-263. The words refuse to fit into a construction, since αἷμα blood is subject and τὸ διερὸν the wet also is; furthermore χαμαί to the ground and πέδοι on the ground are the same. Schol.: πᾶν διερὸν all wet (i.e. ὑγρόν moist, with which the ancients explain) ἐκκεχυμένον εἰς τὴν γῆν δυσαγκόμιστον poured out upon the earth, hard to gather up· τοιοῦτον οὖν καὶ τὸ αἷμα such then is the blood. So period (Hermann) after χαμαί to the ground (and new speaker?), so that χαμαί to the ground is the entire predicate, = ἐν τῆι γῆι in the earth or ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἐστι is upon the earth. The cry of woe παπαῖ alas! is of course directed at the doer; to δυσαγκ hard to gather up. Wecklein compares τίς ἂν πάλιν ἀγκαλέσαιτο who could call it back again Ag. 1020; χύμενον poured like Ch. 401; on πέδωι πέδοι on the ground, on the ground see on Ch. 48. (Wecklein takes τὸ the as relative, which in itself would be permissible, but makes δυσαγκόμιστον hard to gather up the predicate, so that χαμαί to the ground becomes part of the relative clause; that is an impossible position, and the combination τὸ διερόν the wet would have to be understood as article and substantivized adjective.) 264-268. Πελανόν libation cake libation like Ch. 92. Βοσκὰν φεροίμαν may I carry off as food (-ην of which) πώματος δυσπότου of a drink hard to drink (manuscripts) looks like a begun trimeter (on 258), which would have become complete with τοῦ δυσπότου of the hard-to-drink; but the Doric forms point to lyric rhythm, which one obtains by φεροίμαν βοσκὰν may I carry off as food (Wellauer): dochmius with cretic dimeter as at 268 cretic dimeter with dochmius. For the expression cf. Sept. 244: τούτωι γὰρ Ἄρης βόσκεται for on this Ares feeds, φόνωι βροτῶν in the murder of mortals. After 266 one can (Hermann) let the speaker(s) change. On 267 cf. 305 καὶ ζῶν με δαίσεις and you will feast on me while living, 302 ἀναίματον bloodless (3) βόσκημα fodder; already alive he becomes instead of a διερὸς βροτός wet mortal dry like the dead, who ἀλίβαντες dry corpses, and so finally enters the underworld. Ἀντίποιν᾽ ὡς as requital very good Schütz for ἀντιποίνους of requitals (ἀντίποινα πράξειν to exact requital Pers. 476); ματροφόνου of a matricide for -ous already Casaubon.

Ὄψηι you will see, when he has come to Hades. The sinners against the three most important commandments are named; cf. 545 ff. parents and guests, and Hik. 701 ff. ξένοι strangers – θεοί gods – τὸ γὰρ τεκόντων σέβας τρίτον τόδ᾽ ἐν θεσμίοις Δίκας γέγραπται μεγιστοτίμου for the reverence of parents is written third in the ordinances of Justice, most highly honored. So too Polygnotus in the Delphic Lesche, in his painting of the underworld, depicted the punishment of a πατραλοίας father-beater and of a ἱερόσυλος temple-robber, Paus. X, 28, 4 f. According to the tradition, 270f. is formed from dochmius, paeon, dochmius; it is very possible or probable that it was three dochmii as in 274f.; but one can restore these in many ways. (Τιν᾿ οὐκ εὐσεβῶν someone not acting piously Herm., τιν᾿ ἀσεβοῦντες ἢ τοκῆας those who act impiously toward parents Weil.) Ἀσεβεῖν τινα to act impiously toward someone Dial.-Inschr. 705 = I. Gr. Meg. et Boeot. 2418 (Thebes) τὼς ἀσεβίοντας τὸ ἱαρόν those who act impiously toward the sanctuary; see also Ddf. in the Thesaurus (Plut. Mor. 291 C). In 272 the change of τῆς δίκης ἐπάξια worthy of justice to τὴν δίκην ἐπαξίαν the worthy justice (τὴν ἐπ the upon. δίκην justice Blaydes) seems to me indispensable. Prom. 70 κυροῦντα τόνδε τῶν ἐπαξίων confirming this man of the worthy things, Ch. 95 δόσιν τῶν κακῶν ἐπαξίαν a gift worthy of the evils; so the crime would have to stand in the genitive, as also Demosth. 19, 8 δίκην ἀξίαν τῶν ἀδικημάτων λάβετε take justice worthy of the wrongdoings.
To separate or not?

Εὔθυνος Euthynus as Pers. 827 Ζεύς τοι κολαστὴς τῶν ὑπερκόπων ἄγαν φρονημάτων ἔπεστιν Zeus is indeed the punisher of overly arrogant thoughts, εὔθυνος βαρύς a heavy corrector. Δελτογράφωι φρενί with tablet-writing mind image from the γραμματεῖον writing tablet as Prom. 789 ἣν ἐγγράφου σὺ μνήμοσιν δέλτοις φρενῶν which you write in the memory-tablets of your mind. Hik. 179 τἄμ᾽ ἔπη δελτουμένας my words being written on tablets; also Soph. Frg. 535 Ddf.: θὲς δ᾽ ἐν φρενὸς δέλτοισι τοὺς ἐμοὺς λόγους place my words in the tablets of your mind (Weckl.). To this (Jacobs in Schütz) Eurip. Melanippe 508 N.: δοκεῖτε πηδᾶν τἀδικήματ᾽ εἰς θεοὺς πτεροῖσι you think that wrongdoings leap to the gods on wings, κἄπειτ᾽ ἐν Διὸς δέλτου πτυχαῖς γράφειν τιν᾿ αὐτά and then someone writes them in the folds of Zeus's tablet, Ζῆνα δ᾽ εἰσορῶντά νιν βροτοῖς δικάζειν and Zeus, seeing him, judges mortals; –
Ἐπωπᾶν to watch over also 971. Ch. 693, = ἐφορᾶν to oversee, ἐποπτεύειν to watch over.

First he prefaces his invocation of Athena (287 ff.) with the statement that, as one already purified, he has the right to do so. He has already said something similar at 237 ff., when he sat down at the image, and when Athena questions him, he repeats it for the third time at 448 ff. At our passage it is directed against 258 ff., where the Erinyes denied him any legal decision and responsibility.

the transmitted reading πολλοὺς καθαρμούς many purifications cannot be retained and is not supported by the second scholion either: ἐγὼ διδαχθεὶς σὺν κακῶι τῶι ἐμαυτοῦ I, having been taught by my own misfortune, καὶ οἷον διδασκάλοις χρησάμενος ταῖς ἐμαῖς συμφοραῖς and having used my own misfortunes as teachers, ἐπίσταμαι καὶ σιγᾶν καὶ λαλεῖν ὅπου δεῖ I know both to be silent and to speak where it is necessary, ἑκατέρου καιρὸν γινώσκων knowing the right moment for each. Accordingly van Herwerden πολλοῖσι καιρούς for many the right moments, since the latter word, instead of καθαρμούς purifications, probably belonged to the explained reading. Hardly, however, πολλοῖσι for many, cf. κακῶι τῶι ἐμαυτοῦ by my own misfortune, ταῖς ἐμαῖς συμφοραῖς my own misfortunes, but rather ἄλλους τε καιροὺς καὶ λέγειν ὅπου δίκη κτέ other right moments too, and to speak where justice demands, etc.., cf. 726 ἄλλως τε πάντως χώτε δεόμενος τύχοι otherwise in every way, and whenever he happened to be in need, and especially 667 τἄλλα τε the other things . . τεύξω I will accomplish . . καὶ τόνδ᾽ ἔπεμψα and I sent this man. Or πολλῶν τε καιρόν the right moment for many things (καιρόν the right moment Weckl. would prefer), cf. τῶνδε καιρόν the right moment for these things Sept. 65, ψευδῶν καιρόν the right moment for falsehoods Frg. 287, since καιροί right moments is not found in A. (πολλῶν of many things namely ἄλλων of other things), or also ἄλλων τε καιρόν the right moment for other things. On λέγειν κτἑ to speak, etc.. cf. Ch. 582 σιγᾶν θ᾽ ὅπου δεῖ καὶ λέγειν τὰ καίρια to be silent where it is necessary and to speak what is timely. — On the matter see what is adduced in the scholia, and below on 451.

Βρίζειν to be heavy, to slumber: Ag. 275. Ch. 897; cf. Ag. 346 ἐγρηγορὸς τὸ πῆμα τῶν ὀλωλότων γένοιτ᾽ ἄν the pain of the dead would be awake. Μαραίνεσθαι χερός to be quenched from the hand "offhand", without exact parallels; compare, for example, λίθον κεφαλᾶς βαλεῖν to throw a stone from the head Pind. Ol. 1, 58 "from the head", Kühner-Gerth I, 394.

Ἔκπλυτος washed out, effaced as in Plat. Νόμοι ΙΧ Laws IX, 872 E οὐδὲ ἔκπλυτον ἐθέλειν γίγνεσθαι τὸ μιανθέν the polluted thing is not willing to become washed out (scil. αἷμα blood, of parricide), πρὶν φόνον φόνωι ὅμοιον ὁμοίωι ἡ δράσασα ψυχὴ τείσηι before the soul that has done the deed pays murder with like murder. Here, however, the μητροκτόνον μίασμα the pollution of a mother's murder has been washed out (Ch. 967) by καθαρμοὶ χοιροκτόνοι purifications by the slaughter of pigs (cf. on 449 ff.); similarly Frg. 340, which will be from a tragedy about Ixion [Weckl.]). So cheaply? Does A. believe in it? He does not even let Orestes believe in it very much; for the latter appeals besides to the long time that has passed and to his many dealings with other people, here indeed as proof that he brings no pollution and therefore no longer has any, yet at V. 238 ff. and 451 f. as to something that likewise rubs off the stain, just as an actual bloodstain is gradually rubbed off. The Erinyes do not care about any of this in the slightest. But ritually Orestes is pure, i.e., he can speak and associate with anyone, which he was not allowed to do before the purification.

it would become long if I wanted to enumerate from the beginning with whom I have been together without infecting him. Since Musgrave, line 286 has been deleted, not as not originating from the poet, but as added from elsewhere for explanation. If, however, one writes καθαίρει he purifies and not (manuscript) καθαιρεῖ he destroys, then it is by no means foreign to the context, cf. above (Paley). Prom. 981 ἐκδιδάσκει πάνθ᾽ ὁ γηράσκων χρόνος time as it grows old teaches all things, Sept. 682 οὐκ ἔστι γῆρας τοῦδε τοῦ μιάσματος there is no old age for this pollution. Γηράσκων ὁμοῦ growing old together like ἅμα γηράσκων at the same time growing old (βρίζων ἅμα slumbering at the same time Ch. 897).
Εὐφήμως with auspicious words: without defilement.
Ἀθηναία Athenaia also at 299, 614; Ἀθάνα Athana (on 235) likewise three times, and besides Sept. 487.

Ἀθηναία Athenaia is also found in the inscriptions of this period (alongside Ἀθηνάα Athenaa), Meisterhans-Schwyzer 31, 157. — 289 f.: cf. 762 ff. the fulfillment of this promise (see also 671 ff. Apollo). The suppliant seeks to draw the god into his interest, see on Ch. 255 ff.
Ἐς τὸ πᾶν to the whole on 83;
δικαίως justly as at 891 (γαμόρωι εἶναι to be a landowner) δικαίως ἐς τὸ πᾶν τιμωμένηι justly honored in every way.

292 ff. The general form of invocation of a god is that of the various places where he may reside, where he enjoys worship; thus the more numerous and the more distant the places, the greater his power. So already Glaucus in Homer Π 514: κλῦθι ἄναξ hear me, lord, ὅς που Λυκίης ἐν πίονι δήμωι ἔσσ᾽ ἢ ἐνὶ Τροίηι who somewhere in the rich land of Lycia is, or in Troy· δύνασαι δὲ σὺ παντόσ᾽ ἀκούειν ἀνέρι κηδομένωι but you are able to hear everywhere, for a man in distress. Orestes now names two peculiarly chosen places: the Tritonian lake in Libya and the Phlegraean fields in Pallene. The lake had become known to the Greeks through the Cyrenaeans, which is why Pindar also mentions it in Pythian IV, 20; the neighboring Libyans, Αὐσέες Ausees according to Herodot IV, 180, worshipped a warlike goddess, whom the Hellenes immediately identified with their Athena and knew how to reconcile the Libyan mythology, according to which she was a daughter of Poseidon and Τριτωνὶς λίμνη Lake Tritonis, with their own; Athena had given herself to Zeus out of anger she had felt toward her father. Herodotus does not speak at all of a river Τρίτων Triton; according to others, such as Pausan. 9, 33, 7, this was the name of the outflow of the lake situated near the coast. But also in Hellas there were several rivers of that name, and everywhere the legend of the birth of Athena was attached to them, in accordance with the ancient epithet Τριτογένεια Tritogeneia (Homer Δ 515 etc.), which undoubtedly means the one born from the water (Ἀμφιτρίτη Amphitrite, Τρίτων Triton), Preller-Robert Myth. 186 f. Since, however, the opinions of scholars differed about the origin of the name (Schol. Δ 515 ὅτι γενηθεῖσαν ἔτρεσαν αὐτὴν οἱ θεοί that when she was born the gods feared her), the scholiast here remarks: ὅτι διὰ τοῦτο οἴεται αὐτὴν Τριτογένειαν that for this reason he thinks her Tritogeneia. Whether and how Aeschylus combined this conception with that of the birth from the head of Zeus (see line 736) remains unclear.

292 χώρας ἐν τόποις Λιβυστικοῖς in the regions of the Libyan land (M) Wecklein compares with ποῖον γαίας πέδον what plain of earth Sept. 304, χθονός τηλουρὸν πέδον a far-off plain of land Prom. 1; however, χώρα land is never the earth, as at this passage γαῖα earth and χθών ground, but rather the individual land, and for the emphatic fronting the idle "of the land" fits poorly; so Λιβυστικῆς Libyan (Auratus) is preferable, despite passages like 327 ματρῶιον ἅγνισμα κύριον φόνου a maternal purification, authoritative for bloodshed.
Ἐν τόποις in the regions also 703 (Πέλοπος ἐν τ in Pelops' ....). 858 etc.
Χεῦμα stream Hik. 1020 χ ch. Ἐρασίνου of Erasinus, and other passages;
πόρος crossing river at Ch. 72 (366);

γενέθλιος of one's birth connected with birth, cf. 7. Impossible to be correct is 294 ὀρθὸν ἢ κατηρεφῆ πόδα upright or roofed-over foot; for of the covering of the feet by the garment (when sitting or however) κατηρεφής roofed over is entirely unsuitable, since it means "roofing over" or "roofed over", from ἐρέφω to roof (ὄροφος roof), cf. also Arist. Σφῆκ Wasps. 1294 of the tortoises: ὡς εὖ κατηρέψασθε how well you have roofed over . . κεράμωι τὸ νῶτον your back with tiles. (Also νυκτηρεφής roofed by night Ag. 460, which Weil recalls, is quite well understood from this sense.) So whoever is in the open air, as Athena must be when she φίλοις ἀρήγει to aid friends, is οὐ κατηρεφής not roofed over, and so it seems μὴ not should be written instead of ἢ or. Ὀρθὸν πόδα upright foot as Pindar Ol. 13, 72 ἀνὰ δ᾽ ἔπαλτ᾽ ὀρθῶι ποδί and he leapt up with upright foot, cf. the same Frg. 167 of Caeneus σχίσαις ὀρθῶι ποδὶ γᾶν splitting the earth with upright foot. — To seek here an allusion to the battles of the Athenians in Egypt is, because of the spatial distance between Egypt and Libya, entirely inadmissible.

On the plains of Phlegra, the scene of the Gigantomachy, see Preller-Robert Myth. 75 (ἐν πεδίωι Φλέγρας in the plain of Phlegra Pind. N. 1, 75, Φλέγρᾶι Phlegra Eurip. Ion 988, Φλεγραῖον εἰς πεδίον Ἡρ to the Phlegraean plain, Hera. μ m. 1194, τὸ Φλέγρας πεδίον the plain of Phlegra Ar. Ὄρν Birds. 824). Hdt. 7, 123 τὴν νῦν Παλλήνην the present Pallene, πρότερον δὲ Φλέγρην καλευμένην but formerly called Phlegra; naturally this localization of the Gigantomachy comes from the same poets for whom Olympus was the mountain of the gods. On this scene of their battles (against Enceladus Eur. Ion 209) the goddess gladly dwells.
297 κλύει . . θεός a god hears is, as the scholiast correctly notes, a parenthetical clause; one may supply τις someone as subject, cf. on 234.
Λυτήριος Deliverer is of two endings like 646. Hik. 1073; in general those in -τήριος of deliverance, Kühner-Blass I, 536 (σωτήριος savior etc.).

Οὔτις no one: (M first, f g h) is stronger than οὔτοι not indeed (M corrected), and cf. ἤ τις Ἀπόλλων or some Apollo Ag. 55, ποῖος Κιθαιρών what Cithaeron? Soph. OT 421 (and on this Bruhn), μήτηρ οὔτις no mother below 736.
Παρημελημένον neglected cf. Sept. 702 παρημελήμεθα we have been neglected;
301 cf. 423 ὅπου τὸ χαίρειν μηδαμοῦ νομίζεται where rejoicing is nowhere customary of hell. Nowhere in your spirit shall joy find a place, any more than in hell.
302 ἀναίματον bloodless after 264 ff.;

βόσκημα food, pasture recalls 266 φεροίμαν βοσκὰν πώματος δυσπότου may I be carried as food of a bitter drink, and cf. Hik. 620 of the μίασμα pollution: ἀμηχάνου helpless (Stanley for -ανον anon) βόσκημα πημονῆς πέλειν to be food of misery. Weil's punctuation is: ἀναίματον bloodless, βόσκημα δαιμόνων food of the gods, σκιάν shadow, so that ἀναίματον bloodless and σκιάν shadow belong together and are separated by the explanation of ἀναίματον bloodless.

Βόσκημα δαιμόνων food of the gods will thus be correct, without indication of which δαίμονες gods they are, since the context points to the Erinyes themselves; so 22 f. Νύμφας Nymphs, ἔνθα Κωρυκὶς πέτρα where the Corycian rock . . δαιμόνων ἀναστροφαί haunts of the gods, and 801 μηδ᾽ ἀκαρπίαν τεύξητ᾽ ἀφεῖσαι δαιμόνων σταλάγματα nor may you cause barrenness by sending drops of the gods. But the trailing σκιάν shadow is unpleasant and also stems only from Heath, while σκιά shadow is transmitted (also Schol.). This now can be σκιᾶι in shadow, and the dative can belong to βόσκημα food, like ἵπποισι νίκα victory with horses in Pindar and other such things (Kühner-Gerth I, 428); cf. ἰυγμοῖσι βόσκεται feeds on wailings Ch. 26, βόσκεται φόνωι feeds on blood Sept. 244. And if now ἀναιμάτωι bloodless is also written, the connection of these words is clear, and it refers to the fact that even in Hades the Erinyes will not leave the criminal in peace: θανὼν δ᾽ οὐκ ἄγαν ἐλεύθερος and when dead he is not very free 340.

303 ff. Also in what follows the tradition cannot be got through well. If one writes (Paley, Weil now): οὐδ᾽ not even (so also Schol.) ἀντιφωνεῖς you answer, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποπτύεις λόγους but you spit out words, ἐμοὶ τραφείς τε καὶ καθιερωμένος reared and consecrated for me; καὶ ζῶν με δαίσεις κτἑ and living you will feast on me etc.., that gives no good connection, and the sense: "what? you do not even say anything to this, but despise our words?" is little clearly expressed, since λόγους words would rather have to refer to ἀντιφωνεῖς you answer and mean "your words". Thus very good and very easy Weil earlier: σὺ δ᾽ ἀντιφωνεῖς but you answer; (which refers to Orestes' just heard speech); then can follow: ἀλλ᾿ ἀποπτύσηι but you will spit out (-σει sei) λόγους words, ἐμοὶ for me . . καθιερωμένος consecrated, καὶ ζῶν με δαίσεις κτἑ and living you will feast on me etc.., i.e. "but you will yourself abhor your impudent words, under the pain that we inflict on you for them". On ἀλλὰ but cf. passages like Ch. 595; on ἀποπτύειν to spit out Prom. 1070. Ch. 197 etc., but especially Soph. Frg. 616 Ddf. ἀπέπτυσεν λόγους he spat out words (Hippolytus Phaedra's proposals). - V.
304 τραφείς reared like a sacrificial animal, see 305; καθιεροῦν to consecrate Hdt. 1, 92 etc.

- 306 δέσμιος bound (δ d. φρενῶν of the mind 332) recalls the καταδέσεις binding spells (defixiones) on lead tablets buried or hung up in sanctuaries of the underworld gods, Plat. Νόμ Laws. ΧΙ XI, 933 A (Weckl.): μαγγανείαις τε καὶ ἐπωιδαῖς καὶ καταδέσεσι by sorceries and incantations and binding spells, and see the collection of tablets found in Athens in the appendix to the C. I. Att.: Defixionum tabellae Atticae ed. R. Wünsch, where καταδῶ I bind, κατέδησα I bound (τὰς χεῖρας καὶ τοὺς τόδας καὶ τὴν γλῶσσαν καὶ τὴν ψυχήν the hands and the feet and the tongue and the soul), especially with regard to speaking, is carried out.

As often elsewhere, anapests precede the stationary song, during which the chorus takes up the position suitable for the stationary song; so here too the anapest has the character of a marching rhythm.

According to the tradition there are 6 systems, of 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3 verses; but the 3rd system must be supplemented by one anapest or emended so that the paroemiac disappears; I prefer the latter, according to which 5 systems of 3, 2, 4, 2, 3 verses remain. Regularity in the verse numbers is not necessary, see on Ch. 719 ff. – Χορὸν ἅπτειν to kindle the dance as πάλην wrestling Ch. 866 ff.;

μοῦσα Muse appellatively (often Euripides, Ddf.) also Hik. 695. Δοκεῖν to seem in A. wavers between the Attic and the Ionic inflection; for δεδόκηκα I have seemed the Attic would be δέδοκται it has seemed (so Hik. 601), and this active perfect occurs only here at all.

Λάχη τὰ κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπους the lots among men according to the Schol. are the lots of men; on the other hand, according to V. 334. 347. 386 it seems to mean the lot (office) assigned to the Erinyes over men. However, ἐπινωμᾶι allots is so clearly "allots", and the parallel Sept. 727 ξένος δὲ κλήρους ἐπινωμᾶι χάλυβος and a stranger allots the lots of steel so exact, that I follow the Schol. Also the elaboration in 312 ff. connects better in this way, and "how we administer our portion among men" would be rather meaningless. Below 930 πάντα γὰρ αὗται τὰ κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπους ἔλαχον διέπειν for these obtained by lot to manage all things among men; 953 περί τ᾽ ἀνθρώπων φανερῶς τελέως διαπράσσουσιν and they accomplish openly and completely the affairs of men, τοῖς μὲν ἀοιδάς to some songs, τοῖς δ᾽ αὖ δακρύων βίον ἀμβλωπὸν παρέχουσαι but to others a life dimmed by tears (= ἐπινωμῶσαι to allot).
Στάσις faction as Ch. 114. 458;
ἁμή our = ἡμετέρα our, on Ch. 428.
The following verses are disfigured by numerous small corruptions, which can, however, be removed.

Εὐθυδίκαιοι δ righteous in judgment' Hermann, cf. ὀρθοδίκαιον upright in justice 994; then οἰόμεθ᾽ εἶναι we think we are quite easily Ahrens, which is better than ἡδόμεθ᾽ εἶναι we are pleased to be (Hermann after Canter), where the infinitive instead of the participle is not justifiable, and also than εὐχόμεθ᾽ εἶναι we pray to be (Stanley), which is too far from the features. "And indeed we believe (with litotes) that we are very just in the distribution." In 313 the transmitted τοὺς μὲν those who.. προνέμοντας holding out throws the rhythms into confusion, unless one inserts with Hermann: τοὺς μὲν καθαρὰς those with pure | <καθαρῶς purely> χεῖρας προνέμοντας holding out pure hands, or inserts in some other way; that then the singular διοιχνεῖ passes through follows is no different than in the stasimon antistrophe α τοῖς ὁμαρτεῖν ὄφρ᾽ ἂν γᾶν ὑπέλθηι to accompany until he goes under the earth. Perhaps, however, as the same Hermann earlier: τὸν μὲν καθαρὰς χεῖρας προνέμοντ᾽ the one holding out pure hands, not difficult and smoother; Paley compares the corruption Prom. 264 τοὺς κακῶς πράσσοντας those who fare badly instead of (as the verse requires) τὸν κ the one. πράσσοντα doing.
Προνέμοντα holding out: opposite ἐπικρύπτει conceals, Paley; thus προνέμειν to hold out to bring forward, exhibit, extend (Dindorf).

In v. 314 the synapheia is interrupted by hiatus: οὔτις ἀφ᾽ ἡμῶν μῆνις ἐφέρπει no wrath from us creeps upon | ἀσινὴς unharmed; but already Porson and Wakefield corrected οὔτις ἐφέρπει μῆνις ἀφ᾽ ἡμῶν no wrath creeps upon from us.
Διοιχνεῖ passes through cf. εἰσοιχνεῦσιν they enter Prom. 122.
Πράκτωρ avenger Ag. 111. Hik. 646.

Composition and rhythms. The strophic composition of this stasimon, according to the tradition, is as follows: Str. α a Antistr. α a; each in two parts, consisting of a main part and a refrain that is identical in wording both times; Str. β b, with a refrain that one may call γ c, in similar but not identical rhythms to that of α a, and with different words; Ant. β b; Str. δ d, with the refrain γ c repeated rhythmically but not in wording; Str. ε e Ant. ε e, without refrain. At β γ b c the peculiarity is that y attaches itself to β b with the closest syntactic connection, which has not prevented modern editors (since G C W Schneider) from appending an identical ephymnion, thus lacking syntactic connection, also to the antistrophe β b; one repeats this at Str. Ant. δ d, where at least the construction suffers no harm, though the sense certainly does, and so one obtains the regular scheme of αα ββ γγ δδ aa bb cc dd. Correspondingly, it has been done in the last two stasima of the Choephori, where the tradition offers a similar artificial interweaving as here: αβα γμεσ aba cmes. γ δβδ c dbd. and αβα γβγ aba cbc, as here αα βγβ δγδεε aa bcb dcdee. I do not understand how one can thus devastate the sense for the sake of a purely external scheme. Far less harsh, but in my opinion equally false, is the formerly popular transposition of y' after β΄ b', by which likewise the regular scheme ααββ γγδδ aabb ccdd is obtained; see on Antistr. γ c. In the scholia (on 341) is found the name fitting the transmitted form μεσόφθεγμα mesophthong (that which is sung between two strophes). A. has two kinds of ephymnia, identical in wording and only rhythmically identical; the former kind appears Ag. 121. 139. 159 (1 verse). Ch. 961. 972 (likewise); more extensive Hik. 111 ff.; on the other hand the latter Ag. 367 ff., with rhythmic identity throughout the whole stasimon except for the epode, and Hik. 630 ff. likewise except for the last strophic pair, with the same rhythms as in the Agam.; in addition Ch. 783 ff. Str. Ant. β b and the same also Ch. 935 ff. have this character. The rhythms show the same progression from majestic trochees to pathetic iambs as so often in A., see on Ch. 585 ff.. With the trochees are combined here as elsewhere dactyls, and again in pentapodies, Ch. 30 f. (p. 78). 591 f. (p. 143); yet this is not yet the case in the first strophe, but in the second and third to such a strong degree that the dactyls far predominate and there is only one trochaic colon in each. In these strophes, which one will therefore call κατὰ δάκτυλον by dactyl, there occur besides the pentapodies other dactylic verses, see below on Str. β b. Finally, also in the iambic strophe ε e the close is again a dactylic pentapody with trochaic dimeter, as in the iambic Ch. 22 ff.. But the refrain in α a and the strophe serving as refrain γ c have, besides trochees, whose dipody for the most part shows the first arsis resolved and the last thesis suppressed (thus ∪ ∪ ∪ —), in all appearance also the Pherecratean, thus a πούς foot from κατὰ βακχεῖον by bacchius, so at the end γ c (as Ag. 367 ff. at the end and likewise in the following strophes; again 681 ff. at the end and likewise in Str. β γ b c) and according to the tradition also in the middle of the refrain of α a, see below; accordingly it is to be investigated whether the same is also to be recognized at the beginning of α a. Characteristic for the ὕμνος δέσμιος binding hymn are the measures ∪ ∪ ∪ — (almost always with diaeresis after each measure); everything else is found also used elsewhere, in that at least from Antistr. α a onward, outside the refrains, self-conscious majesty presents itself in the song. Strophe α a. The rhythms are according to the tradition unclear precisely at the beginning, but Weil has made something very pleasing out of it, though not without alteration: (Antistr.) τοῦτο γὰρ λάχος διανταία for this lot, piercing | (- -,-∪「,「「) Μοῖρ᾽ ἐπέκλωσεν Fate spun (Eurip. Or. 12 likewise) ἐμπέδως ἔχειν θνατῶν to hold steadfastly for mortals )-)」, ں۔۔۔, -ur, 「「), and accordingly Str.: μᾶτερ ἃ μ᾽ ἔτικτες ὦ μᾶτερ mother who bore me, O mother | Νύξ Night, ἀμαυροῖσι for the dim (ἀλαοῖσ for the blind(ιν in) transmitted) καὶ δεδορκόσιν ποινάν and for those who see, requital. The λέξεις words of the form ποινάν requital and again ταία piercing – θνατῶν of mortals, correspondingly at the close of the cola, make themselves most magnificent, whereas if one divides and measures thus (Rossbach-Westphal): μᾶτερ ἃ μ᾽ ἔτικτες ὦ μᾶτερ Νύξ mother who bore me, O mother Night, ἀλαοῖσιν for the blind | καὶ δεδορκόσιν ποινάν and for those who see, requital, one obtains in the first verse a mixture of trochees and dactyls (or Pherecratean), and as the second the σχῆμα figure وساسا μᾶτερ mother which would be measured as - c, rit, with the form for -- nowhere attested. Ἀλαοῖσιν for the blind and ἀμαυροῖσιν for the dim differ little, and the meaning "blind" is present for ἀμαυρός dim at least in Sophocles, OC. 182 ἀμαυρῶι κώλωι with dim limb, 1639 ἀμαυραῖς χερσίν with dim hands ("dark" also A., Ch. 157 etc.). The connection is as below 387 δερκομένοισι καὶ δυσομμάτοις for those who see and for the dim-sighted, and if ἀλαός blind corresponds even better to δυσόμματος dim-sighted than ἀμαυρός dim, it may have come in as the more familiar word for "blind". Lengthenings as in ἐπέκλωσεν spun are found in A. also the following (J. Rumpel Progr. Insterburg [I. II] 1865. 66): ἐπέκρανεν accomplished Hik. 624 (ἐπικρᾶναι to accomplish Ddf.), ἐπέφλεγεν burned Pers. 395, ἀποκρύψει will hide Prom. 24, ἄτρυτος unwearied Eum. 403, ἰσοτριβής equally wearing Ag. 1443, ἀκραγής not barking (Ddf. ἀκλαγγής not howling) Prom. 803, μηλοτρόφου sheep-nourishing Pers. 763. Thus there seem to be preponderant reasons for the change. The imperfect ἔτικτες you bore corresponds to the rule according to which of persons still living the imperfect and not the aorist is used, Homer Ζ 206 Ἱππόλοχος δέ μ᾽ ἔτικτε Hippolochus bore me, against ἔτεκε bore 196. 199 (not very different 154 τέκετο gave birth to and 155 ἔτικτεν Βελλεροφόντην bore Bellerophon, where the narrative lingers, as it were "has (had) borne"), likewise π p 118 Λαέρτην Ἀρκείσιος υἱὸν ἔτικτεν Arcesius begot Laertes as his son, μοῦνον δ᾽ αὖτ᾽ Ὀδυσῆα πατὴρ τέκεν but his father begot only Odysseus (whom Telemachus holds for dead), αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς μοῦνον ἔμ᾽ ἐν μεγάροισι τεκὼν λίπεν οὐδ᾽ ἀπόνητο but Odysseus, having begotten only me in the halls, left me and had no joy of me (for Odysseus I have been nothing). For the sense of ἀμαυροῖσι ποινάν for the dim, requital Paley rightly compares 175. 340; see also on 302. –
324 ἶνις son still Hik. 43. 251. Ag. 718 (Conington);

326 ἀφαιρούμενος taking away according to the Attic ἀφαίρεσις εἰς ἐλευθερίαν removal to freedom, Meier-Schömann-Lipsius Att. Proc. 658. Πτώξ cowering is in Homer an epithet of the hare or stands for the animal itself, P 676, as in A. πτάξ cowering Ag. 137 (μογερὰν πτάκα θυομένοισιν a wretched cowering creature for those sacrificing), which (πτάκα cowering creature) M also had here at first; is this then the meaning, or "fugitive", after καταπτακών having cowered down 252? Ματρῶιον ἅγνισμα κτέ a mother's expiatory offering. a due expiatory offering to the mother for the murder; it is not absolutely necessary to assume a transposition in relation to the associated noun, since ματρ mother. properly belongs to φόνου of murder (ὄγκον ὀνόματος μητρῶιον the weight of the mother's name Soph. Τr. 817 and other places, Wecklein on 292).
Κύριον lord cf. 127, effective, intended for this purpose. Refrain 329 ff.
Τεθυμένωι to the one sacrificed cf. 304 f., thus already as good as actually sacrificed; to this sacrifice this song.

Παρακοπά madness Ag. 223 (παράκοπος maddened Prom. 581), παραφορά derangement cf. παράφορος deranged and παραφέρεσθαι to be deranged. There is no reason in form or meaning to doubt φρενοδαλής mind-destroying, cf. φρενοβλαβής mind-harming, φρενοπληγεῖς μανίαι mind-stricken madnesses Prom. 878; δήλημα destruction stands A. Frg. 121. But neither do the rhythms: ~, -, -, - Ag. 698; still more similar, -,, -, -, - Ch. 806 f. (Paley). With the conjecture written in M (οἶμαι I think) φρενοδαής mind-destroying nothing can be done; of the newer conjectures (-πλανής wandering, -βλαβής harming, -μανής raging, -δακής biting) none is any more commendable.
Ἐρινύων of the Erinyes is evidently the more terrible, because less transparent name (still 511 chorus, 951 Athena); at the introduction 417 they call themselves Ἀραί Curses.

Ἀφόρμικτος without lyre: thus (as is natural) this song was not accompanied by Apollo's cithara (but only by the shrill and exciting flute). Cf. (Stanley) Ag. 990 τὸν δ᾽ ἄνευ λύρας ὅμως ὑμνωιδεῖ θρήνον Ἐρινύος αὐτοδίδακτος ἔσωθεν θυμός but without the lyre, nevertheless the self-taught spirit within sings a dirge of the Erinys.
Αὑονή drought drought, parching (cf. μάραινε wither 139, ἰσχνάνασα having dried up 267, Pal.) only here; a different word (related to αὔω to cry 'to cry') is αὐονή cry 'cry' in Semonides (Herm.).
Διανταῖος piercing through like Ch. 184. 640. Sept. 895, penetrating, i.e. lasting and eternally determining; ἡ διαμπὰξ τιμωρουμένη she who punishes through and through (Schol.) is not quite correct.
Ἐπέκλωσεν she spun the thread after Homer λ l 139 etc. —

At 336 the manuscripts have a corrupt reading, which in majuscules would be: TOICINAYTOYΡΓ ΡΓIAICΞΥΜΠ ΞΥΜΠACWCI(N)MATAIOI; from this one can make τοῖσιν αὐτουργίαι with their own deeds (but also Schol. αὐτοφονίαις with self-murders) ξυμπέσωσιν they may fall in with (Turneb.) μάταιοι vain, or even more easily τοὶ σὺν αὐτουργίαις ξ those who with their own deeds. μ m., after φόνου δὲ κηκὶς ξὺν χρόνωι ξυμβάλλεται the oozing of blood in time comes together Ch. 1012. Συμπίπτειν τινί to fall in with someone is admittedly said more of sufferings than of deeds, and so stands Soph. OR. 113 τῶιδε συμπίπτει φόνωι he falls in with this murder of the murdered man; thus Weil τοί νιν αὐτουργίαις ξυμπατῶσιν those who trample him with their own deeds, whereby however neither συμπατεῖν to trample in this sense is properly attested, nor νιν him i.e. τὴν Μοῖραν Fate is possible at all. The difficulty of ξυμπίπτειν to fall in with becomes less if at least the criminal is the subject, who in a blinded and reckless sense (cf. Hik. 762 ματαίων ἀνοσίων τε κνωδάλων of vain and unholy beasts, ματαίαις χερσίν with vain hands Soph. Tr. 565, Abresch) commits the crimes that, so to speak, come his way, without hesitation, and so I have preferred τοὶ σὺν those who with.
Αὐτουργίαις with their own deeds cf. αὐθέντης murderer above 212.

Ὄφρ᾿ ἂν γᾶν ὑπέλθηι until he goes under the earth namely τις someone or (Schol.) ὁ τοιοῦτος such a one; cf. on this transition to the singular above on 313 ff., to which passage Wecklein compares Plat. Protag. 324 B: οὐδεὶς γὰρ κολάζει τοὺς ἀδικοῦντας for no one punishes those who do wrong . . τούτου ἕνεκα for this reason, ὅτι ἠδίκησεν because he did wrong. Οὐκ ἄγαν ἐλεύθερος not too free is a powerfully effective litotes; precisely the half-veiled expression terrifies. Then the fearful refrain is repeated, to bind the criminal all the more firmly.

Further development of the thought in the antistrophe α a, also in the direction that they are now separated from the gods precisely by their office; to the office they return in the refrain (strophe γ g).

347 γεινομέναισι for those born Hermann, since 'to be born' at least in the epic poets is not γίγνομαι I become but γείνομαι I am born; see Homer p. 128 = Ω 210 (αἶσα fate or μοῖρα portion) γεινομένωι ἐπένησε λίνωι for him at birth she spun with thread (otherwise WSchulze).

Ἀμῖν to us only here in Aeschylus, frequent in Sophocles, Kühner-Blass I, 591. - The conjecture (ἀθ but. δ᾽ ἄπ᾽ ἔχειν to keep away) γέρας privilege (Evers) for χέρας hands is poorly compatible with λάχη lots, and in ἀπέχειν χέρας to keep hands away there is also no ambiguity, since "to keep the hand from grasping and striking" χ hand. ἀπέχεσθαι to keep oneself away means, Hik. 756, Demosth. Meid. 69. Paley construes the construction thus: it is for the immortals to keep their hands away from us; more naturally, however, ἀθ but is construed with ἀπέχειν to keep away: to keep the hands that seize the murderer (cf. 779 ἐκ χερῶν εἵλεσθέ μου you took from my hands) away from the immortals, not to greet them, etc. (ἐν δ᾽ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί and he grew into his hand Homer).
Μετάκοινος sharing in common 964. Hik. 1039;

συνδαίτωρ fellow-banqueter only here. For the restoration of the following verse, which in ἄμοιρος ἄκληρος without share, without lot shows a metrical error instead of ⏑ – ⏑ – ⏑ - the antistrophic verse is in even worse condition -, first offers itself ἀπόμοιρος without a share (OMüller), unattested, yet cf. ἀπάνθρωπος inhuman Prom. 20, ἀπόμουσος without the Muses Ag. 801, ἀποχρήματος without money [Ch. 275], ἀπόκλαρος without a lot (πόνων of toils) Pind. Pyth. 5, 54. But I am reluctant to efface the ἀ a-- ἀ a--, cf. the same asyndetic accumulation of parallel words with ἀ a-- in ἄτιμ᾿ ἀτίετα dishonored, unhonored 385; more examples at 785. Ἀνέορτος ἄκληρος without festival, without lot (Fritzsche, Weil) lies further off and has hardly any support in the freely paraphrasing scholion. So the transposition ἄκληρος ἄμοιρος without lot, without share is probably the simplest.
Ἐτύχθην I was made = εἰμί I am also Hik. 86, like τέτυκται it is made Ag. 751.
Εἱλόμαν I chose took for myself (867 etc.) in accordance with my office.

Ἄρης Ares: is in general the god of bloody killing, so θηλυκτόνωι Ἄρει with woman-slaying Ares of the Danaids murdering their husbands Prom. 860, cf. also Ag. 1235. In τιθασός tame lies the comparison with the seemingly tamed beast (Ag. 717 ff.).

Διόμεναι pursuing = διώκουσαι pursuing also (385, see below,) Hik. 819 μετά με δρόμοισι διόμενοι pursuing me with their courses, = μεταδιώκοντες pursuing after with tmesis; so Homer H 197 etc. But one gets on badly with ἐπὶ τὸν ὦ upon the one, as transmitted; for ἐπιδιώκειν to pursue after "pursue further" does not fit at all, and an ὦ O or ὤ O as an interjection διὰ μέσου through the middle (Schol.) is strange. So good E. A. J. Ahrens ἐπὶ τὸν ὧδ᾽ ἱέμεναι upon the one thus sending (since ἵημι I send the ι i in A. as in others has anceps, Sept. 310 etc.); the ὧδε thus could (Wecklein) be made vivid by the gestures of the dance. Very difficult is the close: κρατερὸν ὄνθ᾽ ὁμοίως μαυροῦμεν ὑφ᾽ the mighty one, likewise we dim under (ἐφ᾽ upon) αἵματος νέου of new blood, while the antistrophe γ g closes: σφαλερὰ τανυδρόμοις κῶλα δύσφορον ἄταν slippery limbs, a grievous ruin to swift runners, unsuspicious, except that according to the scholia καὶ and can be added before ταν tan.; the rhythms are thus: ◡ ◡ ◡ —, ◡ ◡ ◡ —, — ◡ — ◡ ◡ —, cf. the Pherecrateans in Str. a. Accordingly, in the strophe one must emend, if these are strophe and antistrophe γ g; namely those who repeat the words from γ g after Antistr. β b as part of this strophe, and those from γ g' after δ d′ (according to our numbering, according to the other γ g′), need not trouble themselves about responsion. Dindorf therefore writes (after Hermann, who however finally chose something else) κρατερὸν ὄντα περ ὅμως the mighty one, though nevertheless (ὅμως nevertheless Arnaldus), also very similar in sound to σφαλερὰ καὶ τανυδρόμοις slippery and to swift runners (α a, ερ er, τα ta, ρομ rom, ς s), by which indeed the connection is guaranteed. Cf. Sept. 712 καίπερ οὐ στέργων ὅμως although not loving, nevertheless, γυνή περ οὖσα though being a woman Sept. 1038, καὶ θεός περ ἱμέρωι πεπληγμένος and though a god, struck with desire Ag. 1204, γενναῖός περ ὧν though being noble Soph. Phil. 1068 etc. Also that is no reason against it, that so alone here after ◡ ◡ ◡ — there is no diaeresis. Anapaests and first stasimon. That then ὑφ᾽ αἵματος νέου under new blood comes from explanation, Hermann already saw; now it says in the one scholion διὰ τὸ νέον αἷμα because of the new blood, which can indeed also be taken as explanation of ὑφ᾽ αἵματος νέου under new blood, but arouses the suspicion that the scholiast to νέον αἷμα new blood of the text according to his custom supplied διὰ through, in order to be able to construe the accusative. Just so to δύσφορον ἄταν grievous ruin Ant. γ διὰ τὴν because of the.. ἄτην δύσφορον grievous ruin, and to 378 μύσος pollution: λείπειν φασὶ διά they say to leave because of. On νέον αἷμα fresh blood therefore GHermann had already come; with ὑφ᾽ αἵμ by blood. νέου of a young man this perhaps cannot be explained directly, but these words can be understood as the remnant of a longer paraphrase. The rhythm is now there: — ◡ — ◡ ◡ —; for precisely in these rhythms trochee and spondee respond without objection, to Ch. 619. But now the main thing, the sense.

Νέον αἷμα fresh blood must be a sentence apposition like the corresponding δύσφορον ἄταν grievous ruin, and like (in a passive sentence) νέος ἰχώρ new ichor Agam. 1480; this, like νέον αἷμα fresh blood, means "new bloodshed," cf. there before πρὶν καταλῆξαι τὸ παλαιὸν ἄχος before the old grief ceases. Murder is atoned for by murder.

Here the difficulties are greatest. The manuscript has at the beginning σπευδόμενα δ᾽ and hastening and σπευδόμεναι δ᾽ and hastening; this can also be -μένᾱι to remain, and the singular is recommended by the following ἐμαῖσι with my. We can also, without violence, construct neither σπευδόμεναι hastening nor -μένᾱ to remain (Burges); but Doederlein writes σπεύδομεν αἵδ᾽ we hasten, these, and σπεύδειν to hasten and σπείδεσθαι to make haste (this only Ag. 151, σπευδομένα hastening in dactylic verse as here) are the same in Aeschylus, and ἐμαῖσι with my after σπεύδομεν we hasten is not in the least objectionable. The αἶδε these is understandable, even if unnecessary; for they are not now introducing themselves. But another objection is greater: the Eumenides want to take this care of vengeance away from the gods, especially Zeus, but constantly and not in a single case; but that is expressed by ἀφαιρεῖν to take away and not ἀφελεῖν to take away, which indicates the one-time act, and this act of ἀφελεῖν to take away necessarily lies before us as having happened; therefore σπευδόμεναι hastening must be a participle of the past, and the present σπεύδομεν we hasten is wrong. From this the construction already follows: σπευδομένᾱι δ᾽ ἀφελεῖν and hastening to take away . . θεῶν δ᾽ ἀτέλειαν and exemption from the gods . . ἐπικραίνων fulfilling . . Ζεὺς Zeus . . ἀπηξιώσατο deemed unworthy (cf. for the dative βουλομένωι ἦν it was pleasing to him, ἀσμένωι δέ σοι ἡ ποικιλείμων νὺξ ἀποκρύψει φάος but to you, glad, the many-colored night will hide the light Prom. 23, similarly ἡδομένωι to one rejoicing, ἐλπομένωι to one hoping etc., Kühner-Gerth I, 424 f.). That is, our ancient office is also confirmed by Zeus in the new world. In detail: ἀφαιρεῖν to take away here with double accusative, which is unprecedented for the active; if one writes instead τινί from someone, then the parallels are there (Kühner-Gerth I, 328f.): Xenoph. Kyr. 7, 2, 26 μάχας δέ σοι καὶ πολέμους ἀφαιρῶ but I take away battles and wars from you (cf. 7, 1, 44), i.e. release yourself from them, exactly as here. The τινί from someone sounds somewhat mystical, but need not be meant so; Pauw's change to Δία Zeus is unnecessary.

Ἐπικραίνειν to fulfill is a word very popular with Aeschylus (in the Eumenides also 950, 959); with ἀτέλειαν exemption it could mean "to bring about," if only ἐμαῖσι λιταῖς with my prayers could be construed with it. So one must write ἐπικραίνων fulfilling, to which ἐμαῖσι λιταῖς with my prayers is added in the same way as to the main clause σπευδομένᾱι for her who is hastening.

Ἀτέλεια exemption from public burdens is immunity from all burdens, such as the descendants of Harmodius already had in Athens at that time; likewise, ἀνάκρισις preliminary inquiry is an expression of political life, a preliminary investigation, which in Athens belonged to the archon, the basileus, etc. for their judicial sphere, while the decision was taken away from them (Aristot. Πολ. Αθ. 3, 5 προανακρίνειν to conduct a preliminary inquiry). Thus = ὥστε αὐτοὺς so that they (τοὺς θεοὺς the gods) μηδ᾽ εἰς ἀνάκρισιν ἐλθεῖν not even to come to a preliminary inquiry.

Ἄγκρισις inquiry as δυσάγκριτοι hard to decide Hik. 126; cf. on the apocope above at 243. It further follows that in v. 366 the γὰρ for after Ζεὺς Zeus is to be deleted with f g h (thus not, for instance, to write in the strophe παν all⟨το the⟩λεύκων white-robed); the conjunction could easily have been inserted by someone who did not understand the sentence construction (λείπει ὁ γάρ the γάρ is missing at first; then written above); so it also happened at v. 378. Αἱματοσταγές dripping with blood was long ago (by Bothe) emended to αἱμοσταγές blood-dripping (Eurip. Frg. 388), cf. αἱμόρρυτος flowing with blood Frg. 230, αἱμοβαφής blood-dyed Soph. Ai. 219. Dindorf takes offense at ἀξιόμισον worthy of hatred because this is the only compound with ἀξιο worthy- in Aeschylus and from the other tragedians only ἀξιόθρηνος worthy of lamentation (Eur. Alk. 907), ἀξιοπενθής worthy of mourning (Hipp. 1465), ἀξιόχρεως worthy of note (Or. 596) are added, whereas later these formations appear abundantly, as in Xenophon. Furthermore, also because it would have to be formed from μίσος hatred -μισής hateful, like παντομισής hated by all 644.

᾿Αξιομισές worthy of hatred could now be written; but the suspicion that the whole word is an explanation for a genuine one holds one back; also -ὲς -es -ον -on is prettier than -ὲς -es -ὲς -es would be. Dindorf now uses force not only here, but also in the corresponding verse of the strophe: παλλεύκων δὲ πέπλων ἄμοιρος μούνα ἐτύχθην but of white robes I alone was made without share – Ζεὺς γὰρ αἱματόφυρτον πᾶν ἔθνος τόδε λέσχας for Zeus has made this whole race blood-defiled, apart from the assemblies; that was his manner of rewriting, which rightly no one follows anymore. I have set a cross; according to the strophe εὐμίσητον well-hated lies near, which stands in Xenophon Cyr. III, 1, 9 (with intensifying εὖ well); the opposite εὐφίλητος well-loved Aeschylus has Sept. 107.
Ἔθνος race, nation class of people (τὸ τῶν φονέων the class of murderers Schol.) like Demosth. XXIII, 146 Aeschylus. Anapaests and first stasimon. (likewise Plato, Xenophon);

λέσχη talk, conversation intercourse, conversation also Ch. 665 according to Emperius for λεχθεῖσιν to those who had spoken (which has remained in my text by mistake); ὃς who suus according to Sept. 641; ἀπαξιοῦσθαι to deem unworthy middle only here (-οῦν therefore Eur. Εl. 256; Thucydides and others); but likewise 425 ἠξιώσατο he deemed worthy, Sept. 667 κατηξιώσατο he deemed worthy.
The τ τ' at the beginning of the new thought does not correspond to usage; therefore δ δ' with Bergk.
Δόξαι opinions, reputations existimatio, gloria, cf. Soph. OC. 258.

Ὑπ᾿ αἰθέρι under the open sky i.e. οὐρανῶι in heaven requires the opposite κατὰ γᾶς under the earth (Hermann) and not κατὰ γᾶν on the earth “on earth”; the same corruption is at 838, 871. Μινύθειν to diminish also Sept. 920. Ὀρχησμοῖς ἐπιφθόνοις with envious dances, the envious one, disturbing his happiness; no other emendation of the transmitted ἐπιφόνοις with murderous seems to offer itself, and there is also a certain analogy of sense to μελανείμοσιν with black-robed. But what the ὀρχησμός dance is, not a dance around him, but rather upon him, and why ποδός of the foot, is clarified by the following antistrophe γ γ.

Already Heath and after him Hermann, Dindorf and others transposed this, before 368, so that it now simply becomes part of antistrophe β; but if in this way the form also becomes regular, the sense still suffers.

Μάλα γὰρ οὖν ἁλομένα for indeed leaping “for in truth (Ag. 524. 674. Frg. 308) with mighty leap” etc. has no connection at all with λέσχας ἅς ἀπηξιώσατο the talk which she disdained; on the other hand, with ὀρχησμοῖς ποδός with dances of the foot the very closest, as also especially ποδὸς ἀκμάν the point of the foot refers back to ποδός of the foot 371, and likewise antistrophe δ πίπτων δ falling is now connected, whereas the connection with ὀρχησμοῖς ἐπιφθόνοις ποδός with envious dances of the foot is deficient: how can he fall over from dancing? What kind of dance that is must first be described, and in general after the next description in antistrophe γ γ the ὀρχησμοῖς ἐπιφθ with envious dances. ποδός of the foot sounds quite feeble. — The hiatus after ἁλομένα leaping shows the break of synaphea here; therefore one must not write in tetrameters. Σφαλερὰ τανυδρόμοις κῶλα causing stumbling to the swift-running limbs is explained in the scholia in two ways: τοῖς τανυδρόμοις αὐτῶν κώλοις ἐπάγουσα τὰ σφαλερά μου κῶλα bringing my stumbling limbs upon their swift-running limbs, and ἀπ᾿ ἄλλης ἀρχῆς from a new beginning (with a new sentence) καὶ τοῖς τανυδρόμοις γίνεται σφαλερὰ τὰ κῶλα διὰ τὴν ἐπιοῦσαν ἄτην δύσφορον ὑπ᾽ ἐμοῦ and for the swift-running their limbs become stumbling because of the grievous ruin coming upon them from me. Since in the latter way δύσφορον ἄταν grievous ruin cannot be construed, except if one makes σφαλερὰ stumbling . . κῶλα limbs a parenthesis, and even so only with harshness, I prefer the former: σφαλερά stumbling therefore active, which it can be as well as passive.
Καὶ and before τανυδρ swift-running. can be inferred from the second scholion, although not with certainty as an actual reading; in the other interpretation one wrote 〈γὰρ for〉 (Hermann).

Τανύδρομος swift-running connects with the Homeric τείνειν δρόμον to stretch the course, Ψ 375; so even if he wants to run away, we bring him down in his course. The image of fleeing and pursuing (75 ff., 137 ff., etc.) is, however, used only here and is immediately (377 πίπτων δ᾽ οὐκ οἶδεν κτέ falling, he does not know, etc..) imperceptibly abandoned again.

Ὑπὸ under with dative as at Ch. 28 etc., under the influence of something; the λύμη ruin, destruction is the ruin that clings to him from his guilt, which robs him of clear consciousness; immediately it is also compared to a darkness in which one cannot see. Cf. on 378 Pers. 669 Στυγία γάρ τις ἐπ᾿ ἀχλὺς πεπόταται For some Stygian mist hovers over; here, however, μύσος pollution, defilement (the blood-guilt) is the actual subject, and τοῖον κνέφας such darkness is predicative. On 379 cf. Ch. 51 ff. ἀνήλιοι βροτοστυγεῖς δνόφοι καλύπτουσι δόμους sunless, mortal-hating darknesses cover the house;
φάτις report, saying is the speech of the people, like Ag. 456. Αὐδᾶσθαι to speak, utter middle instead of αὐδᾶν to speak, as at Soph. Phil. 130. 852 etc.

The iambic rhythms that stand out from what precedes are generally clear: two acatalectic dimeters with suppressed arsis in the middle and then a similarly constructed catalectic one, thus ending: CICITči,CICI LUI, CICI - -; then three acatalectic dimeters without syncopated interior and again a catalectic one of the same construction as before; the strophe closes with a dactylic pentameter and a trochaic colon, as already noted above. So Rossbach-Westphal. Some details, however, still require discussion.

Τε μνήμονες mindful at the beginning of the third colon need not be, as Wecklein correctly observes, (antistrophe ἐμοῦ κλύων hearing me), since Ag. 990 ὑμνωιδεῖ sings in hymn – – – and also probably 1459 πολύμναστον much-remembered is measured. But at the beginning of the fourth colon there is indeed in strophe and antistrophe - - -, cf. on Ch. 24 f. p. 77.

At v. 387 λάμπαι torches is transmitted, in the corresponding 395 κυρῶ I meet with, obtain; for this, therefore, Hermann wrote κύρω I meet with, obtain, since as ἐκύρησα ἔκυρσα I met with, I obtained are used side by side by Aeschylus, so alongside κυρεῖν κύρειν to attain, to light upon there is a place, cf. ἔκῦρον they attained Soph. OC. 1157. Conversely Wieseler, Dindorf λ lӑπᾶι to every for λάμπᾶι to a torch, with bad rhythms and without decisive proofs against the spondaic word-form (see below). Hereupon follows in the strophe, as the beginning of the dactylic verse, δύσοδοπαίπαλα hard to traverse, rugged, in the antistrophe regularly καίπερ ὑπὸ χθόνα even beneath the earth. Is it a tribrach instead of a dactyl? Is it a prosodic license? Is corruption to be assumed? Ἀπαράμυθον not to be persuaded, implacable Prom. 187 is still easier than δύσοδο hard to traverse -, since the former can attach itself to ἀθάνατος immortal, ἀκάματος unwearied; but a tribrach instead of a dactyl seems to exist in Euripides (Phoen. 796 ἀσπιδοφέρμονα θίασον ἔνοπλον a shield-bearing armed company = 813 Οἰδιπόδα κατὰ δώματα καὶ πόλιν through the house and city of Oedipus), yet is not easily to be attributed to Aeschylus. Therefore emendation; see below. Somewhat anomalous is the syllaba anceps at the end of the pentapody: τάξιν ἔχουσα holding a position | καὶ and..; for usually the trochaic colon is closely connected, in strophe and antistrophe d even with word-sharing. One could therefore emend: ἔπι δέ μοι γέρας παλαιόν and there is for me an ancient privilege (ἐστιν is) οὐδ᾽ ἀτιμίας κύρειν καίπερ ὑπὸ χθόνα τάξιν ἐχούσαι and not to attain dishonor, even beneath the earth, holding a position. See, however, on Ch. 592, where I conversely remove the synapheia by change. V. 381 ff.

μένει γὰρ for it remains is rightly compared with Ag. 1563: μένει δὲ μίμνοντος ἐν θρόνοις Διὸς παθεῖν τὸν ἔρξαντα but it remains, while Zeus remains on his throne, that the doer suffer; only here the subject is developed in a separate new clause: εὐμήχανοί τε καὶ κτὲ and resourceful and....

Τε καὶ and as in the antistrophe; thus τε and (Wakefield) instead of the manuscripts' δὲ but seems assured. But the new clause would need a finite verb, even if ἐσμέν we are could possibly be supplied; moreover, διόμεναι pursuing (= διώκουσαι pursuing) λάχη allotments, privileges cannot be exactly paralleled, although διώκειν to pursue "to pursue" (μετερχόμεναι going after, pursuing schol.) is common in Attic poetry. Therefore with Heath διέπομεν we manage, we administer, cf. 931. Pers. 106; διόμεναι pursuing may have been repeated thoughtlessly after v. 358. Weil, however, takes a different view: ἄτιμα τίομεν ἀτίεται we honor the unhonored; it is unhonored (thus -ται tai M, and so also the schol.), with slight transposition and minor change. But neither is anything like τίειν λάχη to honor; allotments attested, nor is ἀτίεται it is unhonored correct: οὐδ᾽ ἀτιμίας κύρω and I do not attain dishonor it says later.
Τέλειοι perfect, fulfilled of two endings, like Ag. 1437. Frg. 11, 7, but mostly of three, as at v. 214. Μνήμονες Ἐρινύες mindful Erinyes Prom. 516;
