Σεμναί the August, the Revered is the Athenian cult name of the Eumenides, Preller-Robert Myth. 838; also below at 1041. Heimsoeth and Paley therefore capitalize it; for if it were simply an adjective, the word would have to be joined with καὶ δυσπαρήγοροι βροτοῖς and hard to appease for mortals, which is not a good combination and also gives an unpleasant enjambment.

Δυσπαρήγοροι hard to appease with the same litotes as Prom. 34 δυσπαραίτητος hard to entreat, inexorable; but see also 387 δυσποροπαίπαλα hard to traverse, rugged, 396 δυσάλιον sunless = ἀναλίωι sunless 387, 388 δυσομμάτοις with terrible eyes, in which accumulation there is a certain intention to emphasize the repulsive.
Ἀτίετος unhonored (cf. ἀλάμπετος unlit, ἀμάχετος unconquerable, ἀπεύχετος abominable etc.) also at 839. Hik. 853.

Θεῶν διχοστατοῦντα the gods being divided (Ag. 323) is the same as ἀθανάτων δ᾽ ἀπέχειν κτέ and to keep away from the immortals.... 360 ff. The transmitted ἀνηλίωι sunless Dindorf corrects to ἀναλίωι sunless, likewise 396 δυσήλιον sunless to δυσάλιον sunless; in this strophic pair the Attic forms are almost throughout in the manuscripts, unlike in the other strophes, but at least in this verse λάμπαι to a torch.

Λάμπη Lampē (a kind of froth or scum) according to Hesychius and Photius is παχὺς ἀφρὸς ἐπιπολῆς τοῦ οἴνου thick foam on the surface of wine; Hesychius also has CI λάπην lapē (scum)· βόρβορον mud, ἰλύν slime; in Hippocrates λάπη lapē occurs for thick phlegm (in the verse of Diphilus II 545 K.). It is rightly compared with εὐρώεις moldy, dank; nevertheless, one can also think of the βόρβορος mire of sins in the underworld, Ar. Βάτρ Frogs. 145 etc. There follows the already mentioned δυσοδοπαίπαλα hard to traverse, rugged, explained in the scholia by δυσπαράβατα καὶ τραχέα hard to cross and rough (cf. schol. Ar. Νεφ Clouds. 260), a τριπλοῦν triple more in the manner of the later dithyrambic poets than of Aeschylus, in whom besides ἀτιμοπενθής dishonored in grief 793 only εὐκοινόμητις sharing counsel well Hik. 700 in an otherwise corrupt verse can be compared. Not even this fits, for it is added to κοινόμητις εὖ sharing counsel well, but not to ὁδοπαίπαλος δυσ hard to traverse, rugged-; ἀτιμο dishonored- however is a single concept. Παίπαλά τε κρημνούς τε rugged crags and cliffs Kallimachos Artem. 194; but an adjective παίπαλος rugged, rocky alongside παιπαλόεις rugged, rocky is after all not attested, so that in the end it is advisable, instead of writing perhaps δύσβατα παίπαλα hard to traverse rugged places (Oberdick), to leave τριπλοῦν triple and only emend δυσοδο hard to traverse- to δυσπορο hard to cross- (Heimsöth) (cf. πέλαγος οὐ μάλ᾽ εἴπορον a sea not easy to cross Hik. 470).
Ὁμῶς equally 695. Prom. 736; the sense must be that neither the living nor the dead can escape.
Ἐμοῦ κλύων hearing from me hearing from me.

Μοιρόκραντον fated and ἐκ θεῶν δοθέντα given by the gods summarize what is said in Str. Ant. β 2. In 394 an iambus is missing, which, as it seems, the scholiast no longer found either, since he explains ἔπι upon with ἔπεστι is upon; if, however, οὐδὲ not even 〈νῦν now〉 (Drake in Paley) is the correct reading or indeed the gap is at this place, what was said about the scholiast becomes void. "Ἔτι δέ μοι μένει Yet it remains for me Hermann; others otherwise. On κύρω κυρῶ I attain, I attain see above;
δυσήλιον κνέφας sunless darkness is also dependent on ὑπὸ under (Wecklein); cf. Pers. 839 γῆς ὑπὸ ζόφον under the earth into darkness.
Athena, invoked by Orestes, appears; the parties state their cases, and Athena arranges with them a judicial inquiry and decision, which is to take place under the presidency of the goddess.

397–414. Athene. The first question is how the goddess appears, whether really, as the scholiast on line 405 thinks, in a chariot. But 403 διώκουσ᾽ ἦλθον ἄτρυτον πόδα I came pursuing with untiring foot proves as strongly as possible that she comes without a chariot, also not flying with wings, but striding through the air and thereby supported by the aegis as by a sail (cf. Introduction p. 15); so 405 must be explained metaphorically, if not emended. Now Sept. 371 is said quite similarly of the arriving messenger: σπουδῆι διώκων πομπίμους χνόας ποδῶν in haste pursuing the guiding axle-ends of my feet; so if the feet are compared with the ends of the axle (indeed not without harshness), then here too the body together with the aegis can be designated as ὅδε ὄχος this chariot, and πῶλοι ἀκμαῖοι swift colts can mean the legs. (Hermann, with Wakefield, corrects to κώλοις with limbs: cf. above 372. Prom. 323 etc.; of course this is meant to recall πώλοις with colts; but one can also conversely be reminded of πώλοις with colts by κώλοις with limbs.) Another question is why the poet has the goddess come from the Troad, i.e. from Sigeion. A current interest for the Athenians, which the historically ill-informed scholiast has in mind, Sigeion did not have at that time at all; for after the Athenians had taken it from the Mytilenaeans in the 6th century, it was in any case reoccupied by Athens after the Persian Wars and was then, like Lemnos and Imbros, a tribute-paying allied city, E. Meyer, Geschichte des Altertums IV, § 394. So it is probably meant only to connect with the Trojan War, cf. 456 ff., 631 f., and the first play of the trilogy. As Athene then helped the father, so she now helps the son.
397 κληδών report, rumor here "cry, report", 418 "name", again differently Ch. 505. 1043, = φήμη voice, utterance.
Πρόσωθεν ἐξήκουσα I heard from afar connects with 297 κλύει δὲ καὶ πρόσωθεν he hears even from afar.

398 καταφθατουμένη anticipating occurs only here; the scholiast explains it with καταφθάνουσα anticipating, Hesychius with κατακτωμένη acquiring (manuscript καταντ katant)· κυρίως δὲ τὸ ἐκ προκαταλήψεως properly, that which comes from prior occupation, with which other glosses in him are to be compared: φθατήσηι may anticipate· φθάσηι may anticipate and φθατήσαι to anticipate· φθάσει κτήσασθαι will anticipate acquiring. The connection with φθάνω I anticipate seems clear, but one can take offense at the meaning; for with this acquisition Athene then did not hurry in the least. So perhaps: securing my right as first acquirer.
399 δῆτα indeed in a declarative sentence confirming or assuring, here about = "as is well known", cf. ἢ δὴ or indeed 3 (Paley).
Ἄκτορες Actors Pers. 557, πρόμοι champions Ag. 200. 410. Hik. 904. —
V. 401 αὐτόπρεμνον with the very trunk properly with the stem, αὐτόρριζον with the very roots (Hesych.), cf. πρέμνοθεν from the stump Sept. 71. 1056. In the literal sense of trees Sophocles Ant. 714.

Ἐξαίρετον chosen out 402 belongs in sense actually to the preceding, of the spoil selected for Athena (cf. Ag. 954), yet moving the comma after ἐξαίρετον chosen out would make what follows too bare. Theseus' sons Demophon and Acamas appear only in the later epic, where they find their grandmother Aethra in conquered Troy, see Proclus' excerpt from Arctinus' Ἰλίου Πέρσις Sack of Troy; but this justification of the Athenian claim to Sigeum certainly goes back to the time of Peisistratus. In Euripides' Heraclidae the sons of Theseus are the princes of the land; but in the Eumenides nothing further occurs of them, and according to Aeschylus the Athenian democracy appears as already founded by Theseus, cf. especially Athena's speech to the people 681 ff. — On the dative with δώρημα gift cf. Kühner-Gerth I, 426 f.

Ἄτρυτον unwearied: recalls Ἀτρυτώνη Atrytone (Weckl.). ‘Ροιβδεῖν to make a rushing noise occurs only here (for Homer μ m 106 is ῥυβδεῖν to make a rushing noise the correct spelling), but ῥοῖβδος πτερῶν rushing of wings Soph. Ant. 1004 makes the sense “noisy movement” unambiguous (cf. also Ar. Νεφ Neph. 407); thus = ῥοιζεῖν to whistle (below 424). Since the aegis appears on monuments and vases of the 6th century as laid around like a collar or mantle (see Preller-Robert Myth. 191), it was easy to make of the mantle a kind of billowing sail (Schol.). On κώλοις κτἑ with limbs, etc.. see above.

With καὶ νῦν and now one could be satisfied (cf. Paley), but καὶ νῦν δ᾽ and now (M) demands the correction to καινὴν δ᾽ but a new, a very easy one according to the script of the Aristotle papyrus, where the H shortened at the bottom left and the Y are confusingly similar.
Ὁμιλία company see on 57; exactly as here τῆνδ᾽ ὁμ this company. χθονός of the land 711.
409 ἐφῆσθαι to sit upon with accusative also Frg. 158 (elsewhere with dative, as Ch. 501); likewise ἐφεζόμην I sat upon 446, ἦσθαι to sit Ag. 183, Kühner-Gerth Synt. I, 313 f.
410 Transition to the accusative, which is equally possible with λέγω I say (σέ τοι λέγω I say to you Ch. 456); the dative would have become awkward at 412.
410 σπαρτοί sown generally begotten, including gods and men.

Οὔτ᾽ οὖν neither then as μήτ᾿ οὖν nor then Ag. 359. 474. After μορφώμασιν shapes the following verse is corrupted by unconscious assimilation; for the correctness of the correction ἄμομφον blameless (Robortellus) instead of ἄμορφον shapeless is not to be doubted.

Ἄμομφος blameless also at 475, 678. The scholiast, who had the corrupt text, understands it completely wrongly: you who are ugly will not be able to revile me again; but even if one writes τὸν πέλας the neighbor and makes ἄμορφον ὄντα τ being shapeless π p the object, then with the epithet exactly what should not happen occurs. Also in Aeschylus only οἱ πέλας the neighbors is found (504, Prom. 334, Hik. 373), not, as in others, also ὁ πέλας the neighbor.

On ἀποστατεῖ θέμις right stands aloof cf. especially Frg. 156 μόνου alone (θανάτου of death) δὲ Πειθὼ δαιμόνων ἀποστατεῖ but Persuasion stands aloof from the gods, and 287 ἀπάτης δικαίας οὐκ ἀποστατεῖ θεός a god does not stand aloof from just deceit. — Athena appears in this whole speech as completely humanized with regard to knowledge; as indeed could hardly be otherwise, if she was to appear as a character in the drama; her fine impartiality and consideration toward the Erinyes contrasts with Apollo's behavior and manner of speaking; but he is also a party to the case. Cf. Introduction p. 6.
Stichomythia 415–435, again (as at 198) introduced with 3 verses.

416 αἰανὴς grievous as at 479, 943 (νόσος disease) lugubris, cf. Pers. 635 940, also Pindar several times, and already Archilochus Frg. 38 (αἰηνές grievous, which is explained with δεινὸν καὶ πολύστονον terrible and much-groaning); imitating it Sophocles in Ajax 673 νυκτὸς αἰανὴς κύκλος the grievous circle of night. The spelling varies in Aeschylus between αἰανῆ grievous and αἰανῆς grievous, in Sophocles between αἰανὴς grievous and αἰανῆς grievous; but the form αἰανός grievous has no authority, see Dindorf. Different is αἰανής grievous "eternal" at V. 572 (cf. 672), which seems to be connected with αἰεί always, as the other word with αἰαῖ alas. –
᾿Αραί Curses: cf. ᾿Αρά τ᾿ Ἐρινύς Curse and Erinys Sept. 70, and Introduction p. 2; in this name the thought indeed seems to show clearly through the mythical veil (cf. Soph. OC. 1375 f. [Paley]).
Ὑπαί Beneath as Ch. 615 etc. —
418 οἶδα I know I have now learned. I await further.
Γένος race on Νυκτὸς τέκνα children of Night, κληδόνας names (397, here attached to κεκλήμεθα we are called), ἐπωνύμους named after on Ἀραί Curses.

Ἐπώνυμος eponymous is otherwise always "named after something" or "corresponding to its name" 90, Ch. 190 etc., cf. ἐπωνυμία eponymy, ἐπονομάζω I name after; so here too "corresponding to the dark descent from Night".

Γε μὲν δὴ ge men dē: here, as at γε μήν ge mēn (cf. οὐ μὲν δὴ ou men dē), seems to be continuative, not, as (γε ge) μὲν δή men dē elsewhere, emphasizing a concept in contrast to what follows (Sept. 587. Ag. 661. 887. 1213. Hik. 241. 273; without γε ge above at 106); since that meaning is in fact unattested, an emendation must be made in γε μέντοι ge mentoi, cf. 591. Pers. 386 etc. The words are spoken as if threatening, but Athena answers calmly: so I will learn it, provided that etc. (cf. Hik. 924 ἄγοιμ᾽ ἄν I would lead, and often in the 2nd person = imperative). At βροτοκτονοῦντας those who kill mortals Davies in Paley takes offense, and would like αὐτοκτον self-killing, cf. above 210 ff., below 604 f., where the Erinyes definitely restrict themselves to the murderers of ὅμαιμοι of the same blood. The conjecture seems correct; βροτ mortal- preceded at 412. Τοὺς μητραλοίας ἐκ δόμων ἐλαύνομεν We drive the matricides from their homes 210. At ἐλαύνομεν ἐκ δόμων we drive from their homes Athena attaches the appropriate question: whither and for how long, and then comes the terribly veiled answer ὅπου τὸ χαίρειν μηδαμοῦ νομίζεται where joy is nowhere regarded, i.e. in hell.

Μηδαμοῦ νομίζεται is nowhere regarded is found in no place, as Pers. 498 θεοὺς δὲ τις τὸ πρὶν νομίζων οὐδαμοῦ but someone previously regarding the gods nowhere (cf. also 624); on μη not- (δαμοῦ nowhere) see Kühner-Gerth II, 184. Οὐδαμοῦ nowhere would designate the specific place specifically; but that is precisely what is not intended.

V. 424 ἐπιρροιζεῖν to rush upon only here, in the scholia explained with ἐπιβοᾶις you shout upon and with ἐπιβάλλεις you cast upon. Ῥοιζεῖν to whiz (= ῥοισδεῖν to whiz; Hom. K 502. Hes. Thg. 835) seems to be fairly identical with ῥοιβδεῖν to whiz (V. 404), as ῥοῖζος whizzing (Homer II 361. ι i 315) with ῥοῖβδος whizzing; cf. also ῥοίζημα whizzing Ar. Ὄρν bird. 1182 ῥύμηι τε καὶ πτεροῖσι καὶ ῥοιζήμασιν αἰθὴρ δονεῖται with force and wings and whizzings the air is shaken. "Between" is probably what is meant; see the passages in Homer and Hesiod.
On ἠξιώσατο he deemed worthy 425 cf. ἀπηξιώσατο he deemed unworthy 368.

Athene shows a quick understanding of the matter and a high sense of justice. The reading in M: ἄλλης ἀνάγκης οὔτινος τρέων κότον fearing the wrath of some other compulsion can only be explained with some difficulty: "and indeed not because he feared the wrath of some other compulsion?" The very frequent κότος wrath in Aeschylus is only Ch. 593 αἰγίδων κότον wrath of the aegis not referred to a person. The other manuscripts, however, have ἤ τινος or of someone, which seems more correct; accordingly Dindorf ἄλλαις ἀνάγκαις other compulsions good and clear. The scholiast, however, with μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης τοῦτο πεποίηκεν he did not do this under compulsion offers something else: ἀλλ᾽ ἦ ᾿ξ ἀνάγκης but was it under compulsion, ἤ τινος τρέων κότον or fearing someone's wrath; (ἀλλ᾽ ἦ but was it as Ch. 276. 774. Ag. 276. Hik. 913 ὑπ᾿ ἀνάγκας under compulsionHik. 1032, ἐξ ἀν from compulsion. Soph. Phil. 73). The chorus replies that for this deed there can be no compulsion at all; cf. Aristot. Eth. N. III, 1 p. 1110, a 26: ἔνια δ᾽ ἴσως οὐκ ἔστιν ἀναγκασθῆναι some things perhaps cannot be compelled, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἀποθανετέον παθόντα τὰ δεινότατα but rather one must die after suffering the most terrible things· καὶ γὰρ τὸν Εὐριπίδου ᾿Αλκμέωνα γελοῖα φαίνεται τὰ ἀναγκάσαντα μητροκτονῆσαι for even the things that compelled Euripides' Alcmaeon to kill his mother appear ridiculous. On κέντρον goad cf. 136. 157 and especially below 466. On τοσοῦτον so much (Elmsley) see on 201. — Athene is not satisfied with this, but wants first to hear the other, according to the old saying (ψευδησιόδειον pseudo-Hesiodic Cic. ad Att. VII, 18; probably from the Χίρωνος ὑποθῆκαι Precepts of Chiron, see the exact collection of passages for the saying in Bergk Lyr. Gr. Pseudophocyl. 87): μηδὲ δίκην δικάσηις do not judge a case, πρὶν before (ἂν would added Ar. Σφῆκ Wasps. 725) ἀμφοῖν μῦθον ἀκούσηις you hear the speech of both (saying of Pittheus according to Theophrast Schol. Eur. Hippol. 264, Bergk ibid.). "There are two persons present, so with your statement I have only half of what I must hear." Certainly correct M ἥμισυς λόγου half of the speech, against λόγος speech of the other manuscripts; i.e. ὁ ἥμισυς τοῦ λόγου the half of the speech instead of τὸ ἥμισυ τοῦ λ the half of the speech., Kühner-Gerth Synt. I, 279 c.

429 ff. In the oldest legal procedure, which the Eumenides alone know, there was no other means of proof than the oath of the parties; see the classic passage on this in Platon Ges. XII, 948 B: Ῥαδαμάνθυος δὲ περὶ τὴν λεγομένην κρίσιν τῶν δικῶν ἄξιον ἄγασθαι of Rhadamanthys, in the so-called judgment of lawsuits, it is worth admiring — — διδοὺς γὰρ περὶ ἑκάστων τῶν ἀμφισβητουμένων ὅρκον τοῖς ἀμφισβητοῦσιν ἀπηλλάτετο ταχὺ καὶ ἀσφαλῶς for by giving an oath to the disputants about each of the matters in dispute, he settled them quickly and safely. Plato argues with some irony that this was appropriate at that time, because all people still believed firmly in gods, but is no longer appropriate today because of unbelief and perjury; therefore one must abolish the oath of the interested parties and have only the disinterested judges swear. Aeschylus, who in this very play shows himself to be a political and also juristic thinker, is evidently of the same opinion; for while Attic law did not decide according to the oath of the parties, but still inconsistently demanded this oath (the διωμοσία oath-taking by both parties, Lys. Χ, 11, Demosth. XXIII, 63. 68. 71) in blood courts and elsewhere (ἀντωμοσία counter-oath), Aeschylus in the archetypal blood-court procedure presented here simply omits the διωμοσία oath-taking by both parties, whereas the judges are also sworn in his account. Cf. below on 485 f. Thus Athena also gives as her reason for rejecting the old procedure at v. 432: ὅρκοις τὰ μὴ by oaths the things that are not (μὲν indeed) δίκαια μὴ νικᾶν λέγω I say that unjust things should not prevail. —
At v. 429 in any case θέλοι he might wish is to be written instead of θέλει he wishes, since this fact cannot yet have been established, but otherwise nothing is to be changed.

At v. 430 in M δ d. καίους and burning (but ov on an erasure) and as a transmitted variant δικαίως justly (so fg) are preserved; Dindorf writes δίκαιος just, from which he supplements δίκαια just things to πρᾶξαι to do: "You prefer to be called just rather than to act justly." The reproach would not exactly be deserved, and the parallel verse Prom. 868 (βουλήσεται he will wish) κλύειν ἄναλκις μᾶλλον ἢ μιαιφόνος to be called cowardly rather than bloodthirsty (cf. also Hik. 453 θέλω δ᾽ ἄϊδρις μᾶλλον ἢ σοφὸς κακῶν εἶναι I wish to be ignorant rather than wise in evils) leads in a quite different direction: the emphasis must lie on δίκαιος just, as there on ἄναλκις cowardly. Thus as a question (as the scholiast also understands it, whose explanation is, moreover, useless): do you prefer to be called just or to achieve your purpose, better "to carry out the vengeance" (624)? Or, since thus ἤ or must be rendered with "or", differently from the parallel passages, where it is "than" and attaches to μᾶλλον rather, with the slight change of θέλεις do you wish into
θέλε wish: "prefer to" etc. The chorus does not understand this and asks for instruction, very fittingly, whereas this request would attach less well to the reproach.
Κλύειν to hear can be aorist like πρᾶξαι to do (Kühner-Blass II, 462), but need not be;
δίκαιος just of two endings Eur. Herakl. 902. I.T. 1202 (cf. τέλειος perfect 382) here because of the ambiguity of ΔΙΚΑΙΑ just things. But if θέλε wish, the sentence can also be taken as a maxim.
431 τῶν σοφῶν of the wise neuter;

432 μὴ νικᾶν not to prevail should not prevail; before that τὰ μὲν δίκαια the just things (fg) is better than τὰ μὴ δίκ the unjust things. M: justice should prevail by itself, through clarification of the matter, while injustice seeks to cover itself with oaths.
With ἐξέλεγχε question 433 the questioning of the accused is also permitted;
εὐθεῖαν δίκην straight justice has nothing to do with Attic εὐθυδικία straight justice as the opposite of παραγραφή counter-plea, but rather to εὐθύς straight the opposite is σκολιός crooked.
434 ἢ καὶ or even —: so you are ready for this too?
᾿Επ᾿ ἐμοὶ τρέποιτε turn upon me = ἐμοὶ ἐπιτρέποιτε entrust to me, as (Weckl.) Soph. Aut. 1107 μηδ᾽ ἐπ᾿ ἄλλοισιν τρέπε nor turn upon others.

435 ἐπάξιος worthy is always "corresponding", 271. Ch. 95. Sept. 865. Prom. 70; but the genitive cannot be explained (although the scholiast also had it: ἀξίων of worthy things (scil.) οὖσαν γονέων being of parents), and one can easily emend with Hermann: ἄξι᾿ ἀντ᾽ ἐπαξίων worthy things in return for worthy things, to repay your friendly reception with what is fitting (thus ἄξια worthy things = ἄξιον σέβας worthy reverence). Cf. Ag. 1560 ὄνειδος ἥκει τόδ᾽ ἀντ᾿ ὀνείδους this reproach comes in return for reproach. 1318. Ch. 309. 312. Hik. 966. Whether σέβουσαι revering with M, or σέβοιμεν we would revere, which lies in the reading of fg, is hard to decide; ἄ whichv is easily supplied from τρέποιτ᾽ ἄν would turn to the optative σέβοιμεν we would revere.
Ἐν μέρει in turn: as at 198.
Ξυμφοράς misfortunes the matricide or whatever it is you have done; ἔπειτα κτἑ then etc.. seek to justify yourself.

᾿Αμυνάθου defend yourself (so, not -θοῦ put as Ddf.) cannot be aorist, any more than most of the other forms in -θειν to place Kühner-Blass II, 178f. In A. cf. κατειργάθου you accomplished 566, σχεθεῖν to hold 857 etc. (this aoristic). V. 440

ἑστίας of the hearth: to the ἑστία hearth fled the προστρόπαιος suppliant, Ag. 1587. Ch. 1038. Apoll. Rh. IV, 691; at Apollo's as at Athena's the eternal fire was the symbol of this hearth, Ch. 1037. Paus. I, 26, 6f. (lamp of Callimachus at the old cult image of Athena). ῾Αμῆς our (M) is not to be adopted, because this form is used only under metrical compulsion, as at 311, Ddf.
Σεμνός reverend: cf. 92 σέβας reverence, 151 σέβων revering;
προσίκτωρ suppliant like προσίξομαι I will approach as suppliant Ch. 1035; on Ixion, the prototype of those seeking refuge because of murder, see below on 717f.
443 f. τῶν ὑστάτων τῶν σῶν ἐπῶν of the last of your words would be in nom.-acc. τὰ ὕστατα τῶν σῶν ἐπῶν the last of your words. —

446 ἐφεζόμην I sat upon with accusative as at ἐφημένωι seated upon 409. The tribrach τὸ σὸν ἐ your e-- (or the dactyl -μῆι τὸ σὸν -me your) is one of the few non-necessary ones in Aeschylus (like χρόνον ἐρημώσει πατήρ time will make desolate, father Hik. 516).

V. 447 is, perhaps not without intention, echoing 445: τῶν σῶν ἐπῶν μέλημ᾽ ἀφαιρήσω μέγα I will take away the great care of your words – τεκμήριον δὲ τῶνδε σοι λέξω μέγα I will tell you a great proof of these things. – (448) That the not yet purified murderer was not allowed to address anyone, precisely so as not to defile them with his guilt, was also indicated at 276 ff.; the scholiast quotes from Euripides (Frg. 996 N) τί σιγᾶις Why are you silent?; μῶν φόνον τιν᾿ ἠργάσω Have you committed some murder?; see also Apoll. Rh. IV, 691 ff., of Jason and Medea, who, defiled by the murder of Apsyrtus, turn to Circe: τὼ δ᾽ ἄνεωι καὶ ἄναυδοι ἐφ᾽ ἑστίηι ἀίξαντε ἵζανον They two, speechless and voiceless, rushed to the hearth and sat, ᾗτε δίκη λυγροῖς ἱκέτηισι τέτυκται as is the custom for wretched suppliants, κτἑ etc.. In Euripides, without regard to the purification that has taken place, the behavior of the others toward Orestes remains so until he is acquitted, Iph. T. 949 ff. (951 σιγῆι δ᾽ ἐτεκτήναντ᾿ ἀπόφθεγκτόν μ᾽ In silence they made me speechless, ὅπως δαιτὸς γενοίμην πώματός τ᾽ αὐτῶν δίχα so that I might be without their feast and drink; cf. Orest. 75). Also Telephus came in Aeschylus's Μυσοί Mysians as blood-defiled and therefore ἄφωνος voiceless to Mysia, Aristot. Poet. c. 24 (criticized as ἄλογον irrational), comic poet in Ath. VI, 224E. X, 421D (Frg. 144 Ddf.).
Παλαμναῖος murderer, blood-guilty (from παλάμη palm, hand, cf. ἀπάλαμνος helpless, reckless, Kühner-Blass 1 287, 2) = αὐτόχειρ with one's own hand, Soph. El. 587. Tr. 1207.
— 449 f. to be construed ἀνδρὸς καθαρσίου of a purifying man (cf. 63. 568) αἵματος of blood;
αἱμάτων of bloods (as at 166. 254 and often) would be clearer, and is perhaps what Aeschylus wrote.

Αἵματος – καθαιμάξωσι Blood – they will bloody is of course intentional (like μητροκτόνον mother-killer.. χοιροκτόνοις pig-killers 281 ff.); this is exactly the Heraclitean καθαίρονται ἄλλως they purify in vain (αἵματι with blood) αἵματι μιαινόμενοι defiling with blood (on Ch. 1038).

Νεοθήλου βοτοῦ of a newly born animal of the χοῖρος piglet, which comes fresh from the θηλή teat (cf. εὔθηλος with good teats, Ddf., and χοῖρος εὐθηλούμενος a piglet with good teats Frg. 321). Wecklein wants νεοθήλου newly born, like Hik. 333 νεοδρέπτους freshly plucked, because / - - (word unity in the measure of the ionic a minore), in the 4th and 5th feet does not occur in A.; see, however, (Dindorf Po. Scaen. Praef. 34) Πολυφόντου βία the might of Polyphontes Sept. 498. Πολυνείκους βία the might of Polyneices(ν n) 577. 641. Πολυν Polyn. νεκρὸν corpse 1013. There is also no example in A. where νεο neo- is certainly monosyllabic (cf. on 513), except νοσσός chick Frg. 510. The rite is again described by Apollonius IV, 702 ff.: (Circe) πρῶτα μὲν ἀτρέπτοιο λυτήριον ἥ γε φόνοιο τειναμένη καθύπερθε συὸς τέκος first, a release from unyielding bloodshed, stretching over her the offspring of a sow, ἧς ἔτι μαζοὶ πλήμυρον λοχίης ἐκ νηδύος whose teats still swelled from the womb of birth, αἵματι χεῖρας τέγγεν she wet her hands with blood, ἐπιτμήγουσα δέρην cutting the throat· αὖτις δὲ καὶ ἄλλοις μείλισσεν χύτλοισι and again she appeased with other libations, καθάρσιον ἀγκαλέουσα Ζῆνα calling upon Zeus the purifier, etc. Cf. above on 280ff., also on the fact that according to Orestes' opinion the purification is strengthened by subsequent intercourse on journeys and in houses, V. 451 f., where βατοῖς to those who go must be written for βοτοῖς to cattle (which is certainly assimilated after 450). Cf. 240 ὅμοια χέρσον καὶ θάλασσαν ἐκπερῶν crossing alike land and sea. ῾Ρυτᾶς ἐξ ἁλός from the sea of Rhytas Ag. 1408. The asyndetic beginning 451 stands for ἡμεῖς δὲ πάλαι but we long ago, with emphatic preposing of πάλαι long ago. But striking is ἀφιερώμεθα let us consecrate instead of ἀφωσιώμεθα let us purify (Ddf.): Orestes has not become ἱερός sacred, but only ὅσιος holy, and also ταῦτα these things (the blood-guilt) can fittingly be object only to ἀφοσιοῦσθαι to purify oneself. I would therefore also write ἀφωσιώμεθα let us purify; elsewhere neither this nor that verb is found in the tragedians. 453
ἐκποδών out of the way: namely εἶναι to be;
λέγω I say = κελεύω I command as at 432.
Πεύσηι τάχα you will learn soon at the end of the verse also at 419.
Ἱστορεῖς you inquire 455 = οἶσθα you know, Pers. 454.

῾Αρμόστωρ Harmostor only here, = -στήρ ster -στής stes, which likewise does not occur in the tragedians. On 457 the scholiast correctly says: διὰ τούτων φιλοποιεῖται τὴν θεόν through these things he makes the goddess friendly; cf. on 397 ff. The pleonasm in Τροίαν Troy we remove with Τρώιαν Trojan (adjectivally Wieseler, Headlam; on Ch. 363); for ἄπολιν πόλιν a city without a city one compares νόμον ἄνομον a lawless law Ag. 1142, ἄχαριν χάριν a graceless grace 1545 cf. Ch. 42. Prom. 545, etc.

Κελαινόφρων dark-minded (only here) refers to the dark, cruel disposition, cf. κελαιναὶ Ἐρινύες dark Erinyes and μέλας Ἄρης black Ares Ag. 462. 1511, ἐκ μελαίνης φρενός from a black heart (Solon) 42 Bgk. The epic (κατ kat)έκτα ekta the tragedians seem (against Homer) to measure with ā, Kühner-Blaſs II, 468.
Ποικίλοις with embroidered like τοῦ ποικίλματος of the embroidery of the same garment Ch. 1013;

ἄγρευμα the prey, the catch the same at 1013 there; Orestes refers back to this scene of the Choephori with 461. Ἐκμαρτυρεῖν to bear witness, to testify in the technical sense of testimony from an absent person or about hearsay is even less possible to take here than Ag. 1196; it is nothing but a strengthening of μαρτυρεῖν to bear witness, to testify (this of the same thing Ch. 1010), and Paley correctly compares Eurip. Frg. 553 N.: ἐκμαρτυρεῖν γὰρ ἄνδρα τὰς αὑτοῦ τύχας εἰς πάντας ἀμαθές for to bear witness about one's own fortunes to all is foolish, τὸ δ᾽ ἐπικρύπτεσθαι σοφόν but to conceal them is wise. –
462 κατελθών having returned cf. Ch. 3. Ag. 1283.
On ἀντικτόνοις avenging, murder-avenging (only here) ποιναῖσι punishments, penalties Wecklein compares Soph. El. 248 ἀντιφόνους δίκας retaliatory justice.

465 ff. The scholiast correctly recalls 426. There is nothing to object to in ἐπαίτιος blameworthy, culpable (Homer A 335), except that it already recurs at 467 (ἐπαιτίους blameworthy, culpable (accusative plural)) in the same position; so there the conjecture μεταίτιος sharing in blame, jointly responsible (cf. 199) improves it, which at the same time brings out more sharply the different sense in 465 and 467. No offense is naturally to be taken at the pleonasm κοινῆι μεταίτιος jointly responsible.

Ἀντίκεντρα counter-goads, retaliatory stings cf. 136; on the matter Ch. 271 ff. 1030 ff. In 467 v. Wilamowitz writes well ἔρξοιμι I would drive away, I would keep off, cf. εἰ μὴ μέτειμι if I do not pursue Ch. 273.

Τι τῶνδε any of these things is a kind of litotes = τάδε these things, cf. 142 εἴ τι τοῦδε φροιμίου ματᾶι if anything of this prelude goes astray, Ag. 1059 σὺ δ᾽ εἴ τι δράσεις τῶνδε but if you will do any of these things, 1239 τῶνδε of these things . . εἴ τι μὴ πείθω if I do not persuade.

— 469 = πανταχῆι ἐν σοὶ πράξας ταῦτα στέρξω having done this in every way in you, I will be content; Paley compares Soph. Ant. 634 ἢ σοὶ μὲν ἡμεῖς πανταχῆι δρῶντες φίλοι or we, acting as friends to you in every way, Ai. 1369 ὡς ἂν ποιήσηις as you may do, πανταχῆι χρηστός γ᾽ ἔσηι in every way you will be good, Hdt. 9, 27 πάντηι τεταγμένοι πειρησόμεθα εἶναι χρηστοί in every way we will try to be good (also Pers. 225).
Ἐν in to Ch. 773. With this both parties have submitted to Athena's judgment, even if the Erinyes not so unconditionally as Orestes.

Ἤ τις or someone: for εἴ τις if someone is in any case necessary; for for εἴ τις οἴεται δικάζειν if someone thinks to judge it would have to be δικάσειν will judge or δικάσαι ἄν would judge. But whether βροτοῖς for mortals or βροτὸς a mortal, that can be disputed. With βροτοῖς for mortals human judges are immediately thought of, and these are then somewhat rejected, which does not fit with what follows 483 ff.; with βροτός a mortal one thinks of Orestes' words 468, and Athena thus first raises two objections against a decision by herself: the first not yet serious, but the second introduced by οὐδὲ μὴν nor indeed? for me it is (as a goddess) not in accordance with sacred right (on θέμις divine law, right mostly emphasis) to judge in a blood matter, since this is the affair of the punishing deities (the Erinyes), see the chorus 360 ff.
Ὀξυμηνίτου of sharp wrath, of bitter anger is not to be changed into -ους ous; for of the μῆνις wrath, anger for the δίκη justice, judgment there is talk only from 477 ff.
Δίκας justice, judgment = δίκην justice, judgment as at 224. 682.
473 ff. follows a third reason, which reaches further and makes any decision difficult: I owe consideration to both parties.
Ἄλλως τε καὶ especially since with following main clause also Pers. 689.

Κατηρτυκώς having completed the scholiast takes intransitively as "grown up", because it was said of animals that have completed the entire change of teeth (Eurip. Frg. 42, only a gloss; Nauck Aristoph. Byz. 100); this, however, fits absolutely not. But Eurip. Frgm. 818, 5 stands: νῦν δ᾽ ἀμβλύς εἰμι καὶ κατηρτυκὼς κακῶν but now I am blunt and have completed my evils (κακοῖς with evils Valcken.), and so the sense here must be: you have come through the pollution, are done with it (like an animal with the change of teeth). A closer determination, however, would be desirable, and there offers itself νόμοι laws (Dindorf), cf. what Or. 448 has said. Again, δόμοις houses at 474 needs the closer determination; good then Hermann δόμοις ἐμοῖς in my house (instead of the second ὅμως nevertheless of M; Pauw set it for the first), ἄμομφον δ᾽ ὄντα σ᾽ αἰδοῦμαι πόλει but I respect you as blameless for the city. Also for the city you are ἄμομφος blameless (413. 678), because of the purification and because Argos and Athens are not enemies.

Αἱροῦμαι I choose (M) cannot simply = δέχομαι I receive, as the scholiast explains; for αἰδοῦμαι I respect Hermann compares Hik. 641 αἰδοῦνται δ᾽ ἱκέτας Διός they respect the suppliants of Zeus and Eurip. Herakl. 102 θεῶν ἱκτῆρας αἰδεῖσθαι (ἱκέτηισιν αἰδοίοισιν to respect the suppliants of the gods (with reverent suppliants) Hom.).
Μοῖραν fate cf. 105, the nature and kind given by fate (δυσάρεστοι φύσει εἰσὶν αὗται these are hard to please by nature Schol.).
Εὐπέμπελος easy to send away only here;

οὐκ εὐπέμπελος not easy to send away seems = δυσπέμφελος hard to send away, Homer Il. 16.748 πόντος sea, in Hesiod Ἔργα Works 722 also of a person, δαιτὸς δυσπέμφελος a feast hard to send away, difficult against, so that the scholiast explains correctly. Paley, to be sure, compares χορὸς δύσπεμπτος ἔξω a chorus hard to send out . . Ἐρινύων of the Erinyes Ag. 1190 and below πέμπειν to send 481; against this Lobeck Pathol. proleg. p. 105 (Herm.) already contradicts the identification of -πέμπελος sendable and -πέμφελος sendable. So "you may remain, but these I also cannot easily send away".

Μοῖραν fate remains pretty much what it was. In 477 f. τυχοῦσαι having obtained . . ἰὸς arrow is again anacoluthon as at 95 ff. 100 f.; for πράγματος νικηφόρου of a victorious matter Paley well compares Hik. 233 ὅπως ἂν ὑμῖν πρᾶγος εὖ νικᾶι τόδε that this matter may turn out well for you (below 719 μὴ τυχοῦσα τῆς δίκης not having obtained justice).
Μεταῦθις afterwards also 497; on the poison more at 780 ff. 801 ff.
Φρονήματα thoughts seems here (Ddf.) to be as much as φρένες mind; at least 783 καρδίας heart stands for it. More precisely: the φρένες mind as seat of the mind and wrath.
Πέδοι on the ground to Ch. 48;
ἄφερτος unbearable above 146, αἰαής woeful 416. 943.

Athena draws from 476 ff. the conclusion: if they remain and do not win, their wrath is terrible, and sending them away at once is not even possible (namely, if Orestes stays here). To this fits δυσπήμα grievous suffering<ν n>τα ta with reference to the first (Scaliger; supported by δυσκύμαντα hard to steer Ag. 653) and ἀμηχάνως τ᾽ ἔχει and is in a helpless state (Dindorf after Butler, who ἀμυ amu. ἔχει has) with reference to the second. But since the scholiast explains: πέμπειν αὐτὰς ἀμηνίτως δυσχερές ἐστιν ἐμοί to send them away without wrath is difficult for me, a reading diverging more strongly from M has been suspected here, although δυσχερές difficult corresponds to ἀμηχάνως helplessly, and ἀμηνίτως without wrath can be an addition (ὀξυμηνίτου of sharp wrath above at 475; ἀμηνίτως without wrath Ag. 1036).

Ἀμφότερα both: so - ~~ Pers. 491. 720; cf. μαρτύρια παρῆν witnesses were present in the same verse position Eum. 797 (and μαρτύριά τε and witnesses in another position immediately at 485); also (Dindorf, Poetae scaenici⁵, Preface 35) Hik. 259 τἀπὶ τάδε κρατῶ I have power over these matters, 388 ἐγγύτατα γένους nearest of kin.
V. 481 belongs, like 444, to the verses whose τομὴ ἑφθημιμερής hephthemimeral caesura is obscured by elision, to Ch. 150.
482 ff. Athena explains her decision: as things stand, the trial must take place despite everything (since sending them away is impossible), but according to 471 not by the goddess herself.

Ἐπέσκηψεν he enjoined is intransitive only here in Aeschylus, and this usage can now be attested only from later authors (Plut. Thes. 15 νόσος ἐπέσκηψεν a disease fell upon), but the simple verb Aeschylus also uses thus: Ag. 302. 310 (308) φάος ἔσκηψεν light flashed (ἐς τόδε στέγος to this roof), Prom. 749 Sept. 429 πέδοι σκήψασα(ν) having fixed on the ground. The scholiast explains ὡς σκηπτὸς ἐπῆλθεν as a thunderbolt came upon. After 482 Linwood and Weil assume a lacuna; if, however, with Casaubon one emends ὁρκίων of oaths to ὁρκίους sworn (schol. δικαστὰς ἐνόρκους sworn judges) and αἱρουμένους choosing to -μένη remains, then there is no need for it. The judge also, according to Plato and Aeschylus, has to take the oath; see on 429 ff.;
ὅρκιος of oaths stands thus Soph. Ant. 305. OC. 1637;

αἱρουμένη choosing means: I will occupy myself with the selection of judges, in order to create from it a lasting institution (the contrast to the present is κρίνασα having decided 487). Also θεσμὸν τὸν εἰς the ordinance, the one for – is in Aeschylus a quite ordinary position of the article (Ddf. Lex. 325 ab), so here 10. 35. 66. 87. 227. 242. 391 θεσμὸν τὸν μοιρόκραντον the ordinance, the one fated, etc.; there is nothing to indicate that τὸν the should be taken as a relative.
Θεσμός ordinance is at V. 616 the court itself, and can be that here too.
Ἐγώ I forms the contrast to ὑμεῖς you 485.

Μαρτύρια testimonies and τεκμήρια proofs are also later the chief means of proof, and these are called here according to the manuscripts ὁρκώματα oaths (after 786, 379 (Ddf. Lex. p. 58). πιστὰ καλεῖται is called a pledge. For otherwise not), in that they take the place of the old oaths of the parties and are better and more reliable than these; cf. Ch. 901 τὰ πυθόχρηστα πιστὰ δ᾽ εὐορκώματα the Pythian pledges, the well-sworn oaths (scil. ἡγοῦ lead). The scholiast also read thus (ὑμεῖς δὲ ὅρκους αὐτοὺς αἰτήσατε but you, demand oaths from them, admittedly quite wrongly), and we need not change with Pauw to ὀρθώματα upright things (an unattested word). Nor is the τε and after δίκης of justice (Wellauer) necessary, cf. on ἀρωγὰ τῆς δίκης helpers of justice Ag. 1156 γάμοι ὀλέθριοι φίλων marriages destructive to loved ones, Eum. 578 φόνου καθάρσιος purifier from bloodshed etc., Kühner-Gerth 1, 371.
Καλεῖσθε you are called middle voice as at Ch. 201. 216. Pers. 688 καλεῖσθε τεκμήρια you are called proofs is a zeugma.

V. 487 βέλτατα best things Hik. 1055; so also elsewhere Aeschylus βέλτερος better -τατος most, except βέλτιστον best Ag. For the neuter Wecklein compares Pers. 1 τάδε ἥξω I will come to these things is ἄξω I will lead an easy change by Auratus (for which Heimsoeth compares the scholium on 556 ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ ἄγει δικάσοντας Athena leads those who will judge); τάξω I will arrange Schneidewin, which is also not difficult; but one can also attach the infinitive to κρί judgevada.

V. 489 is ὅρκον πορόντας having provided an oath an emendation supported by the scholium (διδόντας giving); but μηθὲν ἔνδικον φράσειν to say nothing just (Markland) has the difficulty (Paley) that φράσειν to say "to indicate" does not suit a judicial verdict. So better Schütz μηθὲν ἐκδίκοις φρεσίν nothing with unjust mind, with a comma after πορόντας having provided, = γνώμηι τῆι δικαιοτάτηι with the most just judgment, which was the formula in the Attic heliastic oath, Demosth. XX, 118 etc., for cases where (as here) no opposition provided the norm for the decision. Cf. (πρὸς ἐνδίκοις φρεσίν with just mind Ag. 996) 1143 ταλαίναις φρεσίν with wretched mind, Hik. 106 δυσπαραβούλοισι φρεσὶν καὶ διάνοιαν μαίνολιν . . ἔχων with ill-advising mind and maddened thought . . having, 750. Pers. 374 etc.; further for μηθὲν nothing (οὐδὲν nothing) as a strong negation before an adjective 730 οὐδὲν nothing . . βαρύν heavy, Prom. 47. 833. With this Athena departs into the city, and with her probably also Orestes, who is assumed as ἱκέτης suppliant (the scholiast thinks otherwise); cf. Hik. 481. 506 and καλεῖσθε you are called 486, although the Erinyes in fact have no reason to go anywhere for this, and the continuation of the play requires their presence in the theater. The scene changes during the choral song to the Areopagus, see on 566.

Rhythms. This stasimon is composed in four strophes and antistrophes in the usual manner. The first three strophes are wholly or largely trochaic, while the fourth is iambic, thus in the customary sequence of these genres; see on Ch. 585ff.. The first strophes are correspondingly also calmer in ethos; in the last there is more tragic pathos, and certainly also a somewhat quicker tempo. In strophe α a the trochaic dimeter prevails, in the forms -- c-cr- and ----, once also (which is not frequent) acatalectic – ~~~ -ut; only the fifth (middle) of the nine cola is a trimeter, of the form -rc-clcr. Even simpler is the second strophe in eight cola: colon 4 is a trimeter of the same form, all the others dimeters of the one form - (「. This same form also begins the third strophe, repeated twice; but then there is strong variation; a monometer, which one must probably separate off, and now twice 5 + 2 dactyls, the first time without, the second with internal catalexis in the fifth foot, this exactly as Pers. 855: πανταρκὴς ἀκάκας ἄμαχος βασιλεὺς ἰσόθεος Δαρεῖος ἆρχε χώρας all-powerful, guileless, invincible king, godlike Darius, ruled the land. As now in the Persians a brachycatalectic trochaic dimeter is appended, so in the Eumenides the first time a catalectic one, as usual after dactyls (see the first stasimon, strophe β b and δ d); also the second time, if the antistrophe with δωμάτων ἐπιστροφὰς turnings of the house is to be authoritative; cf. on this below. In any case there then follows as the last colon (from κατὰ βακχεῖον in bacchic rhythm, and equal to the last in d) --- Lan. The combination of CICT/IC, -- we also have at Ch. 793f. as a strophe-ending, but not after trochees; before and after such in the middle of the strophe Hik. 1065; otherwise - -, - (a form in which one often closes) is found after iambs, as Ag. 256f. θέλει τόδ᾽ ἄγχιστον ᾿Απίας γαίας μονόφρουρον ἕρκος he wishes this nearest bulwark of the Apian land, guarded by one man, Cicirilicir, ici, -, since indeed this closing colon consists of a choriambus = diiambus and a catalectic diiambus. Thus rhythmically considered, ἐπιστροφὰς δωμάτων turnings of the house antistr. (Heath) = φρενῶν ὁ πᾶσι of the mind, he who to all⟨ν n⟩ φίλος dear strophe is equally possible. The same colon - then also begins the last strophe; there follow five iambic hexapodies: u-ciri- - - twice, --, then --., I finally - lilcir, and as strophe-ending choriambic-iambic - I,II/II, cii. Content. In the first three strophes (στρ strophe. ἀντ antistrophe. α a, στρ strophe. β b) the Erinyes express their view of the impending legal decision: if Orestes is not condemned, then all moral reverence, especially toward parents, will be lost among men. But from the second antistrophe onward general moral principles are preached, in exactly the same manner as later by Athena in her foundation speech 690ff.: without a power that inspires fear, no state can exist; the commands of justice must be observed; whoever does so has blessing, but the transgressor perishes, as is set forth in the closing strophes (str. ant. δ d) in a powerful and vivid way. The political tendency, then, which the play had alongside everything else, already comes to light here. As the addressee one must think of the people of Athens, who are gathering for the impending legal decision (566).

If the first words mean that all is well if Orestes is condemned, then πάντας ἤδη all already etc. connect poorly, since an "otherwise" is supplied only with difficulty. Δίκα καὶ βλάβα Justice and harm, however, must be the just punishment (on Ch. 956); clearly 799 ὡς ταῦτ᾽ Ὀρέστην δρῶντα μὴ βλάβας ἔχειν so that Orestes, doing these things, suffers no harm (see also Ch. 498). Thus we are led to the easy correction ἢ or for εἰ if (cf. 746 f.), so that the first words νῦν now . . θεσμίων of ordinances can mean: now a new justice is set in place of the old. Cf. Dante in Purgatorio I, 46 o è mutato in ciel nuovo consiglio; thus μεταστροφαὶ turnings (with Meineke) for καταστροφαί overthrowings. So Prom. 310 μεθάρμοσαι τρόπους νέους to adapt new ways (Paley).

Θέσμιον Ordinance also Hik. 708. To write ⟨Τε Te⟩ καὶ and (cf. μαρτύριά τε καὶ τεκμήρια testimonies and proofs 485, etc.) is so easy that an irregular responsion of – ᴗ ᴗ – ᴗ ᴗ – and – ᴗ – ᴗ – ᴗ – need not be accepted here; cf. on 525.
With εὐχέρεια facility one compares Plato Republic III, 391 E μὴ ἡμῖν πολλὴν εὐχέρειαν τοῖς νέοις ἐντίκτωσι πονηρίας lest they engender in the young much facility for wickedness;
συναρμόσει will join together (only here in Aeschylus) approximately "accustom to".

Ἔτυμα True things i.e. ἔργωι καὶ οὐ λόγωι in deed and not in word (Paley); προσμένει τινι awaits someone like μένει κτέανά τ᾽ ἐπιγόνοις possessions remain for descendants Sept. 902 τίς δέ μοι τιμὴ μένει what honor remains for me below 894, προσμένειν τινά to await someone "await" in Pindar, Sophocles and elsewhere, so that one need not correct with Weil to προσνεμεῖ will allot.
Μεταῦθις Afterwards 478;
ἐν χρόνωι in time Ch. 1040, Hik. 138. 938 etc.

Ἐφέρψει will creep upon: as at 314. 943, at the second place without object; there is no compulsion for changes, apart from that of οὔτε neither to οὐδὲ nor (cf. μηδὲ nor 508; Pers. 652, where M likewise has οὔτε neither; οὔτι not Casaubonus), since κότος anger can carry the two dependent genitives, Kühner-Gerth I, 337; τιν someone' for τις someone (Weil) is admittedly very close.

Μαινάδες Maenads of the Erinyes only here. The difficult next sentence is at least less unclear at its end. Λῆξιν ὑπόδοσίν τε μόχθων ἄκε a cessation and remission of toils〈ά a〉 τ᾽ οὐ βέβαια and not steadfast, τλάμων δέ τις μάταν παρηγορεῖ but some wretched man consoles in vain gives the sense that one should be consoled by the (even worse) fate of another, though in vain. Ὑπόδοσις remission in the sense of abating (opposite ἐπίδοσις increase) is not demonstrable, even if late authors like Philostratus and Dio Cassius use ὑποδιδόναι to give way in this way, and in the sense of "yielding" (opposite ἀντερείδειν to resist) Aristotle also has it (Π. ζ 7. κινήσ motion. 698 b 15); the scholiast explains διαδοχήν succession, which leads to ὑποδοχήν reception (Paley): ὑποδέχεσθαι to receive Hik. 1022. However, ὑπόδυσιν a slipping under (g, and so Herm.) lies closer and is supported by Homer v 53 κακῶν δ᾽ ὑποδύσεαι ἤδη but you will slip under evils; moreover, ὑποδύεσθαί τι to slip under something means to take upon oneself, which comes close to ὑποδέχεσθαι to receive. In the last colon either μάταν in vain or δέ τις but someone must be removed; μάταν in vain now echoes μεταῦθις afterwards of the strophe, and Hermann supports ἄκεα παρηγορεῖ remedies he consoles with Apoll. Rh. II, 624: Τίφυ Tiphys, τί δή μοι ταῦτα παρηγορέεις ἀχέοντι why do you console me in my grief?. Of the scholiasts, one accepts μάταν in vain, the other does not: ἕκαστος δὲ τῶν φονέων παρηγορηθήσεται each of the murderers will be consoled, so si dis placet not only τλάμων wretched "criminal", but also active for passive. Ἄκεά τε and remedies, which lies closer to the transmitted text than ἄκεα δὲ but remedies, requires after it βέβαι᾽ ἃ steadfast things which instead of βέβαια steadfast (τλάμων wretched 〈ἃ which〉 Hartung, with a different rhythm, which he also restored in the strophe). But in the first words of the sentence πεύσεται will learn contends with προφωνῶν announcing beforehand, and if this is to be connected with τὰ τῶν πέλας κακά the evils of one's neighbors, then πεύσεται will learn is without an object, and vice versa. The simplest solution is probably to emend τὰ the to ἃ which (sua): each tells his misfortune and inquires about that of his neighbor, or rather learns of it, since one tries to console him with it. Ὅς who in the sense of suus already at 367.
Προφωνεῖν to announce beforehand 446, Ag. 882 etc.; οἱ πέλας the neighbors 413.

Κικλήισκω I call upon: (Kühner-Blass I, 185) is the spelling of the second Delphic Hymn (V. 20), Weil Études de littérat. et de rythmique gr. p. 71. Θροεῖν to cry aloud otherwise active, Ag. 104 etc.; but θρέομαι I cry aloud Hik. 111 etc. The insertion of τε and after Δίκα Justice (but goddess here, not δίκα justice) seems unnecessary, since also Str. 3, 3 is an independent dipody; nor even fitting in the pathetic invocation.
513 νεοπαθής newly suffering is according to Wecklein (cf. on 450); to me the ἀνατρέφων rearing up of the antistrophe seems quite unreliable because of the sense, cf. there.

Οἶκτον οἰκτίσαντ᾽ having lamented a lament after ταῦτα these things is very harsh, and οἰκτρὸν pitiable is obvious (as in μέγα στένει he groans greatly Ag. 710, etc.); in τίνα πόλις πονεῖ πόνον what toil does the city toil Pers. 682 the figure is the same as here, even if one writes οἰκτρὸν pitiable.
On πίτνει δόμος Δίκας the house of Justice falls cf. Ch. 646 (below, 539).

Somewhere there must be something that inspires fear and keeps the minds of men within bounds. Thus Athena at 698 καὶ μὴ τὸ δεινὸν πᾶν πόλεως ἔξω βαλεῖν and not to cast all fear out of the city, and Menelaus in Sophocles' Ajax 1084: ἀλλ᾽ ἑστάτω μοι καὶ δέος τι καίριον but let there stand for me also some timely fear.
Εὖ well belongs to δεῖ μένειν καθήμενον it must remain seated (ὅπως χρονίζον εὖ μενεῖ so that it may remain well for a long time Ag. 847). —
στένος narrowness only here, = στεῖνος narrowness in Homer.

— 521 ff. is in thought identical with 699 τίς γὰρ δεδοικὼς μηδὲν ἔνδικος βροτῶν for who of mortals, fearing nothing, is just; τίς who, βροτός mortal, μηδέν nothing, δίκαν justice 9* are repeated. Corresponding to δεδοικώς fearing, from τρέφων nourishing one can make with Paley τρέμων trembling or even more easily τρέων fleeing (426 etc.); from this then follows καρδίαν ἄνα up from the heart, since anastrophe, if not with ἀνά up, is not unusual in Aeschylus (φρυκτωρῶν δία through the beacon-fire Ag. 590, χαρᾶς ὕπο from joy 541. 587, etc.), and just as little is ἀνά up with accusative in a local sense (ἀν᾿ ἄστυ up through the city Sept. 346 ἀνὰ γᾶν ᾿Ασίαν up through the Asian landPers. 584, etc.). Thus μηθὲν ἐν φάει nothing in the light (Ch. 62) becomes nothing standing in the bright light, no manifest higher power (= μηθὲν ἐμφανές nothing manifest, but stronger); the opposite is the fear of hidden powers; which, as one sees, is not sufficient. Since now ἄνᾶ τρέων up trembling is harsh - lengthening of a short final syllable by an initial mute + liquid is very rare -, and the strophe shows two short syllables for - να then, I write (with Hermann) ἄν᾿ up (ἔτι still) τρέων trembling. The πόλις βροτός τε city and mortal is (Dindorf) like Homer B 289 ὥστε γὰρ ἢ παῖδες νεαροὶ χῆραί τε γυναῖκες as for example young children and widowed women.

Μήτε κτἑ. Neither ... (and so on).: so Athene 699 τὸ μήτ᾽ ἄναρχον μήτε δεσποτούμενον ἀστοῖς περιστέλλουσι βουλεύω σέβειν I advise the citizens to honor neither anarchy nor despotism; but in detail Plato Laws III, 693 D—699 D, where by the examples of the Persians and Athenians, in older and in more recent times, it is shown how moderate kingship and freedom not lacking in fear are beneficial, whereas unlimited despotism and unbridled freedom are ruinous. With the Eumenides, however, there is no contact, since the Areopagus is not mentioned. (Cf. Introduction p. 13). - Ἀνάρχετος without a ruler (Wieseler; cf. f g h) relates to ἄναρκτος unruled (M) as ἀπεύχετος not prayed against (Ch. 155. 624) to ἀπευκτός not to be prayed against; but while this occurs in A. (Ag. 638, Hik. 790), he does not have ἄναρκτος unruled, but instead (699) ἄναρχος without a ruler, so that the correction is justified and here too (as at 492) the exact responsion is to be established. (Ἄναρκτος unruled Soph. Frg. 28.) Αἰνέσηις you may praise (aorist) refers to the individual case. For the saying about the right mean one compares again Plato, Πολιτεία Republic X, 619 A τὸν μέσον ἀεὶ τῶν τοιούτων βίον αἱρεῖσθαι καὶ φεύγειν τὰ ὑπερβάλλονθ᾽ ἑκατέρωσε always to choose the middle life among such things and to flee the extremes in either direction; but also already Theognis 335 μηδὲν ἄγαν σπεύδειν to hasten nothing in excess· πάντων μέσ᾽ ἄριστα the middle is best in all things, Pind. Pyth. XI, 52 τῶν γὰρ ἂμ πόλιν εὑρίσκων τὰ μέσα μακροτέρωι ὄλβωι τεθαλότα for I find that the middle things in a city flourish with longer prosperity, μέμφομ᾽ αἶσαν τυραννίδων I blame the fate of tyrannies. Then Euripides Frg. 80 N. βροτοῖς τὰ μείζω τῶν μέσων τίκτει νόσους for mortals, things greater than the middle breed diseases etc. Ἄλλ but’ ἄλλα different things̄ δ᾽ ἐφορεύει oversees (Pers. 7, Hik. 627. 676) can be understood as "the one so, the other otherwise", like ἄλλος ἄλλοθεν one from one place, another from another etc.; however also (Paley) that which is different from the μέσον middle in correspondingly different manner. The first explanation, however, lies closer, and contains more: first, that the deity oversees and directs everything, and then, that it treats different things differently, as is set out in the following verses.

Ξύμμετρον commensurate cannot mean the same as σύντομον concise, as the scholiast explains, but must (like Ch. 229) have the meaning "corresponding", namely to the difference of mental dispositions and their consequences. The impious disposition produces wantonness and the deeds arising from wantonness and the consequences of these deeds; on the other hand, with health of mind all blessing is connected as its consequence, as both are further shown in Antistr. γ γ, Str. Ant. δ δ. Ὑγίεια φρενῶν health of mind forms the opposite to νόσος φρενῶν disease of mind Pers. 750 of Xerxes' arrogance, who believed himself superior to all the gods;
δυσσεβία impiety and εὐσεβία piety (the latter Sophocles) the tragedians use according to the rhythm.
Ἐς τὸ πᾶν for the whole can be understood temporally, as at 83 and 291, but the sense is better taken as 'in general', cf. 52.

Αἴδεσαι you will revere the aorist denotes the individual case: the general validity is expressed by ἐς τὸ πᾶν for the whole. Βωμὸν Δίκας the altar of Justice as Ag. 384 λακτίσαντι μέγαν Δίκας βωμόν having kicked the great altar of Justice, which here is expressed by λὰξ ἀτίσηις you may dishonor with a kick (ἀτίζειν to dishonor Sept. 441, Hik. 733, Frg. 103).

On κύριον authoritative cf. 326; Hik. 732 f. χρόνωι τοι κυρίωι τ᾽ ἐν ἡμέρᾶι θεοὺς ἀτίζων τις βροτῶν δώσει δίκην in time and on the appointed day, whoever among mortals dishonors the gods will pay the penalty.
545 πρὸς τάδε with regard to these things (Pers. 170. 730, Sept. 312) = πρὸς ταῦτα with regard to these things, accordingly;
προτίων honoring Ag. 789 (above all else, especially one's own desires).

Ἐπιστροφὰς δωμάτων turnings of houses (Heath) is an easy correction by transposition, so that (with πᾶσιν for all) strophe and antistrophe are balanced; the other way of balancing requires a double correction: ὑγιεί healthy)ας φρενῶν ὁ πάμφιλος of mind, the all-loving (after Hermann) above and here (ξενοτί honoring strangers)μους δόμων ἐπιστροφάς of houses, turnings (Hartung), or, if δωμάτων of houses, there (Herm.) ⟨αὖ again⟩ φρενῶν ὁ πάμφιλος of mind, the all-loving. Δωμάτων τ᾽ ἐπιστροφάς and turnings of houses also stands Sept. 684 (cf. also Frg. 243. 264);

ξενοτίμους honoring strangers is perhaps to be taken proleptically, "so that thereby strangers are honored." On the double τις anyone Paley compares Hik. 58 εἰ δὲ κυρεῖ τις δοξάσει τις ἀκούειν but if anyone happens to think he hears. On these three foremost commandments see on V. 269 ff.

Wieseler's easy change, ἑκὼν δ᾽ willingly for ἐκ τῶνδ᾽ from these things, gives excellent sense and also makes the responsion exact. For the sense cf. among others Philemon 94 Kock: ἀνὴρ δίκαιός ἐστιν οὐχ ὁ μὴ ἀδικῶν a just man is not one who does no wrong, ἀλλ᾽ ὅστις ἀδικεῖν δυνάμενος μὴ βούλεται but one who, though able to do wrong, does not wish to; the sophistical doctrine, as Glaucon presents it in Plato's Πολιτεία ΙΙ Republic II, denies that such people exist, and claims that οὐδεὶς ἑκὼν δίκαιος ἀλλ᾽ ἀναγκαζόμενος no one is just willingly but under compulsion (360 C, Paley). To the real δίκαιος just man, then, blessing is foretold, cf. Plat. Πολιτ Republic. Χ 613 Α (where an exception is made: εἰ μή τι ἀναγκαῖον αὐτῶι κακὸν ἐκ προτέρας ἁμαρτίας ὑπῆρχεν unless some necessary evil from a previous error was upon him; but the rest, whatever befalls the δίκαιος just man, must end in good). The litotes οὐκ ἄνολβος not unblessed is here too to be taken more fully than the expression suggests, cf. οὐκ ἄγαν ἐλεύθερος not too free 340. — To ἀντίτολμον bold 553 Hermann's proposed conjecture παρβάταν transgressor for περαιβάδαν transgressor fits very well, only one must, if one shortens here, add in the following verse (ἄγοντα leading), which is why Hermann later kept closer to the tradition: φαμὶ I say (καὶ and) παραιβάταν τὰ πολλὰ παντόφυρτ᾽ ἄνευ δίκας a transgressor of many things, all mixed up, without justice, with a very free construction of the accusative with παραιβάταν transgressor. However, already the inferior manuscripts have περβάταν transgressor, and Dindorf recalls Sept. 743, where instead of παρβασίαν transgression Μ παραβ transgression., the inferior manuscripts have the word found in Hesiod παραιβασίαν transgression (see also Hik. 1048). Weil keeps παρβάδαν transgressor, an unattested but still understandable word; but the scholiast explains with παραβεβηκότα having transgressed, and τὸν ἀντίτολμον the bold one does not remain well independent. Ἄγοντα leading 554 Pauw inserted after παντόφυρτ all mixed up', better Weil (ἄγοντα πολλά leading many things. The verb already plays into the comparison with the ship.

On παντόφυρτα all mixed up cf. Prom. 450 ἔφυρον εἰκῆι πάντα they mixed everything at random; ἄνευ δίκας βιαίως without justice, violently belongs together, as just now ἑκὼν ἀνάγκας ἄτερ willingly, without compulsion.
On καθήσειν to lower Linwood in Paley compares Hom. ι 72 καὶ τὰ μὲν and the (ἱστία sails) ἐς νῆας κάθεμεν δείσαντες ὄλεθρον we lowered the sails into the ships, fearing destruction.
ἀκούοντας οὐδὲν hearing nothing as Ag. 396 λιτᾶν δ᾽ ἀκούει μὲν οὔτις θεῶν but no god hears prayers.

560 θερμῶι hot as Sept. 602 ναύταισι θερμοῖς καὶ πανουργίαι τινί for sailors hot and with some villainy, hot-blooded = reckless (Soph. Antig. 88) = wicked. Here for once h has the right reading, instead of the explanation θερμοεργῶι hot-working (M), even if from metrical correction. Αὐχεῖν to boast "to think wrongly" as Ag. 506 οὐ γάρ ποτ᾽ ηὔχουν for I never boasted, Prom. 688 οὔποτ᾽ ηὔχουν I never boasted etc.

Ἰδών having seen: after he has seen the revenge, which is as good as accomplished, he concerns himself no further with it; therefore not ὁρῶν seeing. Λέπαδνον Lepadnon (M) is explained in the scholia with ὑπεζευγμένον καὶ χαλινωθέντα yoked and bridled, thus derived from τὸ λέπαδνον the lepadnon 'yoke' (Ag. 217, Pers. 191); but there is no evidence for such an adjective. Musgrave and Hermann write λαπαδνόν lapadnon (= ἀλαπαδνόν alapadnon Hom.), which is also better insofar as the different images do not mix.

Ὑπερθεῖν ἄκραν to surmount the crest as Eurip. Frg. 229 οὐ γὰρ ὑπερθεῖν κύματος ἄκραν δυνάμεσθ for we are not able to surmount the crest of the wave', and already Theogn. 620 (Weckl.) ἄκρην γὰρ πενίης οὐχ ὑπερεδράμομεν for we have not outrun the crest of poverty. So the waves are already closing over him.
Δι᾿ αἰῶνος throughout his life Ag. 554, Ch. 26; to πρὶν ὄλβον before prosperity, which accompanied him throughout his life and seemed permanent.
Ἕρμα Herma Ag. 1007, explained by the ancients with ὕφαλος πέτρα underwater rock; also the δίνη whirlpool stands in relation to this.

Ἄκλαντος unwept Dindorf restored here and at Sept. 696 for -στος unlamented, cf. Kühner-Blass II, 460; on αἶστος unseen (Porson) at Ch. 396. Paley compares Homeric οἴχετ᾽ ἄϊστος ἄπυστος he went unseen, unheard of (α alpha privative 242). Third episode, part 1: 566 - (777)915. The following trial scene I can only imagine on the Areopagus, which is also named at line (688.) 693; so during the preceding stasimon a small scene change was again carried out. On the Areopagus there was no building, and all proceedings of the blood courts took place under the open sky (Antiphon 5, 11, Aristotle Πολιτ Polites. Ἀθ Athena. 57, 4), to avoid pollution by remaining in the same space; accordingly the scene is to be imagined here as well. Thus the backdrop of a temple building, which was present at the beginning and also later, had to be concealed now, just as for the first part of the Choephori (Ch. Introduction p. 20); but the ekkyklema, which last displayed the interior of the temple with the image of the goddess, could remain, and it was only necessary to draw the image back again and instead to set up seating for the Areopagites. These were, as the scholiast notes, a mute parachoregema; how many there were is not said, and indeed this council had no fixed number of members; twelve, however, as many as the chorus comprised, were fully sufficient, and this number has also been inferred from 711 ff., see below. The people, however, the corona, is present only in imagination (στρατός army, host 566); but a herald had to actually appear, and a trumpeter. These appear, like the Areopagites, in the retinue of Athena, and likewise, I think, her suppliant Orestes. The trial is only in a free manner an image or model of those taking place before the Areopagus. Athena presides and directs, which in reality the βασιλεύς king did; naturally the accuser has the first word, but of the double procedure with πρότερος former, earlier and ὕστερος λόγος later account for each party (Demosth. 23, 69) there is nothing here, rather the speeches are dramatically dissolved into dialogue between the parties. That no diomosia of the parties takes place, which existed before the Areopagus, and indeed in the most solemn manner (Dem. 23, 67 ff.), has already been pointed out (p. 122). According to the later arrangement, here, where the accused admits the deed but asserts its justice, the Areopagus would not have been competent at all, but the court at the Delphinion (Dem. 23, 74 ff.); but rightly and in accordance with tradition Aeschylus has only this one blood court, competent for all cases, founded first. The secret voting with pebbles in urns, as described here, certainly existed also in these courts, as in the ordinary ones.
Στρατός army, host 'people' here often: 569, 668, 686, 762, 889; so also Pindar, as Pyth. 2, 87 ὁ λάβρος στρατός the violent host = δῆμος people.

Κατειργάθου he was being restrained (or perhaps κατεργάθου you were being restrained, as the manuscript, cf. ἄφερκτος unrestrained Ch. 446; but εἰργάθειν to restrain Eur. Ph. 1175, κατειργάθηι he was restrained Soph. OC. 862) is as little an aorist as ἀμυνάθου you were defending 438; the middle voice is justified by the fact that the herald, as an official, belongs to the council. The model for the passage is clearly Homer Σ 503 (court scene): κήρυκες δ᾽ ἄρα λαὸν ἐρήτυον and the heralds were restraining the people (cf. also B 96 ff.).

In V. 567 there is an old variant ἤ τ᾽ οὖν or then for εἴτ᾽ οὖν or then, and the τ the' οὖν then can be compared with οὔτ᾽ οὖν neither then 412, μήτ᾽ οὖν nor then Ag. 359. 474, since this also stands in the second clause; thus the scholiast is right: ὡς μὴ ἀρκοῦντος μόνου τοῦ κήρυκος as if the herald alone were not sufficient. At the beginning the verse is mutilated: perhaps 〈τὸν ἄλλον the rest〉.. The interpreters seem to go far astray who seek in ουν then a form of οὐρανός heaven, while διάτορος piercing just as little as Prom. 76. 181 needs an addition, and the concept 'heaven' has nothing to do here at all. The anachronism in Τυρσηνικὴ σάλπιγξ Tyrrhenian trumpet is noted by the scholia; cf. Soph. Ai. 17 (Pausan. 2, 21, 3, Paley). We do not know that the trumpet had a place in the Athenian judicial system; the σαλπικτής trumpeter Dem. 16, 169 is related to the generals. On 568 cf. μυκτηροκόμπτοις πνεύμασιν πληρούμενοι filled with nostril-proud blasts Sept. 464, on 569 ὑπέρτονον βοάν over-loud shout Aristoph. Νεφ. 1154 (= Eurip. Frg. 625a Ddf., 623 N.).

Βουλευτήριον council chamber is, as at 683, 687, not the space, but the assembly itself (cf. δικαστήριον court), therefore ἡ ἐξ ᾿Αρείου πάγου the council of the Areopagus; πληροῦσθαι to be filled and πλήρης full (ἡ βουλὴ ἐπειδὴ ἦν πλήρης the council, when it was full Andok. 1, 112) are standard for the becoming full of an assembly or manning (Sept. 32 ), πληρουμένης τῆς ἐκκλησίας ), when the assembly was being filled Arist. Eccl. 89. V. 571
ἀρήγει it helps = συμφέρει it benefits Schol. (Pind. Pyth. 2, 94 φέρειν ἐλαφρῶς to bear lightly . . ζυγὸν ἀρήγει the yoke helps).

With θεσμοί ordinances the establishment of the Areopagus and specifically of the entire legal procedure before it is indicated (484, 615, 681); one must not now think that the establishment speech of Athena (681 ff.) would have to follow here immediately, but rather from the θεσμοί ordinances a part appears at once with the constituting council, for which reason at 615 Apollo addresses the council as Ἀθηναίας θεσμός the ordinance of Athena. On the one hand this concerns the whole city, for now and for all future time, 572 (αἰανῆ everlasting to 416), on the other hand it concerns the present lawsuit, which is to be conducted first: 573 καὶ τῶνδ᾽ and of these (τόνδ᾽ of this) ὅπως ἂν εὖ καταγνωσθῆι δίκη so that the case may be decided well. Compare with this below in the speech of Athena: 707 ff. ταύτην μὲν ἐξέτειν᾿ ἐμοῖς παραίνεσιν ἀστοῖσιν ἐς τὸ λοιπόν this advice I have extended to my citizens for the future; ὀρθοῦσθαι δὲ χρὴ καὶ ψῆφον αἴρειν καὶ διαγνῶναι δίκην but you must stand upright and cast your vote and decide the case. – Since καταγιγνώσκειν δίκην to decide a case against someone ordinarily means not 'to recognize exactly' but 'to decide to someone's disadvantage', Paley demands διαγνωσθῆι to be decided (cf. 709), for which, however, εὖ well is not the correct adverb. Cf. Aristoph. Ἱππ Hipp.. 46 (Wakef.), Xen. Oecon. 2, 18.

Τῶνδε of these is better than τόνδε of this, with δίκη case (of Orestes and the Erinyes); the πόλιν τε and the city corresponding to καὶ τῶνδ᾽ ὅπως and of these, so that is indeed freer in construction, but still understandable: and for the present, so that the lawsuit of the parties present may be accurately decided.

Meanwhile Apollo has appeared (cf. his promise at 81 ff.), and the chorus wants to drive him away. In response, Apollo declares that on the one hand he is a witness (cf. Athena's summons to the parties at 485f.), which he justifies by his close relationship to the accused as his ἱκέτης suppliant, and on the other hand a legal advocate, who conducts Orestes' case as his own, as the author (αἴτιος cause) of the matricide. The scholiast does not explain quite correctly: σύνδικοί εἰσιν οἷς ἴσον μέτεστιν ἐν τῆι δίκηι τῆς αἰτίας syndikoi are those who have an equal share in the case of the accusation, for according to 761 the Erinyes are σύνδικοι syndikoi of the mother, and in Athens this is the name for legal advocates, whom, for example, the people elect for a contested law, Dem. 20, 146, each tribe for an accused belonging to it, Andok. 1, end, Dem. 23, 206 (Meier-Schömann-Lipsius Att. Proc. 123f.).

At V. 576 f. the tradition is corrupted: ἔστι γὰρ δόμων for he is of the house (δήμων of the people M first) ἱκέτης ὅδ᾽ ἀνὴρ καὶ δόμων this man is a suppliant and of the house (δόμος house M first) ἐφέστιος at the hearth (thus and -έστιως of the hearth M, -εστίων of the hearths f g h) ἐμῶν my.

Ἐφέστιος of the hearth is found constructed in both ways: σῶν δόμων ἐφέστιον the hearth of your house (Hik. 365. 503), and δόμους ἐφεστίους houses with hearths Ag. 851 (Sept. 73). Schütz changes the first δόμων of the house to νόμωι by custom (cf. above 473), but is ἐστὶν ἐφέστιος is at the hearth factually correct? It seems better, with H. L. Ahrens, to change the second δόμων of the house to μυχῶν of the inner chambers (cf. 39. 170. 180), and then to adopt ἐφεστίων of the hearths.

Καθάρσιος purifier 63. 449. Αἰτίαν ἔχω I am held responsible can be understood as at 99 'I am accused', see V. 199, but also 'I have the guilt'. Then Apollo turns to Athena, who according to Attic usage is εἰσαγωγεύς introducer of the trial (Meier-Schömann-Lipsius 45, 13); this procedure (present tense) may now go forward, and finally, according to the wisdom of the goddess (ὡς ἐπίστασαι as you know 667, ὅπως ἐπίστασαι in whatever way you know Prom. 374; ὅπως how 'however'), the trial may be brought to an end and decided (aorist τήνδε κυρῶσαι δίκην to bring this case to fulfillment by the judges). On ἐπίστᾶι he knows see on 86. Thereupon Athena gives the Erinyes the floor and sets up the general (though self-evident) principle, in words strongly reminiscent of the opening formula of later Attic court speeches, Lysias 12, 3 πειράσομαι ὑμᾶς ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὡς ἂν δύνωμαι δι᾽ ἐλαχίστων διδάξαι I will try to instruct you from the beginning as best I can in the fewest words. 585–608. The Erinyes correspond to the (later and certainly also customary in Aeschylus' time) form of an accusation only in the one respect that they too promise brevity; of ἐξ ἀρχῆς διδάσκειν to teach from the beginning, however, nothing is to be noticed, nor of a connected exposition, since in place of the entire accusation speech comes the questioning of the accused. Such questioning also occurs in later court speeches, only not as the main thing or replacing the accusation (so Lysias 12, 25); since Orestes now not only answers with yes and no but defends himself, the whole hearing for and against is already given in essence. When afterwards Apollo appears as defender, the Erinyes in between also make their arguments, and likewise at greater length; thus there are two hearings, only to be compared with accusation and defense insofar as in the first the accusation has the first word, in the second the defense. So as in Aristophanic dispute scenes: in the Clouds first the δίκαιος λόγος just argument presents his case, with objections from the ἄδικος λόγος unjust argument, and then the latter with corresponding participation of the opponent, and in the Frogs Aeschylus and Euripides likewise. Since the promised brevity in V. 585 is contrasted with the great number of the Erinyes, Weil has rightly inferred that the individual ones speak one after another: the first with two verses, then ten with one each, then the last with two. Thus the number twelve of the chorus results here, as in Agamemnon 1348 ff., unless one assumes there, which seems to me fundamentally wrong, that the three choreuts who previously heard the cries of woe from the palace and initiated the deliberation are thereby dispensed from expressing their opinion. For the Erinyes everything actually reduces to the question of fact, yet they also go somewhat into the motives, according to Athena's instruction at 426.
586 ἐν μέρει in turn 198. 436. So with this the stichomythia is indicated, which here too, as at 198. 415, is introduced with three verses.

- 588 δ d’ is inappropriate; γ g’ is correct (Ag. 368, Pers. 738). On 589 cf. schol.; hence ἀτρίακτος unwrestled Ch. 339. τριακτήρ wrestler Ag. 171. Also Plato Phaedr. 256 B (Paley): τῶν τριῶν παλαισμάτων τῶν ὡς ἀληθῶς Ὀλυμπικῶν ἓν νενικήκασιν they have won one of the three truly Olympic wrestling bouts. 590. The dative as with λέγειν to speak. 591: according to the scholiast, by ὅπως how the motives are meant, and Orestes misunderstands; but ὅπως how quite unambiguously denotes the manner of the murder, on which something also depended, cf. 629 ff. — 592 Orestes answers unshaken and confident, as he behaves throughout the drama. The expression χειρὶ πρὸς δέρην τεμών cutting with his hand at the throat is somewhat peculiar, but Homeric βεβλήκει πρὸς στῆθος he had struck at the chest (Δ 108) and the like offer ample comparison. 595 “Incredible! The μάντις prophet (169) and ἐξηγητής expounder of holy law commands this?” ᾿Εξηγοῦ Expound! also stands at 609; Plat. Πολιτ. IV, 427 C οὗτος γὰρ δήπου ὁ θεὸς περὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις πάτριος ἐξηγητὴς ἐν μέσωι τῆς γῆς ἐπὶ τοῦ ὀμφαλοῦ καθήμενος ἐξηγεῖται for this god, I suppose, is the ancestral expounder for all men in such matters, seated at the navel of the earth, and he expounds.

596 δεῦρό γ hither' αἰεί always is found besides in the unknown verse which the scholiast cites, also Eur. Ph. 1209 δεῦρ᾽ ἀεὶ γὰρ εὐτυχεῖς for you always fare well here, Οr. 1663, Med. 670, Arist. Lys. 1135 (Weckl.); on the schol. cf. Harpocration ἀεί always (Stanley). “I have not fared badly, but am still safe.” 601 πέμψει he will send for πέμπει he sends is restored according to the scholiast. With this Orestes brings the second point of his justification (again at 605): I had to avenge my father.
602 πέπισθι trust like ἐπέπιθμεν we trusted Homer; ἴσθι know, δείδιχθι fear (Kühner-Blass II, 402, see Nic. Alex. 443 Schneider after II). - 603

προσβολάς attacks: cf. κακὸν προσέβαλεν πόλει he brought evil upon the city Pers. 781; thus like πόλει πρόστριμμ᾽ ἄφερτον ἐνθείς inflicting an unbearable stain upon the city Ag. 395 (Weil). Μιασμάτοιν two pollutions Elmsley writes according to the rule that δυοῖν two combines only with dual, so also in A. in ten examples (only here and Ag. 1389 plural transmitted).

— 604 Schol. πανούργως φασί they say cunningly, μὴ ἡμᾶς δίδασκε do not teach us, ἀλλὰ τοὺς δικαστάς but the judges, and of course in τοὺς δικάζοντας those who judge lies that the chorus does not care what Clytemnestra has done. With 605 now Orestes brings also the third point of his justification: Clytemnestra was a husband-murderer, which is no less bad than mother-murder, see the discussion between Apollo and the Erinyes 211 ff.

606 τοιγάρ therefore 901, Ch. 894 and often: so you must pay for your murder with death, as she paid for hers; as long as you live, we pursue you. Ἐλευθέρα φόνου free from murder (M) like ἐλεύθερος πημάτων free from troubles Ch. 1060, but the sense requires the dative (Schütz).
606 ἐν αἵματι in blood within the blood relationship, as one says ἐν μένει in might (Eurip. Alk. 904). — 607

πῶς γάρ σ᾽ ἔθρεψεν for how did she nourish you: namely, if not with her blood (Weil); this sense, however, only emerges with ἔθρεψ᾽ ἄν would have nourished (Hik. 586 τίς γὰρ ἂν κατέπαυσεν Ἥρας νόσους for who would have stopped the diseases of Hera, "who else"). On ἐντὸς ζώνης within the girdle cf. Ch. 992; ἀπεύχηι you pray away strong for ἀπαρνῆι you deny (Schol.). With this the accusation closes emphatically. 609—613 Orestes. The defense begins also without a special granting of the floor, since there had already been dialogue: Orestes calls upon Apollo to give testimony (594) that he had ordered the deed, and then to instruct about the right of the deed, which is a position more worthy of this god than that of a σύνδικος advocate. Σφε them singular as at 234.—611
ὥσπερ ἐστὶν as it is: cf. Ag. 1171 τὸ μὴ πόλιν μὲν ὥσπερ οὖν ἔχει παθεῖν not to have the city suffer as it does.

612 δίκαιως justly cannot be construed, whereas it stands correctly at 615; δίκαιον just . . αἷμα blood can be said just as well as δίκαιος φόνος just murder Demosth. 23, 74 (since αἷμα blood = φόνος murder, 752. 359 etc.), and because of δρᾶσαι to do preceding, an adverb could easily be set. Ὡς τούτοις φράσω As I will tell these again presupposes Orestes as the defender; in fact, however, he now says nothing more until 744. 614-673 Defense by Apollo, with interjections from the Erinyes. Apollo is thus now really an advocate and behaves somewhat as such a one behaved. Did the role of exegete, which Orestes just assigned to the god, seem to A. too lofty even for tragedy? We would rather say this: Apollo would then have had to teach why this murder was just, and (what is the same thing) why he had commanded it to Orestes, and which murder is just at all and which not; but then the matter was actually decided by an infallible mouth, and no longer a legal dispute, for which judge could have rebelled against it? But the result was to come out differently: equal number of votes against equal, and as the myth is, gods stood against gods; so instead of the exegete, the advocate now speaks, heightening and appealing to the feelings more than clarifying the question, and finally even remarkably sophistically. He speaks four times, at considerable length; the interjections of the chorus comprise only 3, 4 and 5 verses.

The first two verses are the proem for everything. He wants to speak justly, as is fitting before such a court (θεσμός ordinance on 571), and to say nothing false, which as a seer he may not. Now he traces with all emphasis all his oracles back to Zeus (on 19), without further expressly testifying that he gave this to Orestes (μαρτυρήσων about to testify 576, μαρτύρησον testify 609; cf. μαρτυρεῖ testifies 594, and what Ap. already said at 579f.); thereby he gives his pronouncements the highest conceivable authority, but - on the opposite side stand still older deities.
For κελεύσει he will command the correct change is κελεῦσαι to command (Hermann), Kühner-Gerth Synt. II, 427 f.

620 πιφαύσκω I make known (Pers. 661, Ag. 23, Ch. 279; as Soph. and Eurip., Ddf. Lex. 290) is otherwise as in Homer, "(to) indicate", here synonymous with κελεύω I command, and also constructed so. Ὕμμε you (pl.) is attested in A. only here (in Soph. Ant. 846 in a lyric passage); also of the 1st person only the dative ἄμμι us Sept. 156 occurs in a dochmiac verse (Ddf. Lex. 337. 100).

Ὅρκος Oath: so also no oath of judges; cf. what Pylades says at Ch. 901f.. 622-624 Chorus. The Erinyes pretend that they cannot believe in such a command of Zeus (ὡς λέγεις σύ as you say, in contrast to Zeus), since father and mother would then be treated quite unequally. The argument is the same as that already put forward at 603. On πράξαντα having done cf. Ch. 511, Pers. 476. Τιμὰς νέμειν to distribute honors differently than at 747:

νέμειν to distribute = νομίζειν to consider, and it is rather to be compared with 423 ὅπου τὸ χαίρειν μηδαμοῦ νομίζεται where joy is nowhere considered, thus = to hold in no account. Wecklein cites Soph. Tr. 56: εἰ πατρὸς νέμοι τιν᾽ ὤραν if he paid any heed to his father. 625-639 Apollo. The advocate now in fact maintains that the father and husband as such has greater claims to consideration, especially if he is such a one as Agamemnon, king and commander of the army. The spirited exposition, which at the same time brings out the treachery of the murder, but yet allows the main point, that it is his own wife who is the murderess, to recede very much into the background, is subject to what Cicero says in the Pro Milone (§ 17): non alio facinore clari homines, alio obscuri necantur: intersit inter vitae dignitatem summorum atque infimorum; mors quidem illata per scelus isdem et poenis teneatur et legibus; nisi forte magis erit parricida, si qui consularem patrem, quam si quis humilem necarit. 625

ταὐτόν the same: as when a woman is killed. Τι what? belongs to οὐ not like Prom. 268 οὐ μήν τι not at all. On τιμαλφεῖν to honor see above on 15; διόσδοτος given by Zeus also Sept. 948 (Ag. 1391 according to Porson's emendation); besides only Pindar P. 8, 96, Frg. 137. The scholion must refer to this, that Epicharmus mocked Aeschylus for his constant use of this ὄνομα name; for τιμαλφεῖν to honor is a ῥῆμα verb. The σκῆπτρον scepter of the Pelopids already in Iliad B 100 ff.

627 γυναικός of a woman of a woman (not 'his wife'); θούριοι rushing and θοῦρος rushing are not rare in Aeschylus, e.g. Ag. 112 θούριος ὄρνις rushing bird, Sept. 42 θούριοι λοχαγέται rushing leaders, roughly 'warlike'.

629 ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἀκούσηι but so that he may hear κτέ etc..: he holds the attention. On 631 cf. Ag. 602 ἀπὸ στρατείας ἄνδρα σώσαντος θεοῦ πύλας ἀνοῖξαι to open the gates of the god who saved the man from the campaign; here ἀπὸ στρατείας from the campaign is combined with δεδεγμένη having received.
