Ἠμποληκότα having traded (properly 'having done business') = πεπραγότα having done, as Soph. Αi. 978 ἆρ᾽ ἠμπόληκας ὥσπερ ἡ φάτις κρατεῖ have you traded as the report prevails?, for which Lobeck cites from Hippocrates Π. νούσων of diseases Δ 12 (Littré VII, 580, c. 49) κάλλιον ἐμπολήσει ὁ ἄνθρωπος the man will trade more nobly = (as it is called elsewhere) βέλτιον ἀπαλλάσσει he departs better. Thus (Schütz) he had accomplished most things for the good, at least in the eyes of the right-minded (the contrast is Clytemnestra), as Ch. 109 φθέγγου χέουσα κεδνὰ τοῖσιν εὔφροσιν speak, pouring out good words to the well-minded, and (what Schömann compared) Soph. Ant. 904 καίτοι σ᾽ ἐγὼ ᾿τίμησα τοῖς φρονοῦσιν εὖ and yet I honored you among those who think well. The comparatives like ἀμείνων better (ἄμεινόν ἐστι it is better 'is good') and κρείσσων stronger are often used without an expressed comparison (Homer A 22 σαώτερος ὡς κε νέηαι safer that you may return, where the scholiast notes: τὸ σαώτερος ἀντὶ τοῦ ἁπλοῦ the 'safer' instead of the simple). Ἄμεινον Better or ἀμείνον᾽ better doubtful. For the thought compare what the herald says at Ag. 551ff.. So after this verse one should not assume a lacuna with Hermann; but in 633 we cannot get through without a change. The scholiast read δροίτηι in the tub in the dative, to ἐπὶ τέρματι at the end he supplies τῶν λουτρῶν of the baths; about περῶντι crossing he says nothing. Now it seems that περισκηνοῦν to encamp around fits better with δροίτηι in the tub than with a περῶντι crossing lying in αὐτῶι to him: the canopy was set up over the tub, apparently as a further honor which the wife had apparently thought of only afterwards; therefore it was also such a costly garment. And then the frame fell over, seemingly by chance, and so on. If one now writes περῶντος of one crossing, and takes κἀπὶ τέρματι and at the end as the scholiast does, no difficulty remains; also ἐπὶ τέρματι at the end and ἀτέρμονι endless now form a contrast: only seemingly was he through.

V. 634 had an x, because of the elision of the i of περὶ around and because of the συζυγία conjugation (conjugation, i.e. -άω -aō or -όω -oō) of the verb (Schol.); there were (as M shows) the readings παρε pare-- and περε pere-- and further -νωσεν -nōsen and (lemma of the Schol.) -νησεν -nēsen, as indeed elsewhere σκηνάω skēnaō and σκηνόω skēnoō go side by side. Περεσκήνωσεν Pereskēnōsen is necessary: πέροδος perodos Pindar, περεβάλοντο perebalonto Ai. Agam. 1147 (περιβ perib-. Turneb.).
Ἄνδρα Man here probably 'her husband'; δαίδαλος cunningly wrought also Pind. Nem. 4, 59.

636 As before at 629f., so now afterwards the horror of the deed is rhetorically emphasized. Cf. Ag. 1628 to Aegisthus: ἀνδρὶ στρατηγῶι τόνδ᾽ ἐπόρσυνας μόρον for a man who was a general you prepared this fate;

— 638 ταύτην τοιαύτην verlangt nach ἀνδρὸς μὲν durchaus ein δέ, und auch ταύτην ist unpassend; also gut Weil τὴν δ᾽ αὖ τοιαύτην (vgl. 954 u. s.) Und doch hat Apollon gar nicht alles gesagt, und von dem Ehebruch mit Aigisthos ganz geschwiegen; diese verächtliche Persönlichkeit kommt in der ganzen Tragödie auch nicht andeutungsweise vor. Λεώς von den Areopagiten wie 681; zu δηχθῆι vgl. Pers. 846.

Chor 640–643. Nun geht die Argumentation ganz von der Hauptsache ab: indem die Erinyen auf 616 ff. zurückgreifen, wiederholen sie, was sie 622 ff. gesagt (τῶι σῶι λόγωι wie dort ὡς λέγεις σύ), aber mit einer scharfen Spitze gegen (den mythologischen) Zeus, der doch selbst seinen Vater gefesselt hat. Der Scholiast wehrt die Meinung ab, als sei es auf Schmähung des Zeus abgesehen; Apollons Behauptung nur, daſs Zeus diesen Spruch gegeben, werde bekämpft. Ich denke im Gegenteil, daſs die „alten Göttinnen" ebenso wie 719 den Zeus nur äuſserlich schonen. Früher galt der Vater so wenig, daſs Zeus seinen eignen gefesselt hat. Und dies Argument scheint ihnen so wichtig, daſs sie die Richter eigens auffordern, dies ja zu hören. Vgl. zu 657 ff. Μαρτύρεσθαι mit Inf. in abgeschwächter Bedeutung, = dringend auffordern, wie Hdt. 5, 92, 7, Thuk. 6, 29, 2 ἐπιμαρτύρεσθαι steht.

Der Hieb hat gesessen, darum wird Apollon zum ersten Male heftig und gibt seinerseits den Gefühlen der jungen Götter gegen die alten Ausdruck, ähnlich wie oben 179 ff. Sein Argument aber: Fesseln sind lösbar, Blut ist nicht zurückzurufen, gilt natürlich nicht weniger gegen Orestes als für ihn, vgl. 653.—644 κνώδαλον Ch. 586 u. öfter;
στύγη θεῶν Ch. 1028.

V. 645 ist Weils πέδαι μὲν ἂν λυθεῖεν ebenso möglich wie Dindorfs (πέδας —) λύσειας (dies wie εὑρήσεις 698). Zeus hat doch den Kronos und die Titanen befreit, nach dem Prometheus λυόμενος schon zu Herakles’ Zeiten; also das überlieferte λύσειεν „er kann lösen", von Zeus, scheint für die Sache zu wenig, und wie auch der Zusatz zeigt (ἔστι τοῦδ᾽ ἄκος κτἑ.), auch Menschen können das; also besser auch vorher allgemein λυθεῖεν oder λύσειας. Man kann fragen: weshalb wird nicht die Lösung direkt ausgesagt? War das etwa zu sehr Geheimlehre? In den Eumeniden gibt es nur gewöhnliche Mythologie, wie sich am stärksten 728 zeigt.

Μηχανὴ λυτήριος wie μηχανὴ δραστήριος Sept. 1041. Der Gedanke von 647 f. steht auch Ag. 1018 ff. τὸ δ᾽ ἐπὶ γᾶν πεσὸν ἅπαξ usw., wo τίς ἂν πάλιν ἀγκαλέσαιτ᾿ ἐπαείδων dem τούτων ἐπωιδάς hier entspricht.

V. 651 f. are often misunderstood, while the sense is simple: in all else his omnipotence is unbounded, and effortlessly he transforms things, this way and that, as he wills (Schütz, Paley), see Hik. 99 πᾶν ἄπονον δαιμονίων every effortless work of the gods· †ἥμενον ἄνω φρόνημά πως αὐτόθεν ἐξέπραξεν ἔμπας ἑδράνων ἀφ᾽ ἁγνῶν seated above, he somehow accomplishes his purpose from there, seated on his holy throne. And οὐδὲν ἀσθμαίνων μένει he remains without panting (dative) is exactly like Sept. 393 ἵππος χαλινῶν ὡς κατασθμαίνων μένει (μένος as a horse, panting against the reins, remains (strength also Eum. 128. 832. 840).

The Erinyes somewhat connect with what was last said: αἷμ᾽ ἐκχέας πέδοι having shed blood on the ground like αἷμ᾿ ἀνασπάσηι κόνις the dust may draw up the blood 647, and make vivid the seemingly impossible consequences of an acquittal.

Ὑπερδικεῖν to plead on behalf of (Plat. Phaid. 86 E with gen.; Phryn. Bk. An. 68, 24 explained with ὑπέρ τινος εἰπεῖν δίκην to speak a case on behalf of someone) compares with ὑπερστατεῖν τινος to stand over someone Hik. 342; even closer stands Soph. Ai. 1346 σὺ ταῦτ᾽ Ὀδυσσεῦ τοῦδ᾽ ὑπερμαχεῖς ἐμοί you, Odysseus, are fighting on my behalf in this (as in general the Ajax offers many parallels to the Oresteia). But φεύγειν to flee does not fit where 'acquittal' is the sense; also at γάρ for Casaubonus and Schütz rightly took offense; so Dittenberger's πῶς τἀποφεύγειν how to escape is good. —
Πέδοι on the ground 267. 479; on βωμοῖς altars cf. Ch. 293;
φρατέρες brothers in A. only here;
χέρνιψ lustral water Soph. OT. 240; see also Ag. 1037.

I have already noted in the introduction to the Choeph. p. 12 that the last argument of Apollo seems directed against the old view, according to which the bond of the child with the mother, which was not in doubt, was considered the most sacred, while with the higher culture that followed from the introduction of marriage, the father received at least equal standing. Cf. Telemachus' jest α a 215: μήτηρ μέν τέ μέ φησι τοῦ ἔμμεναι my mother says I am his· αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε οὐκ οἶδ᾽ but I myself do not know· οὐ γάρ πώ τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω for no one yet has recognized his own offspring, and Clearchus in Athenaeus XIII 555 D (cited by Wecklein): ἐν δὲ Ἀθήναις πρῶτος Κέκροψ μίαν ἑνὶ ἔζευξεν in Athens, Cecrops first yoked one woman to one man, ἀνέδην τὸ πρότερον οὐσῶν τῶν συνόδων καὶ κοινογαμίων ὄντων since previously their unions were promiscuous and marriages were communal. διὸ καὶ ἔδοξέ τισιν διφυὴς νομισθῆναι for which reason some thought him to be of double nature, οὐκ εἰδότων τῶν πρότερον διὰ τὸ πλῆθος τὸν πατέρα since those of earlier times did not know their father because of the multitude. Cf. above on 640 ff. The theory that the father is the true begetter is also clearly found in Euripides, who will have taken it from here and uses it in the Or. (552 ff.) for the same purpose, see also (Schütz) Frg. 1048. Anaxagoras (see Wilamowitz Übers. p. 43, 1) seems to have taught the same, Aristot. De gen. anim. Δ 1 p. 763 e 31 ff. (Diels Vorsokrat. 325); but another testimony contradicts this (ibid. no. 111). Paley also cites Plut. Quaest. Conv. IV, p. 651 C: τὸ σπέρμα μὴ προγεγονέναι τὸ γόνιμον διὰ κατάψυξιν the seed had not previously become fertile because of cooling (lacunose), ἀλλ᾽ ὕλην μόνον καὶ τροφὴν παρέχειν τῶι ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄρρενος but provides only matter and nourishment to that from the male. Actually the same view lies in the Attic ἐπ᾿ ἀρότωι παίδων γνησίων for the sowing of legitimate children: the earth, with which the mother is compared, is after all only τροφὸς κύματος νεοσπόρου nurse of the newly sown wave, and we have this clearly developed in the papyrus fragment from Aeschylus' Europe: καὶ τρὶς πονοῦσα τοὺς γυναικείους πόνους ἐκαρτέρησ᾽ ἄρουρα κοὐκ ἐπέμψατο τὸ μὴ ᾿ξενεγκεῖν σπέρμα γενναίου πατρός and thrice enduring the pains of women she endured as a field and did not send forth the seed of a noble father.
657 μάθε learn to the Erinys, whom he wishes to instruct better.

658 the tradition is divided between κεκλημένου called (M) and -μένη remains (fgh). Apollo wants to ascribe the τίκτειν to bear exclusively to the father, so τέκνον child must also be referred to him and not to the mother, and μήτηρ τέκνου mother of a child in the sense of "her child" is not a proper expression. Therefore κεκλημένου called. On the other hand, the expression μήτηρ mother could in no way be challenged as improper. As for the general usage, in A. himself τίκτειν to bear is hardly ever used otherwise than of the mother, as at v. 666; Ch. 690 τὸν τεκόντα the one who begot stands in relation to τοὺς τεκόντας the parents parents 681; πατέρων τε καὶ τεκόντων of fathers and parents 329 can indeed only be referred to the father; besides he has τοκῆας parents parents often (270, 497, etc.). Homer, however, has τίκτειν to bear also of the father, and famously Plato in Diotima's speech Sympos. 206 ff. τίκτειν to bear (τόκος birth) and γεννᾶν to beget as synonyms, whereas Euripides, precisely in the passage of the Orestes, ascribes the τίκτειν to bear to the mother, the φυτεύειν to plant to the father (Weckl.; on τεκών the one who begot, τοκῆας parents in Soph. and Eur. see P. Menge De poetarum scaen. sermone [Gtg. 1906] 34 ff.) - 659 κῦμα wave = κύημα embryo, Ch. 128; cf. ἐγκύμων pregnant generally.

660 θρώισκων leaping the spelling correctly demanded by Herodian, which the Medicean does not preserve here, but does at Ch. 846 and Pers. 457. Hesychius: θρώσκων κνώδαλα leaping beasts· ἐκθορίζων καὶ σπερματίζων ejaculating and emitting seed, γεννῶν begetting. Αἰσχύλος Ἀμυμώνηι Aeschylus in Amymone (Frg. 13); cf. θορός semen Hdt. 2, 93 and others.

”Ἔρνος shoot again 666, Ag. 1525 ἐμὸν ἐκ τοῦδ᾽ ἔρνος ἀερθέν my shoot raised from this one (likewise other poets); with ἅπερ ξένωι ξένη just as a stranger to a stranger one must think of guest-friends living spatially separated and a deposit (schol.). Οἷσι to whom refers to both parents and is not to be changed into αἶσι to whom; on the missing ἄν would see on 211.
662 ff. Apollo continues to address the Erinys;

δείξω I will show can actually be understood. He now shows awareness of his superiority; he and Athena belong together as children of Zeus, the new and better ruler, and from the reference to Pallas he turns directly to her. The gap before 665 seems clear, because of οὐδ᾽ nor and Aeschylus. μ not because in fact something more than the single v. 665 is required here; on the other hand, that 663 πατὴρ μὲν ἂν κτἑ a father might, etc. stands without an expressed contrast (Ddf. Lex. p. 210) does not compel the assumption of a second (Weil) after 666. Rather, if it continued after 666: ἄνευ δὲ πατρὸς τέκνον οὐκ εἴη ποτ᾿ ἄν but without a father there could never be a child (this is the sense Weil wants, see Eur. Or. 547), that would tear apart a close connection.
666 θεός goddess certainly feminine, as at 883 and occasionally elsewhere; θεά goddess (671) is more common and would be clearer here (Weil).

looks like a captatio, but is addressed to the presiding goddess and not to the Areopagus, and is meant to emphasize the harmonious cooperation of the two deities. At the same time the conclusion of the speech is clearly marked, as with an epilogue, and accordingly Athena now closes the proceedings. If one has seen an argument ἔξω τοῦ πράγματος outside the matter in the verses and recalled that such were forbidden before the Areopagus (cf. on 674), there is still a long way from that to deleting verses 667–673 as an insertion made at a revival after Aeschylus's death (so Weil). Ending at 666, Apollo's defense would be without any conclusion. — 667
ὡς ἐπίσταμαι as I know: see on 581; not as much as ὅσον δύναμαι as much as I can (schol.), but confidently and firmly (ὡς as, not ὅπως so that).
— 670 ff. Reference to the alliance between Athens and Argos, 762 ff.
— 672 Τάδε these things belongs to τὰ πιστά the pledges (alliance, Ag. 631), τῶνδε of these to ἐπισπόρους future generations. 674–680, conclusion of the proceedings.

Κελεύω I order has rightly been changed by Robortellus to κελεύσω I will order, because it contradicts 708; that Athena does not want to force a conclusion but only proposes it is clearly shown by 678. Kirchhoff and Weil even make the sentence a complaint, and κελεύσω I will order into the subjunctive. Athena may indeed actually follow the custom of the Areopagus, allowing nothing ἔξω τοῦ πράγματος outside the matter, by cutting it off immediately.
Ἀπὸ γνώμης from judgment see on 488 f.; Stanley compares Plut. Mor. 44 DE ἀπὸ γνώμης from judgment (ἀκούειν to hear, of judges). — 676

ἡμῖν μέν for us: the contrast is the other party; so again a μέν on the one hand without δέ on the other hand (663). In πᾶν τετόξευται βέλος every arrow has been shot ἅλις λελεγμένων enough of words is confirmed (Wecklein);

μένω δ᾽ ἀκοῦσαι I wait to hear etc. not without a threat, cf. 711 etc. (μένω I wait with infinitive as at 732, Homer Il. 4.247, α a 422). The question at 678 must of course be addressed to the other party, for whom Apollo answers more appropriately than Orestes; so at 679 ΑΠ Apollo instead of ΧΟ Chorus, rightly Karsten.

Τιθεῖσα placing = ποιοῦσα making as so often, without any relation to the θεσμός ordinance at 681, since the question is only: end or not, and the answer corresponds. Logically it should be: πῶς τιθῶ how shall I place, ἵνα πρὸς ὑμῶν ἄμομφος ὦ so that I may be blameless in your eyes; but so also interwoven Ch. 14, see there. —

679 ὧν ἠκούσατε of what you have heard, i.e. what it is not necessary to repeat. The expression is common, with various shades: Ag. 1287 πράξασαν ὡς ἔπραξεν having done as she did, Soph. OC. 273 ἱκόμην ἵν᾿ ἱκόμην I came where I came, etc., Wecklein on Ag. 1170.

The surprise that this institution is only now being established, although it was already announced at 571 ff., led Kirchhoff to want to move it to after 573 (which is clearly impossible because of the conclusion at 708 ff.), and Wecklein to bracket it from beginning to end as interpolated here (while originally something similar stood after 573). If such assumptions are necessary, one will still prefer to try to come to terms with what is transmitted, and can do so quite well, cf. on 571. The court is first convened for this case, then it is to become a permanent institution; this case, then, is first submitted to it for due cognizance (573), and it now has to function and decide for the first time; at this point belongs the address to it, which only further on, as the goddess establishes it for the future, becomes an address to the whole people. For Ἀττικὸς λεώς Attic people (cf. 638) . . κρίνοντες judging 681 f. are the judges alone. After 682 Hermann (Dindorf) places verses 704-6, which is, however, inadmissible; for after them 683 f. would be quite idle. Dindorf, to be sure, declares these together with the following up to 699 to be an interpolation. One is not obliged to refute all such complicated hypotheses 1), but may regard them as refuted if what is actually transmitted proves tenable. In this, there is a close connection between 682 and 683: πρώτας δίκας κρίνοντες ἔσται δὲ καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν judging the first cases, and it will be for the future as well –, with the same connection as already appeared twice, 483 f. and 571 ff.: immediate purpose and permanent institution. I do not think there can be any doubt about Canter's emendation αἰεὶ δικαστῶν always of judges 684 for αἰεὶ δ᾽ ἑκάστων always of each; but thus δικαστῶν of judges agrees with δίκας cases 682, ἀεί always however with εἰς ἅπαντα χρόνον for all time 484 and ἐς τὸν αἰανῆ χρόνον for eternal time 572; in addition βουλευτήριον council chamber to 570, and στρατῶι for the army to 569.

Αἰγέως of Aegeus, however, fits with Θησέως of Theseus 686, and this with Θησέως τόκοις to the children of Theseus 402 and χθονός Θησῆιδος of the land of Theseus 1025 f. I have already pointed out earlier that the poet presupposes in Athens a kind of democracy, namely the one founded by Theseus (see on 402). 1) See also Weil, Revue des études grecques 1888, p. 12, p. 10*. Now if further, from 685 onward, an archaeology of the Areopagus is given, this agrees with the archaeology of the Delphic prologue, and indeed also in character insofar as here and there the legends that reported strife between gods are set aside. The legend of the Areopagus is given by Euripides, who certainly did not invent it, El. 1258 ff., I.T. 945 ff.: Ἄρειος πάγος Hill of Ares is named from the fact that Ares, who had killed Halirrhothios, son of Poseidon, was judged here by the gods themselves. In place of this Aeschylus sets the legend of the Amazons, who as daughters of Ares had sacrificed to him here, and here he perhaps innovates, since nowhere else does the Areopagus appear as occupied and fortified by the Amazons. On the battles between Athenians and Amazons, from which panegyric rhetoric as well as the plastic and pictorial arts so gladly took material, Plutarch treats precisely in Theseus ch. 27, especially after Cleidemus; according to him the Amazons had their camp in the region of the Pnyx, which is at least adjacent to the Areopagus, but one reads nothing of a foundation of a city, even if the battles lasted some months. Yet Stanley cites Etym. M. Ἄρειος πάγος Hill of Ares and Eustath. on Dionys. Perieg. 653, where the name is derived from the fact that the Amazons, daughters of Ares, had come there on their expedition (thus somewhat differently than here). What Aeschylus actually says, however, must first be examined. The sentence beginning with πάγον δ᾽ Ἄρειον the hill of Ares runs anacoluthically, and one cannot even see on what, according to the first intention, this accusative should depend; since now also the name Ἄρειος of Ares is explained only at 690, where it occurs again, it has been conjectured that the first time it crept in erroneously, in place of the verb or participle governing the accusative. Nearest at hand is πάγον δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἕξει and he will hold the hill, from which the corruption could easily arise; cf. δ᾽ ἄρα and then Sept. 646, Pers. 568 (ἄρα then pointing to the present appearance).

To relate the Θησέως κατὰ φθόνον Theseus' [deed] out of envy (686) to something like the rape of Antiope seems to me inadmissible; rather, this must find its explanation in what follows, where something is corrupt in καὶ πόλιν νεόπτολιν τῆνδ᾽ ὑψίπυργον ἀντεπύργωσαν τότε and they built a high-towered new city against this city then. Theseus had, through his συνοικισμός synoecism (political unification), created a new great Athens, a πόλις νεόπτολις new-founded city, which naturally also included the Acropolis, but not the Areopagus; out of envy at this came the Amazons, from whom Theseus had abducted Antiope, and built high bulwarks against it, precisely also on the Areopagus, from which, according to Hdt. VIII, 52, the Persians in 480 besieged the Acropolis opposite. To obtain this sense, one must write πόλει city (Orelli) νεοπτόλει new-founded, from which a τῆνδ᾽ ὑψίπυργον this high-towered [city] is supplied to πόλιν city. Objection has also been taken to τότε then (πόλει city for it Weil); but the adverb probably points to the different present, when this city was again destroyed.

Πόλει νεοπτόλει city new-founded and ὑψίπυργον ἀντεπύργωσαν high-towered they built against can be compared with ἄπολιν Ἰλίου πόλιν city of Ilium without a city 457, ἀνήμερον untamed . . ἡμερωμένην tamed 14, παρθένου φίλας φίλοι dear friends of a dear maiden 999, etc.; for ἀντιπυργοῦν building towers against Paley compares Eurip. Bakch. 1097 ἀντίπυργον ἐπιβᾶσαι πέτραν having mounted the rock that faces the enemy.
Ἐν δὲ τῶι And on the: dwelling on this;

σέβας awe (700) 'what inspires awe'; on σέβας awe and φόβος fear as opposites see Ch. 54 ff.; but they can also be taken together, for which Wecklein recalls ἵνα γὰρ δέος for where there is fear, ἔνθα καὶ αἰδώς there is also reverence (Cypria in Plato Euthyphr. 12 A) and Homer O 657 ἴσχε γὰρ αἰδὼς καὶ δέος for reverence and fear hold; also Sophocles Ai. 1079 δέος γὰρ ὧι πρόσεστιν αἰσχύνη θ᾽ ὁμοῦ for fear, when accompanied by shame.

Σχήσει will hold: the future of the aorist can just as well encompass the entire future, as the aorist the entire past; to be supplied is αὐτοὺς them (τοὺς ἀστοὺς the citizens), and τὸ μὴ the not (ἀδικεῖν doing wrong) is added as at 220 after χαλᾶις you slacken. For τόδ᾽ ἦμαρ this day Wecklein would like πεδ᾽ ἦμαρ after day = μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν after day; but πεδά after is not found in Aeschylus (though πεδάρσιος aloft and the like are). Τό τ᾽ ἦμαρ the day (Grotius) = τήν θ᾽ ἡμέραν the day seems at least not inadmissible; but better κατ᾽ ἦμαρ by day Weil, as with καὶ κατ᾿ εὐφρόνην and by night also Soph. El. 259 stands.

At 693 a condition is now set that evidently refers to Ephialtes' legislation enacted shortly before: through these new laws the Areopagus had been deprived of its supreme oversight over the entire life of the state. For the corrupt πικαινόντων defiling the best restoration (better than 'πικαινούντων defiling and πικραίνόντων embittering) is ᾿πιχραινόντων defiling upon, since although not this compound, yet χραίνω to stain, defile is familiar to Aeschylus in the meanings 'to moisten, to defile' (170, Hik. 266), and ἐπι upon- indeed occurs again in ἐπιρροαῖσι with streams (although for this Wieseler's μή τι lest anything is worth noting); to this then belongs the punctuation after ἐπιρροαῖσι with streams and the replacement of ϑ the' by δ the'.

Βορβόρωι in mud etc. was a proverb; Diogenian. III, 55 etc. (according to which likewise one should punctuate before βορβόρωι in mud, G. Hermann, which has also been done in the manuscripts); one compares Eur. Hik. 222 λαμπρὸν δὲ θολερῶι δῶμα συμμείξας τὸ σόν but having mixed your bright house with muddy water; Theogn. 961. The poet expresses himself sharply and decisively, yet at the same time cautiously; likewise in what follows, in which the admonitions from the last stasimon (517 ff.) are partly repeated verbatim, incidentally also one of the arguments that Dindorf makes against the authenticity of these verses, against which Weil recalls Ag. 1219 ff. = 1096f., 1275 f. = 1138 f., 1287 f. 1171f., and Soph. El. 303f. = 164 f. But also the Eumenides themselves are full of repetitions, to the advantage of exegesis and criticism, and if ever, then in these principles the saying held: καὶ δὲς τὸ καλὸν καλόν ἐστιν ἐνισπεῖν and twice to speak the good is good.

V. 697 βουλεύειν to deliberate, advise 'to advise' as Prom. 204; περιστέλλειν to protect, cherish 'to hold in honor, to cherish' of laws Hdt. 2, 147. 3, 31. 4, 80 (Paley). The Areopagus with its unrestricted supreme oversight over everything had previously been a power in the state to be feared, from which the people now freed themselves.
Σέβας reverence, awe: here as often concretely the object of reverence (τὸ σεβαστόν the revered thing, Ch. 157 etc.); with
ταρβοῦντες fearing = φοβούμενοι being afraid again expresses the combination of reverence and fear, as at 690 f.

In ἔρυμά τε χώρας καὶ πόλεως a defense of the land and city the τε and is placed irregularly. The Scythians had from ancient times the reputation of lawfulness, Frg. 203 ἱππάκης βρωτῆρες εὔνομοι Σκύθαι eaters of mare's-milk cheese, law-abiding Scythians, and already Homer N 5 f. Ἱππημολγῶν γλακτοφάγων Ἀβίων τε δικαιοτάτων ἀνθρώπων of the mare-milkers, milk-drinkers, and the Abii, most righteous of men, from which again A. Frg. 198 is drawn, who calls them Γάβιοι Gabii and in any case read Γαβίων of the Gabii in Homer. On -ηισιν -eisin see on Ch. 569. With Πέλοπος ἐν τόποις in the places of Pelops the εὐνομωτάτη Λακεδαίμων most law-abiding Lacedaemon is thought of.
now emphatically the actual institution, which stands here entirely appropriately.

Βουλευτήριον council chamber as above (684), now without mention of the judicial function, although one can see an allusion to it in κερδῶν ἄθικτον untouched by gain; or does this refer to the prosecutions that Ephialtes had conducted against a number of individual Areopagites περὶ τῶν διωικημένων concerning the matters administered, Aristot. Πολιτ Politeia. Ἀθ Athenaion Politeia. 25, 2? The character as a supervisory authority emerges especially in εὑδόντων ὕπερ ἐγρηγορὸς φρούρημα γῆς a wakeful guard over those who sleep, for the land; for naturally one should not think, with the scholiast on εὕδοντες those who sleep, of murdered persons, nor of a night police, but it is spoken figuratively, cf. Ch. 881, Ag. 1357.

Φρούρημα guard equally concrete Sept. 449. So according to the poet all this power is an original attribute of the Areopagus, while the democrats recognized originally nothing but the jurisdiction over bloodshed.

707 ἐξέτεινα I extended is a proof that Athena's speech was not as short as Dindorf makes it; for the contrast cf. 571ff. 711-733 voting of the Areopagites, and meanwhile exchange of speeches between the parties in distichomythia, concluded by three verses of the chorus. There are 10 × 2 and then the three verses, without any relation to the number of choreutae; whether in relation to that of the voters? But there must not have been eleven, but an even number, so that equality of votes could result; what the scholiast on 743 says, that there were 51, is a transfer from the number of the Ephetae. O. Müller therefore assumes that one voted after 711, and again one after each speech of the parties, which yields 12; Weil earlier posited the loss of two pairs of verses and did not count the last three verses, with the same final result; Wecklein achieves this still differently and with much greater violence. The exchanges themselves, however, only at the beginning refer to the voting and then become pure altercatio (almost λοιδορία abuse) of the parties; I therefore miss the sufficient reason to demand a parallelism between these invectives and the voting.

711 βαρεῖαν τῆνδ᾽ ὁμιλίαν χθονός this grievous company of the land as at 406 καινὴν new.. τῆνδ᾽ ὁμιλίαν χθονός this company of the land, and 720 βαρεῖα χώρᾶι τῆιδ᾽ ὁμιλήσω πάλιν I shall again be a grievous companion to this land (which also belongs to the repetitions of this piece mentioned at 696 ff.).

Ξύμβουλός εἰμι I am a counsellor threatening precisely through the litotes. Apollo's reply corresponds (to Ch. 489 ff.): μηδαμῶς ἀτιμάσαι by no means to dishonour — μηδ᾽ ἀκαρπώτους κτίσαι nor to make fruitless (= ποιῆσαι to make, 17, Ch. 1060). — 715
σέβεις you revere: cf. 92. 151; for the thought 166ff. Οὐ λαχών not having obtained by lot: although these are not your office (but ours).

- 718 προστροπαῖς supplications σφάλλεται is deceived, through the supplication. The story of Ixion, the first murderer and first ἱκέτης suppliant (so more correctly Ἰξίων Ixion; cf. Welcker Aesch. Tril. 549), A. had treated in the Περραιβίδες Perrhaebides and the Ἰξίων Ixion, probably as it is presented in Diodorus 4, 69; at least there, as in A. (Frg. 88 in Schol. Pind. P. 2, 39), Ixion's father was called Antion. Ixion had lured his father-in-law Eioneus, to whom he owed the bride-price (cf. Περρ Perrh. Frg. 184) and who had seized his horses as security, to him under false promises of payment and pushed him into a pit filled with fire (Frg. 185). No one wanted to purify him for this murder; then he became a suppliant of Zeus (Frg. 340 πρὶν ἂν παλαγμοῖς αἵματος χοιροκτόνου αὐτός σε χράνηι Ζεὺς καταστάξας χεροῖν until with sprinklings of blood of a slain pig Zeus himself purifies you, pouring it over your hands). According to Frg. 381 (ἐν ταῖς Περραιβίσιν in the Perrhaebides according to Reitzenstein's manuscript of the Etym. M.), the murderer had also, to secure himself against revenge (similarly as through the μασχαλίζειν to mutilate, at Ch. 439 ff.), taken blood from the murdered man into his mouth and spat it out. Yet Zeus took pity on this wicked murderer and purified him; but he repaid it by trying to seduce Hera, and for that he came to the wheel. So, say the Erinyes, Zeus certainly acted wrongly in accepting this ἱκέτης suppliant, who repaid him thus: λέγεις you say "you say it" (so correctly Wilamowitz), as in the Gospel σὺ λέγεις you say "you say it", a form of affirmation where for some reason one does not want to assert openly (more fully Phaedra in Hippolytus 352 σοῦ τάδ᾽ these things are yours, οὐκ ἐμοῦ κλύεις not mine you hear). One would like to know how in the drama the so entirely undeserved grace of Zeus was motivated. But it is incomprehensible to me how critics (Merkel, earlier Weil, Wecklein) could have destroyed this close connection between 718 and 719 by transposing 719-23 after 730. The chorus, out of respect, does not go further into this matter and repeats (with the same expressions) its first threat.
Δίκης of Justice 'lawsuit' (cf. 729); 477 μὴ τυχοῦσαι πράγματος νικηφόρου not having obtained a victorious outcome.
Πάλιν Again 'in the future', as μεταῦθις afterwards 478.

721 ff. Apollo: that you will lose will happen; for you count for nothing, of course not among (ἐν in, see Wecklein) the younger gods, to whom you do not belong, but also not as one of the older ones (cf. what he said at 69f.). Thereupon the chorus: that will then be a counterpart to what you accomplished in the case of Admetus.

In ἀφθίτους θεῖναι βροτούς to make mortals immortal there is of course deliberate exaggeration. The story was treated by Phrynichus in the Ἄλκηστις Alcestis; whether with the crude detail that Apollo made the Fates drunk with wine (mentioned with φασί they say by the scholiast on Eur. Alc. 33), one does not know. Euripides Alc. 12 Μοίρας δολώσας having deceived the Fates; 33 Μοίρας δολίωι σφήλαντι τέχνηι having tripped the Fates with a cunning trick. The story stood in Hesiod (schol. Eur. Alc. 1), certainly with this detail; but A. sometimes likes to bring out quite crude details of the story, e.g. Hik. 300f.

725 σέβοντα revering as Eurip. Alk. 10ὁσίου γὰρ ἀνδρὸς ὅσιος ὢν ἐτύγχανον for being a holy man I happened upon a holy one (when Zeus had given Apollo into servitude to Admetus because of the killing of the Cyclopes, which A. perhaps presupposes, perhaps cancels). 726

τύχοι he might happen: optative in the subordinate clause of a general statement, as Prom. 636 and often in Sophocles, OT. 315. 979 etc., Bruhn Appendix p. 78. On 728 cf. 172 παλαιγενεῖς δὲ μοίρας φθίσας having destroyed the ancient fates. Παραπατᾶν to lead astray occurs only here; very probable and very easy is Davies' conjecture παρηπάφησας you deceived, from παραπαφίσκω I deceive Hom. Ξ 360, ξ x 488.
729 again with parallelism: σύ τοι you indeed. 730.
On ἰόν going cf. 478. 782; οὐδὲν βαρύν not heavy against βαρεῖα heavy 720. –
731 f. καθιππάζει he rides down as at 150 and again 779;
μένω ἐπήκοος γενέσθαι I wait to become a listener = μένω ἀκοῦσαι I wait to hear 677 (ἐπήκοος listening as Ch. 980; δίκη justice legal decision).

Ἀμφίβουλος ambiguous only here, not yet decided, wavering to both sides, and thus as much as οὔπω βεβουλευμένη not yet resolved. Wecklein cites for the connection with only one infinitive, without disjunction, Homer Θ 167 διάνδιχα μερμήριξεν he pondered in two ways, ἵππους τε στρέψαι καὶ ἐναντίβιον μαχέσασθαι to turn the horses and fight face to face.

After the voting has been completed, Athena rises once more to give one final rule; from her speech the manner of the voting that has taken place also becomes clear, as not entirely identical with the later one described by Aristoteles Πολ. Ἀθ. Col. 35. Two urns were also in use later, but a bronze one for the valid ψῆφοι votes, and a wooden one for the invalid; the juror, however, received two ψῆφοι votes, one πλήρης full for acquittal and one τετρυπημένη pierced for condemnation, and threw one into each urn, while completely preserving the secrecy of the vote. Here, by contrast, as also in the Ag. 813 ff., each voter has only one ψῆφος vote, and throws it into the one or the other vessel (τεῦχος vessel Ag. 815, Eum. 742), according as he condemns or acquits. In order for this vote to be secret, the vessels had to stand in a concealed place. That this manner of voting continued through the 5th century is evident from Aristoph. Σφῆκ Wasps. 987 f. and from Phrynichos Μοῦσαι Muses in Harp. καδίσκος voting-urn: ἰδοὺ δέχου τὴν ψῆφον Look, receive the vote. ὁ καδίσκος δέ σοι ὁ μὲν ἀπολύων οὗτος This voting-urn of yours is the one that acquits, ὁ δ᾽ ἀπολλὺς ὁδί and this one condemns. That Athena likewise would have voted now was G. Hermann's opinion, which was contested by Müller and especially by Schömann; it is hardly shared by anyone any longer. That the vote that took place was secret emerges clearly from what follows; how then can Athena take part in this vote and vote publicly? She also does not say προστίθημι I add, but προσθήσομαι I will add, namely for the case of an equality of votes in the urns, and there it is surely clear that the whole expression is figurative and not literal, and only the principle that was also valid later in Athens is being set up (Aristot. Πολ. Ἀθ. Col. 35): ἂν δὲ ἴσαι but if they are equal, ὁ φεύγων the defendant (νικᾶι wins). Thus ψῆφος vote and everything else stands figuratively in the passage of the Agamemnon, and in many places of the Suppliants (640. 645. 739 etc.) ψῆφον τίθεσθαι to cast a vote and the like of the decision of the Argives made by show of hands;

τῆνδε this one (fem.), however, is not deictic, referring to an actual voting pebble held in the hand, but is to be understood with reference to the preceding verse. In Euripides (El. 1265, I.T. 965, 1472) the representation is no different; he traces the principle of acquittal on a tie vote back to this case. Athena ostensibly motivates her vote for Orestes mythologically: being herself a woman, she would, as someone might think, have to be for the woman; but as the motherless daughter of Zeus she votes for the man. In fact, however, the true nature of the matter emerges in v. 739f.: the murderess of her husband deserves no vengeance; for ἄνδρα man . . δωμάτων ἐπίσκοπον guardian of the house means 'her husband'.

── 736 οὔτις . . ἥ no one . . who (fem.) (not ἥτις whoever (fem.)) is regular; see Kühner-Gerth, Synt. II, 403, n. 7. On 738 Abresch compares Eur. Εl. 1103 οἱ μέν εἰσιν ἀρσένων some are of males, οἱ δ᾽ αὖ φιλοῦσι μητέρας μᾶλλον πατρός others again love mothers more than father.

── 741 Orestes is the victor, even if the verdict is by equal votes? Rather, the present νικᾶι he is victorious is used of what is indeed future but is immediately given along with another future event, as in Eur. Andr. 381 ἢν θάνηις σύ if you die, παῖς ὅδ᾽ ἐκφεύγει μόρον this child escapes death, Kühner-Gerth I, 136. Below at 744 stands κριθήσεται he will be judged, not κέκριται it has been decided.

742 f. presuppose the custom, which also existed later, that the votes were counted out by some judges specially appointed for the purpose, Aristot. Πολ Pol.. Ἀθ Ath.. Col. 35, 28 οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τὰς ψήφους εἰληχότες διαριθμοῦσιν αὐτάς those who have been allotted to the votes count them out.
The ψήφοι votes, however, are called here and at 753 πάλοι lots 'lots', from the similarity of the procedure in casting lots and in voting.

Ἐπέσταλται τέλος the office has been entrusted exactly like Ag. 908 of commission and office, Ch. 760. 744-753 counting and announcement of the result. During the counting so much is said that one imagines a larger number than 12 voting, especially also according to Apollo's words at 748 ff.

── 746 ἀγχόνης τέρματα the ends of a noose like θανάτου τέλος the end of death (Sept. 906); ἀγχόνη hanging the last resort of despair, probably more proverbial than literal, after passages such as Eur. Bakch. 246 (Pentheus speaks) ταῦτ᾽ οὐχὶ δεινῆς ἀγχόνης ἔστ᾽ ἄξια are these things not worthy of a terrible hanging?; Herakl. 246 (Demophon) καὶ τάδ᾽ ἀγχόνης πέλας and these things are near to hanging, Soph. OT. 1374, Aristoph. Ach. 125 etc. (Wecklein). ── 747

ἡμῖν γὰρ for us: we too are risking something, not you alone. Ἔρρειν to go to ruin 301, 884; νέμειν to distribute in the active is no less correct than at v. 1017 Παλλάδος πόλιν νέμοντες dwelling in the city of Pallas; πρόσω forward 'henceforth, further' (often spatial, as Ag. 294). ── ἐκβολάς outlets concrete, plural because from two urns whose contents had to be kept apart. The scholiast wrongly speaks of black and white stones.
749 σέβοντες revering 'revering you' as in Pers. 694 σέβομαι I revere, construed as a negative verb with μή not (not in the passage from the Persians).

Γνώμη judgment = ψῆφος vote; ὤρθωσεν it set upright shows that γίγνεται it becomes too is to be taken gnomically and generally. Βαλοῦσα ψῆφος the vote having been cast cannot be satisfactorily explained in any way, neither in that of the scholiast (ἡ ψῆφος δὲ βαλεῖν τε καὶ ὀρθῶσαι οἶκον δύναται the vote is able both to cast and to set upright a house), nor in that of G. Hermann, = βαλὼν τὴν γνώμην εῖς ψηφιζόμενος having cast his judgment in voting, for that would at least have to be (Dindorf) βληθεῖσα having been cast. Μολοῦσα having come (aorist like ὠρθωσεν it set upright) is graphically very close and is a favorite word of the poet (155 ὄνειδος ἐξ ὀνειράτων μολόν a reproach coming from dreams etc.); παροῦσα being present H. Voss, Wecklein. 754–777 Orestes.
755 σύ τοι you indeed as just now at 727, 729.
— 756 καί τις Ἑλλήνων ἐρεῖ and some one of the Greeks will say in Homeric fashion; cf. Soph. Ai. 500 with Homer Z 462 (Wecklein).
757 ᾿Αργεῖος Argive as a citizen of Argos. 759

πάντα κραίνοντος accomplishing all things: cf. Ag. 1486 f. Διὸς παναιτίου πανεργέτα of Zeus, the all-author, the all-worker. τί γὰρ βροτοῖς ἄνευ Διὸς τελεῖται for what is accomplished for mortals without Zeus?; Zeus as the ultimate author has directed everything thus, and just as he comes as the third to the two tutelary gods, so he has also shown himself as σωτήρ savior, just as to him as σωτήρ savior the third libation is due; cf. Hik. 27 (after the ὕπατοι θεοί highest gods and the χθόνιοι gods below) καὶ Ζεὺς σωτὴρ τρίτος and Zeus the savior as the third (also Ag. 1387). The με me at 761 shows that the fictitious speech extends no further than σωτῆρος of the savior. Αἰδεσθείς having felt shame stands in the general meaning of 'to have regard for', cf. σέβειν to revere (92) 151. Συνδίκους advocates on 579.

the political reference to the alliance between Athens and Argos is unmistakable; see also already vv. 289 ff.; 671 ff. Here, however, unlike at 671, the talk is chiefly negative, about the avoidance of all hostility, already at 765 f., but developed in vv. 767 ff., which Dindorf considers a later interpolation. If, however, one follows him in excising 767–774, the oath becomes not only very short but also unclear: he has sworn that no Argive will ever march against Athens; but how can he guarantee such a thing? To this, 767 ff. give an answer, but according to Dindorf none. Thus the excision is untenable, and whoever thinks of the times of the Peloponnesian War as being in the author's mind thereby posits a completely impossible confusion of Argos and Sparta. Since, then, the historical Argives never thought of a campaign against Athens, the poet in fact keeps himself at the height proper to him, above contemporary history and momentary interests. Euripides does similarly in the Suppliants 1187 ff., where Adrastus swears the oath for Argos, and where in place of 767 ff. there stands a curse upon the Argives in case of breach.

Πλειστήρης Pleistērēs (a proper name) 763 only here; πλειστηρίζομαι pleistērizomai (to act as Pleistērēs?) only Ch. 1029, see on that passage; the -ήρης ērēs has lost its force, and the sense is approximately = αἰώνιος aiōnios (everlasting).
Πρυμνήτης Prymnētēs (a proper name) 765 as at 16.

Κεκασμένος kekasmenos (furnished, equipped) 766 does not have the Homeric meaning 'pre-eminent, distinguished', as at Δ 339 δόλοισι κεκασμένε doloisi kekasmene (you who are furnished with wiles), but it was evidently understood differently, as 'ornatus, instructus', and the gloss was used accordingly: Pind. Ol. 1, 27 ἐλέφαντι φαίδιμον ὦμον κεκαδμένον with ivory, his shining shoulder equippedEur. Εl. 616 φρουραῖς κέκασται δεξιαῖς τε δορυφόρων phrourais kekastai dexiais te doryphorōn (he is furnished with garrisons and the right hands of spearmen), Aristoph. Ἱππ Hipp. (Hippolytus). 685 πανουργίαις μείζοσι κεκασμένον panourgiais meizosi kekasmenon (furnished with greater villainies) (Hesych. κέκασται kekastai (he is furnished)· κατεσκεύασται kateskeuastai (he has been equipped), ὥπλισται hōplistai (he has been armed), τέτακται tetaktai (he has been drawn up); Phot. κεκασμένον kekasmenon (furnished)· κεκοσμημένον kekosmēmenon (adorned). Lobeck, however [on Buttmann Ausf. Sprachl. § 114], compares precisely with our passage Hesych. κάδμος kadmos (Cadmus)· δόρυ dory (spear), λόφος lophos (crest), ἀσπίς aspis (shield), = equipment.) Δόρυ Dory (spear) is collective like Sept. 216 (cf. 416): πύργον στέγειν εὔχεσθε πολέμιον δόρυ pyrgon stegein euchesthe polemion dory (pray that the tower may ward off the enemy spear). –
768 νῦν nyn (now) attributive to ὁρκώματα horkōmata (oaths);

παρβαίνουσι they transgress as at παρβάταν transgressor 553, παρβασία transgression Sept. 743, παρβατός transgressed Hik. 1048. In what follows Paley, with Abresch, keeps the reading of the Medicean manuscript: πράξομεν we will do (will bring about) ὡς αὐτοῖσι μεταμέληι πόνος so that toil may be a cause of regret to them; but then it would have to be ὥστ᾽ so that (ὡς so that).. μεταμέλειν πόνον to cause regret for toil. For although πράττειν to do (to work toward) can also be construed with ὅπως in order that (ὡς so that) and the subjunctive, yet after ἀμηχάνοισι δυσπραξίαις with helpless misfortunes the consequence, not the purpose, must be expressed. At any rate this explanation is better than Weil's restoration: ἀμηχάνους helpless/παρέξομεν we will provide | δυσπραξίας misfortunes; namely παρέξομεν we will provide is what the late Codex Augustanus has, probably only to make it a verse: ἀμηχάνοις helpless (M. and Aug.) παρέξ provide. δυσπραξίαις misfortunes. The πράξομεν δυσπραξίαις we will do misfortunes too (cf. on 687) we would rather not obliterate. But if one transposes, then all becomes well: τοῖς παρβαίνουσιν to those who transgress.. ὁδοὺς ἀθύμους τιθέντες making their paths despondent, ὡς αὐτοῖσι μεταμέληι πόνος ἀμηχάνοισι so that toil may be a cause of regret to them, helpless etc.; thus the ἀμήχανοι δυσπραξίαι helpless misfortunes come after the final clause. ᾿Αθύμους ῾ despondent'despondent' precisely because of the lack of good signs and the appearance of bad ones;

μεταμέλειν to be a cause of regret personal, as at Aristoph. Νεφ. 1098 etc. They would finally have to turn back, even if they do not wish to, as the signs are fulfilled and the failures become ἀμήχανοι helpless. V. 772
ὀρθουμένων being set upright: namely τῶν ὁρκωμάτων of the oaths, rather than τῶν πραγμάτων of the affairs, which Paley also considers (after ξυντυχόντων having happened Sept. 274).

At V. 774 I take offense at ἐσμὲν we are, since the explanation given for νικᾶι he/she/it conquers 741 can hardly be applied here; therefore ἐσόμεθ we will be'; for ἡμεῖς we I would prefer χἠμεῖς and we (as at χαίρετε χὐμεῖς farewell, and you too 1003).

the blessing can naturally refer only to the people and not to the goddess; but for that it suffices to punctuate strongly after λεώς people, and ἔχοι may he/she/it have would not even be better, since the people too is present in its representatives.

Πολισσοῦχος city-protecting A. also says elsewhere in the senarius (so below 883. 1010) for πολίοχος city-protecting (Sept. 109) or πολιοῦχος city-protecting (there 312. 822, Hik. 1020, all passages of different meter), cf. πολισσονόμος city-ruling Pers. 852, Ch. 864. No other poet has these forms.
Πάλαισμα wrestling-bout cf. 582, Ag. 63;
ἄφυκτος inescapable Prom. 903. 1016, Hik. 109.

Δορὸς νικηφόρον victory-bringing spear – νίκην δορὸς φέρον bringing victory of the spear (Wecklein). With this Orestes departs, and Apollo as well. The final scene of the play, in which the strife of the old and young gods is resolved into harmony and upon Athens, instead of the threatening curse of the angry Erinyes, comes all the blessing of the reconciled Eumenides, is laid out in the following manner. The anger expresses itself in two pairs of strophes and antistrophes, in which in a peculiar way strophe and antistrophe are each time identical; what the chorus sings is separated by trimeters of the admonishing Athena: ΧΟ CHORUS. ΑΘ ATHENA. ΧΟ CHORUS. ΑΘ ATHENA. ΧΟ CHORUS. (στρ strophe. β beta) ΑΘ ATHENA. ΧΟ CHORUS. ΑΘ ATHENA., thus like Agam. 1407 ff. CHORUS (Str.) ΚΛΥΤ CLYTAEMESTRA. (Trim.) CHORUS (Antistr.) ΚΛΥΤ CLYTAEMESTRA. (Trim.). But Athena's final speech (881-891) prevails, and now the reconciliation is accomplished in stichomythia, ending with the chorus's question what it should wish upon the city, to which Athena gives answer in 903-915. So now (916-1020) the blessing, in three strophe pairs; between these and each time strophe and antistrophe lie anapests of Athena; after the 3rd antistrophe trimeters of the goddess (1021-1031), which lead over to the exodos. This is thus the form as also in the kommos of Agamemnon 1448ff., where Clytemnestra always speaks in anapests, but the chorus predominantly uses lyric rhythms, and in the parodos of Prometheus 128 ff.: chorus lyric, Prometheus in anapests. The difference, however, is that in Agamemnon and Prometheus there is mutual reference to what has been said or sung, whereas here the Eumenides choose entirely independently what they want to sing, so that their entire song is like a choral ode interrupted only by pauses. Athena fills the pauses, and she naturally refers to what has been sung, but speaks predominantly to the citizens.

Str. α alpha. In the rhythms here too, as already in 145 ff., 255 ff., trimeters and dochmiacs are mixed, but the determination of the individual parts is partly difficult, since because of the verbatim repetition in the antistrophe we are actually in the case of ἀπολελυμένον free-standing (metrically independent). Unmistakable trimeters are 779. 80. 87; in these, therefore, the ordinary dialect is also to be preserved (with the manuscripts), ἡ τάλαινα the wretched woman 780. The first verse is composed of iambic dimeter and dochmius, cf. Ch. 938 f. etc.;

781 is a single dochmius; then in any case ἰὸν ἰὸν ἀντιπενθῆ μεθεῖσα καρδίας sending forth a grief-requiting cry from the heart is to be taken together, as twice -, -, -,-; for trochees seem inappropriate.

Σταλαγμὸν χθονὶ a dripping upon the earth and ἄφορον ἐκ δὲ τοῦ barren, and from this are dochmiacs, but detached from one another; cf. on 149 and below on 837 ff. Further, at 785 λειχὴν ἄφυλλος ἄτεκνος a leafless, childless lichen -- ~ - ~~~ -? The resolution is still in the way, for one cannot lengthen as with ---, nor insert a pause, which here would fall in the middle of a word. Pure dochmiacs remain if one (Paley) transposes ἄφυλλος λειχὴν ἄτεκνος ὦ leafless lichen, childless, O (instead of the manuscript reading, after Hermann and others) δίκα πέδον ἐπισύμενος justice rushing upon the ground. Others restore a trimeter: λειχήν ἄφυλλος ἄτεκνος ὦ δίκα lichen, leafless, childless, O justice (δίκα justice), or something similar, in which, however, the ā is striking. In v. 769 the bacchiacs (according to the metrical terminology) seem unambiguous, cf. Ag. 1103, where likewise tetrameters; further on dochmiacs; at the close as at 170, see there.

779 καθιππάσασθε you have ridden down now for the third time in the same usage, see 150, 731. The sentence beginning with ἐγὼ δ᾽ ἄτιμος ἡ τάλαινα βαρύκοτος but I, dishonored, wretched, heavy in wrath (this word only here) has no continuation, since instead of a finite verb μεθεῖσα having released follows; the scholiast explains this with μετοχὴ ἀντὶ ῥήματος participle instead of verb and cites the classic example from Homer 307, where the Aristarcheans similarly remark on βριθομένη laden that either ἐστί is is to be supplied, or this very enallage is to be assumed. Against this, Weil (1861) hit upon the very subtle idea of transposing verses; ἐγὼ I.. βαρύκοτος heavy in wrath/ στενάζω I groan; τί ῥέξω what shall I do?; |γένωμαι δυσοίστα πολίταις I become unbearable to the citizens (789f.) | ἐν γᾶι τᾶιδε in this land, φεῦ alas |.. μεθεῖσα having released, by which the entire construction is put in order and, moreover, a correct sequence of thought is established. For if the Erinyes already now announce their vengeance, why afterwards the deliberation τί ῥέξω what shall I do?? Finally, πολίταις to the citizens (790) is strange in its present surroundings; on the other hand, it is motivated and clear in the vicinity of ἐν γᾶι τᾶιδε in this land 781. This last, however, can also be resolved by emendation, and τί ῥέξω what shall I do? may be more an exclamation of passion than deliberation; but the anacoluthon is precisely as such suited to the pathos, cf. on 94 ff. Weil himself also returned to the usual order.

782 ἰὸν ἰὸν alas, alas shows an epanadiplosis more frequent in Euripides than in Aeschylus; cf., however, also in the latter χαίρετε χαίρετε farewell, farewell 996, 1014, αἰνῶς αἰνῶς terribly, terribly Pers. 930, μυρία μυρία countless, countless 981, ἔλιπες ἔλιπες you left, you left 985, (ἄλαστ᾿ ἄλαστα unforgettable, unforgettable 990, ἔταφον ἔταφον unburied, unburied 1000, etc. But the thought, with similar expression, already stood at 478; cf. also 801.

χθονί to the land is a kind of dative of disadvantage, and it is not necessary, with Heimsoeth, to make φθοράν destruction out of ἄφορον barren; for thus, or rather: thus is the following ἐκ δὲ τοῦ κτἑ and from this.... Elaboration of what is contained in ἄφορον barren or φθοράν destruction.

783 λειχήν lichen also [Cho.] 281, there however of human disease; the length of the first syllable (manuscripts in both places with 1) is guaranteed by Martial XI, 98, 5. With Paley's proposed transposition ἄφυλλος λειχὴν ἄτεκνος leafless, childless lichen (see above) I cannot agree, since the two adjectives with a- are better kept together: σέβας δ᾽ ἄμαχον ἀδάματον ἀπόλεμον unconquerable, untamable, unwarlike reverence Ch. 53 ἄγαμον ἀδάματον unmarried, untamedHik. 143 ἀκέλευστος ἄμισθος unbidden, unpaidAg. 979, above 385 ἄτιμ᾿ ἀτίετα dishonored, unhonored, 564 ἄκλαυτος αἶστος unwept, unseen, etc., although one could compare ἀπό'τροπον ἅγος ἀπεύχετον averted pollution, abominable Ch. 155 for the other order. ἄφυλλος ἄτεκνος λειχήν leafless, childless lichen, ὦ Δίκα O Justice, πέδον ἐπισύμενος rushing upon the ground. Cf. 511 Δίκα Justice Pauw for ἰὼ io! Δ. Μ; Δίκα Justice is in any case to be written as there.

Ἄφυλλος leafless and ἄτεκνος childless can be referred to the lichen itself, which has neither leaves nor fruits; better, however, to understand them of the effect on plants and trees. Τέκνον child of fruit is certainly unusual, but no more so than κάλυκος ἐν λοχεύμασιν in the birth-pangs of the bud Ag. 1392; in any case, leaves and children are an impossible combination, and at least the fruits must be thought of as well. At line 803 the threat uttered here is referred only to the seed.

Ἰὼ δίκα O Justice is διὰ μέσου through the middle (schol.) as before φεῦ alas!; on ἐπισύμενος rushing upon cf. σύμεναι to rush 1007, Ag. 746; alongside stands in Aeschylus συθείς having rushed. The 6 should be doubled, as well as in ἐπισσύτοις rushing upon 924; however, Euripides also has ἔσυτο ἐπέσυτο rushed, rushed upon, Kühner-Blass II, 534.

Βροτοφθόρος destroying mortals Hik. 264, where the arising of snakes and other harmful creatures is traced back to the staining of the earth with blood; from the ἀκαρπία barrenness (801) naturally result diseases and destruction of men.

On κηλίδας ἐν χώρᾶι βαλεῖ to cast stains upon the land cf. Hik. 265 αἱμάτων μιάσμασιν χρανθεῖσα γαῖα the earth defiled by the pollutions of blood. The synonymous expressions γῆ earth, χθών ground, πέδον soil, χώρα land are all combined in this sentence. Then again διὰ μέσου in the middle: στενάζω τί ῥέξω γένωμαι I groan; what shall I do? What will become of me? (δύσοιστα hard to bear), where, if δύσοιστα hard to bear, the final short syllable is striking in bacchiacs (or syncopated iambs); therefore Müller δυσοίστα hard to bear, to connect with γένωμαι I will become and πολίταις for the citizens, after which ἔπαθον I suffered comes to μεγάλα great things. But this is unbearably weak: rather μεγάλα δυστυχεῖς greatly unfortunate as (Wecklein) μέγ᾽ εὐδαιμον greatly fortunate Prom. 647 περίσσ᾽ εὐκαρδίωι exceedingly stout-heartedEur. Hek. 579, and δύσοιστα πολίταις ἔπαθον hard to bear for the citizens I suffered as the scholiast, with a threatening double meaning: suffered by the citizens, and hard for the citizens to bear. The connection with the previous sentence required because of πολίταις for the citizens (cf. above), and the necessary long final syllable of the last bacchius we gain by inserting ὡς as after δύσοιστ hard to bear (α a).

Τί ῥέξω; γένωμαι What shall I do? What will become of me? Hermann supports with Eur. Ion 1446 (same rhythms) τίν᾿ αὐδὰν ἀΰσω what cry shall I utter?; βοάσω I will shout; (πόθεν μοι κτέ whence for me....); τί γένωμαι what will become of me? (as an exclamation διὰ μέσου in the middle) stands Sept. 297, and is like τί πάθω what shall I suffer?; τί νύ μοι μήκιστα γένηται what then will happen to me at the last?; Homer & 465.
Στενάζω I groan probably not interrogative, but like πνέω τοι πένος I breathe toil 840. The wild fury finds its true expression at this point. –

Ἀτιμοπενθής dishonored in grief see on δυσποροπαίπαλος hard to turn aside 387. Fittingly they close with an exclamation about their misfortune and the dishonoring of the old gods (ἄτιμος dishonored 780, ἀτιμοπενθεῖς dishonored in grief 793). was.

The speech has 14 verses, the next (824 ff.) 13; one has wanted to equalize them one way or another, while yet afterwards in the speeches after Str. Ant. β b the greatest inequality prevails, and only by strong deletion in the one and by assuming a lacuna in the other (Wecklein) does the symmetry emerge.
794 On βαρυστόνως heavily groaning cf. στενάζω I groan 789, on ἀτιμίᾶι with dishonor 796 cf. ἄτιμος dishonored – ἀτιμοπενθεῖς dishonored in grief 780. 793.

On δίκη justice (legal decision as at 732) ἐξῆλθε came out cf. Soph. ΟΤ. 88 τὰ δύσφορ᾽ the grievous things, εἰ τύχοι κατ᾿ ὀρθὸν ἐξελθόντα if they should come out rightly, 1011 μή μοι Φοῖβος ἐξέλθηι σαφής may Phoebus not come out clear to me, 1084 (also we similarly 'come out').

Ἀληθῶς truly in accordance with the truth, since the matter was really doubtful. To οὐκ ἀτιμίᾶι not with dishonor the clause with ἀλλὰ but attaches itself, which at the same time gives a reason, therefore ἀλλὰ but . . γὰρ for (Prom. 941, Ch. 375, yet with a different use of the ἀλλὰ but). The testimonies of Zeus consist in Apollo's assurance that he has spoken here as elsewhere on his father's commission, 616 ff. (μαρτύρια testimonies -10—/ ‿ ‿, like νηφάλια wineless 107).

Αὐτὸς.. αὐτὸς himself... himself exactly as in Frg. 281 (Paley): ὁ δ᾽ αὐτὸς ὑμνῶν the same man singing, αὐτὸς ἐν θοίνηι παρών himself present at the feast, αὐτὸς τάδ᾽ εἰπών himself having said these things, αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ κτανὼν τὸν παῖδα τὸν ἐμόν he himself is the one who killed my son. –
V. 799 ὡς as (= ὥστε so that, 36)..
ἔχειν to have: so that no punishment (βλάβη harm 491) befell Orestes for his deed (δρῶντα doing like ἔχειν to have, the action involves no punishment). — The corrupt words

have been essentially healed by Weil through the transposition of μὴ θυμοῦσθε do not be angry in V. 800; the unparalleled middle σκήψησθε you should not pretend (assimilated to θυμοῦσθε you are angry) was already corrected by Elmsley to σκήψητε you should pretend. Through the transposition we also get rid of the strange dative with σκήψητε you should pretend, though not according to Weil, who places μὴ θυμοῦσθε do not be angry after ὑμεῖς δὲ but you; then one would still have to correct (Blaydes) into μήτ᾿ neither (μηδ nor') ἐς τήνδε γῆν β into this land b. κ k. σκ sk. (Ag. 310 ἐς τόδε σκήπτει στέγος it hurls upon this house, Eur. Med. 1333 τὸν σὸν δ᾽ ἀλάστορ᾽ εἰς ἔμ᾽ ἔσκηψεν θεός but the god hurled your avenging spirit upon me). For the verse ending on μὴ not cf. verses like 238 τε πρὸς and toward/, 255 πάντα all, μὴ not/ (dochmiacs), Prom. 865 τὸ μὴ the not, Ag. 1354 γὰρ ὡς for as/. Σκήπτειν to hurl is used intransitively by A. except here and Ag. 366.
Μὴ θυμοῦσθε Do not be angry "be angry no longer"; μὴ σκήψητε do not hurl aorist of what is yet to come.

Δαιμόνων of the gods: cf. 302 βόσκημα δαιμόνων food of the gods; a change is not necessary (πλευμόνων of the lungs Wakefield, δαΐων σταλαγμάτων of hostile drops without comma Hermann). Αἰχμὴ spear-point 'sharpness, point' only here (whereas otherwise A. speaks of the γνάθος jaw in such a transferred sense, Ch. [289]. 325, Prom. 368), yet probably not inadmissible; βρωτῆρας devourers as feminine like σωτήρ savior Ag. 664 etc.; ἀνήμερος savage 14, Prom. 716.
804 πανδίκως with full justice Ch. 241. 681, Hik. 419, Sept. (173). 670; here in all faithful', Wecklein.

805 κευθμῶνας hiding places points, like other things, to the fact that the sanctuary of the Σεμναί the August Goddesses on the Areopagus (Paus. I, 28, 6) had its underground chambers. The ἐσχάραι hearths are altars as at 108; before these, then, stood (stone?) θρόνοι thrones, and these were, like other sacred stones, made greasy and shining with oil, for which one cites Theophr. Char. 17 τῶν λιπαρῶν λίθων τῶν ἐν ταῖς τριόδοις of the shining stones at the crossroads, Pausan. X, 24, 6 Lukian Alex. 30; in addition Homer y 408 of the seats before Nestor's house: λευκοί white, ἀποστίλ βοντες ἀλείφατος gleaming with oil. Λιπαρόθρονος with shining throne Bergk Lyr. Adesp. 190, of Dike and Eirene.
– 807 τιμαλφουμένας being honored 15.
Chorus Antist. a, 808-823. The verbatim repetition means that the chorus pays no attention at all to what it has heard, if it has ever heard it.

Once again reference is made to ἀτιμοπενθεῖς unhonored by mourning 823, but this is denied only very briefly; then she asks them to desist from their threats and from carrying them out, in the course of which she too uses a mild threat (which also has its effect), and finally repeats her promises.

Δύσκηλος Duskelos (ill-omened) (only here) must have been formed after the already Homeric εὔκηλος eukelos (at ease) (= ἔκηλος ekelos (at ease)); Weil writes δύσκηλιν duskelin (ill-omened) from κηλίς kelis (stain) 817.
Θεαὶ βροτῶν Goddesses of mortals: of the poor mortals, who are powerless against you goddesses.

826 καὶ τί δεῖ λέγειν and why need I say formula of passing over something when one considers it superfluous to say (Ag. 598, Eur. Herakles 1270, Plat. Symp. 217 C καὶ τί δεῖ λέγειν and why need I say; οὐδὲν γάρ μοι πλέον ἦν for it would have been no advantage to me), or avoids it for another reason (Eur. Andr. 929. 943), as here too Athena deliberately holds back the threat. See Paley. Athena, however, becomes somewhat more explicit. With 827 f. one compares Eur. Tro. 80, where Athena says of Zeus: ἐμοὶ δὲ δώσειν φησὶ πῦρ κεραύνιον but he says he will give me the thunderbolt, βάλλειν ᾿Αχαιοὺς ναῦς τε πιμπράναι πυρί to hurl at the Achaeans and burn their ships with fire. —
829 εὐπειθής eupeithes (easily persuaded) (so also here in the manuscripts): see on Ch. 259. —

830 γλώσσηι ματαίαι with a vain tongue Prom. 329 ματαίαν γλῶσσαν a vain tongueAg. 1662; yet here ματαίας vain is more 'wicked', 'evil', cf. 337, Hik. 229. 762, Ἔπος ἐκβαλεῖν to cast out a word Ch. 46, Aeschylus. ἐκβαλεῖν ἔπη to cast out words Ag. 1663; so Wakefield's conjecture seems correct so far, and also χθονί in the earth is easier to understand than χθόνα the earth, which, like the dative, would have to be construed with what follows, as subject accusative to πράσσειν to do.

Καρπός fruit so metaphorically Sept. 618 εἰ καρπὸς ἔσται θεσφάτοισι Λοξίου if there will be fruit according to the oracles of Loxias. From the σταλάγματα drops have now, less mythically, become curses.

Κοίμα koima (put to sleep) 832 follows asyndetically according to the manuscripts; but also κοίμησον koimeson (put to sleep) aorist (Ag. 1247) is absolutely expected, unless one writes before it 830 μὴ ἐκβαλοῦσα not having cast out: refrain from curses, and then calm yourself further.
Κοιμᾶν to lull like Homer µ 169 κοίμησε δὲ κύματα δαίμων and a god lulled the waves to sleep; also πικρὸν μένος bitter wrath (on 651) remains within the metaphor.
— 834 πολλῆς much namely οὔσης being; so the sacrifices will be numerous.

Πολύς much 'great, wide', like ἄλω πολλήν a large threshing floor Sept. 489 λίμνη μεγάλη τε καὶ πολλή a lake great and wideHdt. 4, 109. What is attested here is (cf. Schol.) that to the Σεμναί the August Goddesses first-fruit offerings (of grain) were brought for marriage and fertility of children, προτέλεια γάμων preliminary offerings for marriage (Schol.; Plato Laws VI 774 E), in which they appear as earth-goddesses similar to Demeter, Preller-Robert Myth. 841.

Θύος incense Ag. 1409, Eur. El. 1141 (Homer Z 270); Hesychius explains θύη incense offerings with †θαύματα wonders (θυ thu⟨μι mi⟩άματα amata?), ἀρώματα aromata, yet with the concept of θύειν to offer sacrifice (properly burnt offering) that of θύος incense has also been extended.

Πρό before as much as ὑπὲρ on behalf of, as in Ag. 1008 (Homer, Euripides, Herodotus); on τέλος γαμήλιον marriage rite cf. Soph. Antig. 1240; Pollux 3, 38: ἡ δὲ πρὸ γάμου θυσία προτέλεια the sacrifice before marriage is a preliminary rite.... προτελεῖσθαι δ᾽ ἐλέγοντο οὐ μόνον αἱ νύμφαι ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ νυμφίοι not only the brides but also the bridegrooms were said to be consecrated beforehand cf. Sophocles loc. cit. O.), καὶ τέλος ὁ γάμος ἐκαλεῖτο and marriage was called a rite of completion, καὶ τέλειοι οἱ γεγαμηκότες and those who had married were called 'complete'. Διὸ καὶ Ἥρα τελεία Therefore Hera is also called 'the Fulfiller' (above 214) ἡ συζυγία the union· ταύτηι γὰρ τοῖς προτελείοις προυτέλουν τὰς κόρας for with these preliminary rites they consecrated the maidens, καὶ Ἀρτέμιδι καὶ Μοίραις and to Artemis and the Fates (cf. below 961).

Chorus strophe β b, 837-847. The rhythms are mainly dochmiac; difficulties are not lacking here either, since the antistrophe again agrees even in the words. Φεῦ Alas! 837 must be taken by itself, ἐμὲ παθεῖν τάδε that I should suffer these things as a dochmius (Hermann); it was different at line 811, where φεῦ alas! belongs to the dochmius.
839 ἀτίετον φεῦ μύσος unhonored, alas, pollution two cretics; without φεῦ alas! it would again be a dochmius, and Hermann transposes φεῦ alas!, after μύσος pollution.
840 two dochmii without synapheia, cf. on 813;
841 οἰοῖ δᾶ φεῦ alas, alas, earth, alas would become a dochmius by a second φεῦ alas! or by οἰοιοῖ alas, alas.
842 requires emendation, see below, to become a dochmiac dimeter; then still θυμὸν ἄϊε μᾶτερ hear my spirit, mother – ὠ O –, and two dimeters. The heavy ending of the foot on – – is quite frequent.
Exclamatory infinitive, Kühner-Gerth II, 23, as in Ag. 1662, Soph. Ai. 410 etc.

To ἐμὲ παθεῖν τάδε that I should suffer these things belongs the epanalepsis ἐμὲ παλαιόφρονα me, ancient in thought (cf. 847; the word also Hik. 593, of Zeus); then follows a second infinitive clause κατά τε γᾶς οἰκεῖν and to dwell beneath the earth etc. The transmitted κατὰ γᾶν beneath the earth had to be emended already at 369; for οἰκεῖν to dwell Hermann οἰχνεῖν to go (Soph. Ai. 564, El. 165, εἰσοιχνεῖν to go into A. Prom. 122), since after Athena's reply (851. 857) the departure must have been indicated. They dwell under the earth also in Athens (1007 etc.).

In ἀτίετον unhonored it is shown that the chorus has again heard nothing of Athena's words; likewise in μύσος pollution, for which Apollo's words at 195 provide the explanation. Thus the young gods position themselves against the old ones (845f.).
Πνέω μένος I breathe fury (832) after Homeric μένεα πνείοντες breathing fury; κότον πνέων breathing wrath Ch. 33 cf. 951 (Ag. 1236).

Οἰοῖ δᾶ Alas, alas, earth as in Ag. 1072. 1076 ότοτοτοῖ τοτοῖ δᾶ alas, alas, alas, alas, earth (Prom. 568); δᾶ earth allegedly a dialectal by-form of γῆ earth, contained in Δαμάτηρ Demeter (Schol.; Preller-Robert Mythol. 747, 6); οἴ alas or οἱ alas singly and doubled or tripled Pers. 1003. 931. 954 etc. The verse stands in connection with the following; cf. Ag. 1214f.: ἰοὺ ἰοὺ alas, alas, ἰὼ κακά alas, evils. ὑπ᾽ αὖ με δεινὸς ὀρθομαντείας πόνος στροβεῖ again a terrible pain of true prophecy whirls me.

Ὑποδύεσθαι τινά to slip under someone Homer 8 735, here with accusative of the whole and of the part as at 88 νικᾶν to conquer. But the verse has no rhythm, which is restored in various ways: τίς μ᾽ ὑποδύεται τίς ὀδύνα πλευράς who slips under me, what pain in my sides Hermann, τίς μ᾽ ὑπ who under me. πλ pl. αὖ δύα again misery Dindorf, in which, however, δύα misery (miseria aerumna Ddf. Lex.) is no improvement for ὀδύνα pain; if one inserts τίς who, one need not rearrange: πλευρὰς sides (τίς who) ὀδύνα pain, and one can attach θυμόν spirit, which is a quite unsuitable object for ἄ a. Nowhere in Aeschylus is θυμός spirit unambiguously 'anger'.

Αΐειν to hear A. also has Pers. 633. 873, Ag. 55, Hik. 58. At V. 815 δαναιᾶν of the Danaans (Prom. 794. 912) is a happy correction by L. Dindorf; the construction αἴρειν to take (take away) τινὰ ἀπό τινος someone from someone is otherwise unattested, but seems not impossible, cf. on 213, where I write παρ᾿ οὐδὲν ἦρκας ὣς Ἥρας τελείας καὶ Διὸς πιστώματα you counted as nothing the pledges of Hera Teleia and Zeus. The παρ᾽ οὐδὲν as nothing (as nothing) is in any case common to the passages.
Δυσπαλάμως helplessly Hik. 867; εὐπάλαμος resourceful Ag. 1531.

The speech has an even milder character than the previous one; for the Erinyes too have at least not repeated their threat, frightened by the reference to Zeus' omnipotence. With ἐργὰς ξυνοίσω σοι I will join my wrath with you there is particular connection to 840, with γεραιτέρα older to παλαιόφρονα of ancient mind 838, likewise with σοφωτέρα wiser . . φρονεῖν to think 848 f.; finally with 851 ἐς ἀλλόφυλον ἐλθοῦσαι χθόνα having come to a foreign land yet to κατὰ γᾶς οἰχνεῖν to go beneath the earth 838, see above. Συμφέρειν τινὶ ὀργάς to share one's wrath with someone is similar to συγγιγνώσκειν to sympathize; exact parallels are lacking, but Paley cites Eurip. Herakles 1366: τἀμὰ συμφέρειν κακά to share my troubles, Blaydes Med. 870 τὰς δ᾽ ἐμὰς ὀργὰς φέρειν εἰκός σε it is fitting for you to bear my wrath (before that αὐτοῦμαί σε I ask you . . συγνώμον᾽ εἶναι to be sympathetic).
848 seems well emended by Wakefield, even if the scholion διὰ τὸν χρόνον because of time does not exactly provide proof for τῶι to the.
851 ἀλλόφυλος of foreign race in the tragedians only here; moreover, the patriotic pride of the Athenian begins to show itself.
Προυννέπω I foretell 98. – To
V. 853 cf. ὑπορρέοντος τοῦ χρόνου as time flows on Aristoph. Νεφ. 1289.

The δόμοι Ἐρεχθέως the house of Erechtheus 855 denote the Erechtheion and the Acropolis; the sanctuary of the Eumenides lay on the slope of the Areopagus that faced the Acropolis, U. Köhler Hermes VI, 100. After 855 a lacuna is rightly assumed, since ὅσην as much as 857 has no reference and is not well emended either in ὅσ᾽ ἂν as many as (Ahrens) or in ὅσων of as many as (Pauw); with ὅσων of as many as the sequence after στόλων of expeditions and the accumulation of genitives is disturbing.
Στόλων processions must, just as at 1027, mean a festive procession; accordingly, women were predominantly involved in this cult; for ἀνδρῶν of men cannot well be dependent on στόλων of processions.

Σχέθοις you may hold aorist, see on Ch. 832, 'you can obtain' (μετασχεῖν to share in 869). Lines 858–866 or 869 are excised by some (Dindorf, Wecklein) as an interpolation, especially because they interrupt the connection. But it is fitting that Athena now also speaks of the Eumenides' return service, and only thus can the summing up be correctly made (868): εὖ δρῶσαν doing well, εὖ πάσχουσαν faring well. Here the return service is expressed only negatively, as abstention from harm (differently after the reconciliation, 903 ff.); the Erinyes have indeed no longer threatened, but they have not retracted their threat, which is why similar things stand in the following speech, 888 f. — Because in the Teubner text edition the order is changed: 858–866 after 912, which seems to me even more wrong: after the reconciliation has taken place, such hostile activity of the Erinyes can no longer be spoken of at all.

Line 859 θηγάνη whetstone whetstone (σιδηροβρῶτι θηγάνηι νεηκονής with iron-devouring, newly sharpened whetstone Soph. Ai. 820) in another transferred use Ag. 1537; cf. τεθηγμένους λόγους sharpened words Prom. 311, Sept. 715 ἀκράτωι τῆς διανοίας ὀργῆι τεθηγμένον sharpened by the unmixed anger of his thought Alcidamas in Aristotle Rhetoric 3, 3, p. 1406 a 9.

The σπλάγχνα inward parts, as the seat of the emotions, are, as it were, sharpened and thereby become bloody, and the angry person is provoked to bloodshed. Such disturbances were thus attributed to the angered spirits of the deep.

Νέων of the young need not be made dependent on σπλάγχνων of the inward parts, but can be an attribute, cf. νέα νηδύς young belly Ch. 757 νέωι θράσει with youthful boldnessPers. 744 (iuvenilis Ddf.). But impossible is ἀοίνους wineless (M perhaps first -οις ois) ἐμμανεῖς θυμώμασιν maddening surges of anger, from which (after Prom. 675 ἐμμανεῖ σκιρτήματι) with maddened leaping) is easily restored ἀοίνοις ἐμμανέσι θυμώμασιν with wineless maddening surges of anger, raging surges of anger, such as can come from wine, but are produced by the avenging spirits without wine.
Θύμωμα surge of anger from θυμοῦσθαι to be angry only here;

ἐμμανέσι with maddening —, ◡ ◡ like μαρτύρια παρῆν witnesses were present 797, νηάλια μειλίγματα wineless propitiatory offerings 107, τυμβοχόα χειρώματα tomb-pouring handiworks Sept. 1122. — Weil quotes from Goethe: Trunken müssen wir alle sein, Jugend ist Trunkenheit ohne Wein.

861 ff. the overall sense and the comparison are surely clear: the ἐνδομάχας ἀλέκτωρ cock that fights at home Pind. Ol. 12, 14 denotes the Cretans who fight only at home among themselves. But ἐξελοῦσα καρδίαν having taken out the heart 'taking out the heart' does not even seem to have been the reading of the scholiast, who explains with ἀναπτερώσασα having stirred up. Ἐκζέουσα boiling out however (Musgrave) does not lie very close to the features, and also gives nothing characteristic for the cocks; the other conjectures are equally unconvincing. So I keep (with Sidgwick) the transmitted text and only set the punctuation somewhat differently: ὣς so (Ch. 106. 506 etc.) for ὡς as and comma before ἐξελοῦσα having taken out and after ἀλεκτόρων of cocks, "as if you had taken out the heart of cocks, to implant it in the citizens (ἱδρύσηις ἐν κτἑ you may establish in etc..)."
Ἄρη Ares: cf. 355; in πρὸς ἀλλήλους θρασύν bold against one another the emphasis lies on πρὸς ἀλλήλους against one another.

V. 864 οὐ μόλις not hardly the scholiast explains with οὐ μακράν not far; cf. Ag. 1082 ἀπώλεσας γὰρ οὐ μόλις τὸ δεύτερον for you have destroyed not hardly the second, according to Triclinius = ταχέως quickly; Eur. Hel. 334 θέλουσαν οὐ μόλις καλεῖς you call her willing, not hardly, where no other meaning than 'utterly' is possible. This fits also in the Agamemnon; here this and that, also to what follows: "so much the more will mighty desire for glory inflame the hearts". The pride of the fighter of Marathon comes out here, as also below 913 ff. A. can also think of the battles with Boeotians and Chalcidians; of the civil strife, when Cleomenes occupied the citadel, he had experienced something as a boy, and upon these had quickly followed those heavy battles. Δεινὸς ἔρως dreadful desire Plat. Theait. 169 B, δ but. ἵμερος longing Hdt. 9, 3. —

V. 866 οὐ λέγω I do not say as Ch. 989 Αἰγίσθου γὰρ οὐ λέγω μόρον for I do not speak of the fate of Aegisthus, Ag. 871 τὴν κάτω γὰρ οὐ λέγω for I do not speak of the one below. I do not mean and do not want the fighting spirit.
V. 868 double anaphora, to Ch. 628.
Chorus 870—880, antistrophe β b. The chorus still does not react, but repeats even now what was last presented.
Shorter repetition of what has just been said in detail.
881 τἀγαθά the good things ῾ 'what is also good for you'.
Πρός towards 882 with ἔρρειν to go to ruin as at 100, Prom. 92, Ch. 419 with παθεῖν to suffer, Eum 627 with θανεῖν to die; a kind of passive sense tends to be present (Wecklein).

Πολισσοῦχος guardian of the city: see on 775. Τῆσδε γῆς ἀπόξενος stranger to this land Ag. 1282, Ch. 1042, of whom φυγάς exile; here of the rejected stranger. That they have been rejected by her, at least that Athena wants to make it impossible for them to say.

V. 885 ἁγνὸν Πειθοῦς σέβας the holy majesty of Persuasion comes very close to the line quoted from the Myrmidons, σέβας δὲ μηρῶν ἁγνὸν οὐκ ἐπηιδέσω you did not respect the holy majesty of my thighs, ὦ δυσχάριστε τῶν πυκνῶν φιλημάτων O you ungrateful one, despite my many kisses (address to Ares, whose φιλήματα kisses are the wounds; Patroclus was wounded ἐς κενεῶνα in the flank; pederastically misinterpreted by Athenaeus and Plutarch, despite the clear ἁγνόν holy). Here, however, ἁγνὸν holy is predicate, = εἰ μὲν ἅζηι τὴν σεμνὴν Πειθώ if you revere august Persuasion (σέβας majesty 92. 545. 703); the elaboration of Πειθοῦς σέβας the majesty of Persuasion is γλώσσης ἐμῆς μείλιγμα the soothing charm of my tongue (107, Ch. 15) καὶ θελκτήριον and enchantment (here substantival; adjectival θελκτηρία enchantments Ch. 670).

Σὺ δ᾽ οὖν μένοις ἄν You then may remain (= μένε remain) as σὺ δ᾽ οὖν δίωκε you then pursue 226, where δ d' οὖν then as everywhere contains the idea that one does not wish to speak further of something. The promises have all been stated, and this is recalled by εἰ μὲν ἁγνόν ἐστι κτέ if it is holy, etc.. "Well then, stay" 888 ἐπιρρέπειν to incline transitive as Ag. 250 Δίκα δὲ τοῖς μὲν παθοῦσιν μαθεῖν ἐπιρρέπει. Justice inclines to those who have suffered, so that they may learn..

890 γαμόρωι to the husbandman (Dobree's brilliant emendation) as Hik. 613. The compounds with γῆ earth have in the tragedians also in dialogue γα ga- (as also γάποτος earth-drinking Ch. 97. 163), Dindorf Lex. 64 a.
Δικαίως justly cf. 291. 1025. ἀτιμοπενθεῖς unhonored in mourning. 894 Μένει remains cannot be
Stichomythia 892–902. At last the unwearied friendly encouragement has prevailed.

893 ἀπήμον᾽ οἰζύος free from misery as οὐκ ἄπαππον Ἰδαίου πυρός not without a share of Idaian fire Ag. 311; more often Sophocles, OC. 786 κακῶν ἄνατος without share of evils etc., Wecklein, Blaydes. One must also think of the misery that the Erinyes could bring; yet their own is first denied: 780 τάλαινα wretched, 791 f. μεγάλα δυστυχεῖς you are greatly unfortunate . . ἀτιμοπενθεῖς unhonored in mourning. 894 καὶ δὴ δέδεγμαι and now I have accepted hypothetical, see on Ch. 566. Μένει remains cannot be 'awaits', where the accusative would have to stand, but must mean 'remains', 'is not snatched away'. They are still in doubt. The answer 825 is surprising and calls forth the astonished question 826.
Εὐθενεῖν to prosper also 908. 944.

V. 897 συμφοράς misfortunes neuter; related is the passage 1017 ff. μετοικίαν δ᾽ ἐμὴν εὖ σέβοντες οὔτι μέμψεσθε συμφορὰς βίου if you honor my residence, you will not blame the misfortunes of life. Ὀρθοῦν to set upright as Ch. 584.
Πρόπας all Ag. 1011, Prom. 406 etc.; thus Abresch correctly wrote πρόπαντος of all, although the πρὸ παντὸς before all of the manuscripts (= ὑπὲρ παντὸς above all, 835) would not be impossible.
Ἐγγύην τίθεσθαι to make a pledge = ποιεῖσθαι to make, as ὅρκους θεμένη having sworn oaths Ag. 1570 (Blaydes).
899 is said with fine wit and self-assurance.
901 τοιγάρ therefore 603; κατὰ χθόν᾽ οὖσ᾽ κτἑ being beneath the earth, etc.. You will therefore not go away, but remain here and win new friends.
902 τί οὖν what then with the usual hiatus (Blaydes): Hik. 306, Pers. 787, Sept. 208. 704. The friendship must now show itself on both sides.

On νίκης of victory cf. 1008 τὸ δὲ κερδαλέον πέμπειν πόλεως ἐπὶ νίκηι to send what is profitable to the city for victory, victory and excelling in everything, except in battles, for victory in στάσις faction, civil strife (861 ff., 976 ff.) is nothing good. Differently νίκη κακή evil victory (cowardly) Sept. 716. Ἐπίσκοπος overseer, guardian from σκοπός mark, target aim, aiming at, as Soph. Αi. 976 ἄτης τῆσδ᾽ ἐπίσκοπον μέλος a song that watches over this ruin, i.e. ἐστοχασμένον aimed at according to the scholia, ἐπίσκοπα τοξεύειν to shoot at a mark Hdt. 3, 35.
Γῆθεν from the earth as Sept. 247;

δρόσος dew, moisture generally means 'moisture', as Ag. 1363 φοινίας δρόσου of bloody dew of blood; of sea- or river-water Eurip. I. T. 255. 1192 (ἐναλία of the sea, θαλασσία of the sea), Hippol. 192 (ποταμία of the river).

V. 905 suffers from confused construction, unless one writes τἀνέμων the winds for κἀνέμων and winds (the crasis of τὰ the (neuter plural article) is especially frequent, τἀγαθά the good things 881 etc., Dindorf Lex. 233a). The emphasis lies on εὐηλίως in sunny weather: not storms with dark sky and bad weather. Cf. Eurip. Med. 837 ff. of Attica (μετρίας ἀνέμων αὔρας moderate breezes of winds). After the ἐξ οὐρανοῦ from the sky has thus been carried out at once, the γῆθεν from the earth is returned to, and there follow the three items usually combined (also in curses): fruits — herds — children. Cf. Hik. 674 ff., Soph. OT. 270f. (herds not mentioned, but see 25 ff.), Hdt. 3, 65, Aeschin. 3, 111 (Weckl.), and e.g. the Cretan inscription DI 5058, 40 ff.: τέκνων ὄνασιν γίνεσθαι καὶ γᾶν ἔνκαρπον φέρειν καὶ πρόβατα εὐθηνεῖν that there be enjoyment of children and that the land bear fruit and the flocks thrive.
Καρπός fruit, crop is transferred by zeugma to the βοτά flocks, herds;
ἐπίρρυτον flowing upon, abundant 'abundantly', cf. ὄλβου δ᾽ ἐπιρρυέντος when wealth flows in Eur. Med. 1229 κακῶν ἐπιρροάς streams of evils Andr. 349.
