V. 909 in σωτηρίαν salvation, deliverance the object of ἐφυμνῆσαι to sing in praise emerges again. 911

ἐκφορωτέρα more carrying out: while you protect the offspring (909), you may rather proceed in the opposite way against δυσσεβοῦντες the impious (comparative with a kind of litotes, which has a threatening effect by virtue of the hint); ἐκφέρειν to carry out to carry out, as the gardener does the weeds.
Φιτυποίμην may I produce naturally only here;

912 τῶν δικαίων τῶνδε of these just men reference to the citizens present. Cf. Demosth. 20, 39 καὶ γὰρ Ἀθηναίων τινές εἰσιν ἴσως φαῦλοι for some of the Athenians are perhaps worthless — ἀλλὰ τὸν δῆμον νομίζων χρηστόν but considering the people good (fictitious speech of Leucon). V. 913
σούστί it is yours = σοί ἐστι it is to you, you have as your office (others σοῦ ᾿στί it is of you; but that would be σά ἐστι it is yours).

Ἀρείφατος slain by Ares, warlike in Aeschylus is nothing but ἀρήιος warlike, martial, with the second part no longer felt, Frg. 145 ἀρείφατον λῆμα warlike spirit, explained by Hesychius with ἰσχυρόν strong, ἀντὶ τοῦ Ἄρει ἐοικός instead of 'like Ares'.

Πρεπτός conspicuous, distinguished also Aristoph. Lysistr. 1298; πόλιν ἀστύνικον ἀγώνων a city victorious in contests as 37 ποδωκείᾶι σκελῶν with swiftness of feet, and δορὸς νικηφόρον victorious with the spear 777;
ἀστύνικον victorious in the city predicative.
Οὐκ ἀνέξομαι I will not endure is forcefully said, as the whole thought is forceful and proud (on 864);
τὸ μὴ οὐ the not Prom. 787. 918.

The rhythms in the whole choral song are predominantly trochees, mostly, as usual, catalectic dimeters. So it was also in the stasima, except that in those, toward the end, tragic pathos came to expression in iambs; here there was no place for that. Therefore in this first strophe, as the third-from-last colon, ἐπισσύτους βίου τύχας ὀνησίμους the onrushing fortunes of life, beneficial, an iambic hexapody, cannot stand; rather one must attach it to the preceding θεσπίσασα πρευμενῶς having prophesied graciously: ICICICI-, just as already before τὰν καὶ Ζεὺς ὁ παγκρατὴς Ἄρης τε φρούριον θεῶν νέμει which both Zeus the all-powerful and Ares hold as a stronghold of the gods, and in the stasimon at 496 (325). The form 「「 by itself at the beginning of the colon at 918, at the end of a colon, in connection with the next in strophe and antistrophe, 920 ῥυσίβωμον ῾Ελλά altar-protecting Hellas-. But difficult is 925 γαίας of the earth † ἐξαμβρῦσαι to cause to miscarry = 947 πλουτόχθων ἑρμαίαν earth-wealthy, of Hermes, according to Rossbach-Westphal consisting of nothing but three-time lengths and therefore a hexapody. What one expects, however, precisely at this penultimate place of the strophe, are dactyls, like Ch. 30 - -, - -, - -, -, - -, before ----; 591 likewise, but dactyls in the first four places; likewise Eumen. 387, and dactyls are also mixed in afterward in Str. β γ β γ, pentapody and tripodies. A tripody, to be sure consisting of nothing but spondees, I therefore assume here as well; for that the antistrophe with its six lengths must be authoritative is not doubtful. - In strophe and antistrophe there is continuous synaphea. In content, the first strophe is a general introduction to the song of blessing.
Ἄρης Ares: with a new allusion to the victories (or also to the Areopagus, 689? In any case Ares had a temple nearby there, Pausan. I, 8, 4, just as Zeus had the great Olympieion);

φρούριον stronghold here 'citadel', 'guarded place', while at 949 πόλεως φρούριον stronghold of the city and Prom. 801 it means the guards. Therefore (Pers. 348) θεοὶ πόλιν σώιζουσι Παλλάδος θεᾶς the gods save the city of Pallas the goddess. In what follows, the connection ῾Ελλάνων δαιμόνων of the Hellenes, of the divinities is after all impossible according to the sense, and that of ῾Ελλάνων of the Hellenes with ἄγαλμα glory, ornament, of δαιμόνων of the divinities with ῥυσίβωμον altar-protecting (Wecklein) is against the word order, according to which one must connect and understand ἄγαλμα δαιμόνων glory of the divinities (like τέκνον δόμων ἄγαλμα child, the glory of the house Ag. 208, cf. 741, Ch. 200, Prom. 466) ῥυόμενον τοὺς βωμοὺς τῶν Ἑλλήνων protecting the altars of the Hellenes. Better, however, is to insert after δαιμόνων of the divinities a τ τ': "jewel of all Hellenes and of the gods themselves". Correctly one has referred ῥυσίβωμον altar-protecting to the protection that Athens gave to all Hellas against the Persians, who destroyed altars and temples (Pers. 809 ff.).

It is natural to take the νέμει he distributes as synonymous with νομίζει he regards as customary; see on 624; however, at 1015f. δαίμονές τε καὶ βροτοὶ Παλλάδος πόλιν νέμοντες both divinities and mortals inhabiting the city of Pallas stands unambiguously, and the double accusative is also possible with this νέμειν to distribute.

At line 921 κατεύχομαι I pray as at Ch. 88. 139, with no other sense of the κατά down than that of intensification; θεσπίσασα having prophesied (Ag. 1210. 1213) 'prophesying'; the aorist does not contradict the κατεύχομαι I pray, since this too, transposed into the past, would yield κατηυξάμην I prayed (cf. πρόσσω κατανασσαμένη I will accomplish, having settled 928f.). In general, in what follows the form of the wish prevails, not that of prophecy; though when mighty divinities wish, there is hardly a difference between 'may' and 'shall' or 'will'; see what Athena says at 949ff. Ἐπίσσυτος rushing upon Ag. 887. 1150; I see no reason to correct to the synonymous and only weaker ἐπιρρύτους flowing upon (907), where even of flowing things Ag. 887 κλαυμάτων ἐπίσσυτοι πηγαί rushing fountains of tears stands. Bright sunshine (906) will make all other good things sprout from the earth in richest abundance, like the fruits; for the gods and spirits of the deep send all fortune and again all misfortune (Ch. 147, Pers. 222 etc.). Ἐξαμβρῦσαι to make gush forth seems correctly emended except for the tense; at least from later authors such as Himerius and the Anacreontea Lobeck on Ajax p. 77 brings enough evidence for factitive βρύειν to swell. But the aorist I cannot understand; better the future, connected to θεσπίσασα having prophesied.

Between the five anapestic passages of Athena there is, as G. Hermann recognized, a responsion, though not corresponding to that of the strophes and antistrophes by which they are separated. Rather, this first passage responds with the last, 1003-1013, but the three middle ones with each other. In a and e a sentence begins in each case with three dimeters; the second, belonging to the same system, can be written as dimeter monom. dim. monom. paroem., if in a after πληγαὶ βιότου blows of life one supplies the missing verb. There follows now a second system in dim. dim. monom. paroemiac.

928 δυσαρέστους hard to appease 'hard to appease', now for Athena and in quite a different measure for humans who transgress against them. Κατανάσσασθαι to settle belongs to the factitive ἔνασσα I settled Pind. Pyth. 5, 71, κατένασσα I settled down Hesiod Thg. 329, Frg. 168. With 930f. cf. 310. In 932 either βαρεῶν of the heavy ones or μὴ not must be changed: "whom they do not meet graciously" or "whom they meet in anger"; the latter is supported by γε μήν yet indeed (Prom. 871 σπορᾶς γε μὴν ἐκ τῆσδε φύσεται θρασύς yet from this seed a bold one will be born, cf. also above 51, where it is strongly adversative), while the former is not so easy. Ahrens corrected the accent: the Attic dialect also knows for these adjectives -έα one instead of -εῖα one: θρασέα bold Philemon, ἡμίσεα half inscriptions, Thuc., Plat., πλατέα broad Xenophon, Kühner-Blass I, 443.

933 οὐκ οἶδεν ὅθεν he does not know whence, namely that ἐκ τούτων from these; if after 'know' and the like the relative as representative of the interrogative denotes something definite, then the definite relative and not the indefinite ὅστις whoever must be used. Πληγή blow as Pers. 251. 906; as verb Hermann supplies προσέπαισαν they struck.

Ἀπλάκημα error as ἀπλακών having erred Eurip. Alk. 241 (manuscripts ἀμπλ error. as here), under metrical constraint; cf. in Homer ἀνδροτῆτα ι Προτέρων manliness of earlier men as Ag. 1338 εἰ προτέρων αἷμ᾿ ἀποτείσει if he pays the blood of earlier men, Ch. 402 ff. βοᾶι λοιγὸς Ἐρινύν destruction cries out for the Erinys, παρὰ τῶν πρότερον φθιμένων ἄτην ἑτέραν ἐπάγουσαν ἐπ᾽ ἄτηι from those who perished before, bringing another ruin upon ruin. Without twisting and distorting, however, it is impossible to bring into ἐκ προτέρων ἀπλακήματα from earlier errors a reference to those murdered earlier, and Blaydes rightly compares Eur. Hippol. 831: πρόσωθεν δέ ποθεν ἀνακομίζομαι τύχαν δαιμόνων ἀμπλακίαισι τῶν πάροιθέν τινος from somewhere far off I recover a fortune, through the errors of some of those before, see also passages like Ag. 1500 ff. –

V. 935 σιγῶν ὄλεθρος silent destruction as Hes. Erga 102 νοῦσοι αὐτόματοι φοιτῶσι diseases come of their own accord.. σιγῆι in silence, ἐπεὶ φωνὴν ἐξείλετο μητίετα Ζεύς since Zeus the counsellor took away their voice. The opposite is μέγα φωνοῦντα speaking loudly (Sidgwick).

On ἀμαθύνει destroys utterly cf. Homer Il. 9.593 πόλιν δέ τε πῦρ ἀμαθύνει and fire utterly destroys a city, so Aeschylus πόλιν διημάθυνεν utterly destroyed the city Ag. 824 (fr. 239 κύνες διημάθυνον ἄνδρα δεσπότην dogs utterly destroyed the man, their master, the Actaeon). Similar in overall thought are the choral song at vv. 368 ff., the chorus's antistrophe α a, 938–948. Blessing on agriculture, livestock, mining; cf. 905–908. Δενδροπήμων βλάβα tree-harming damage of storms that damage the trees (olives especially); φλογμὸς φυτῶν flame of plants refers to the young plantings, which the storms do not harm, but which lose their buds through the fire; νόσος ἄκαρπος fruitless disease however to the seed (καρπὸν γαίας fruit of the earth 907). Whether χάριν favor is the object of λέγω I say (cf. δολοφόνου λέβητος τύχαν σοι λέγω I tell you the fortune of the murderous cauldron Ag. 1129), or (Dindorf) τὰν ἐμὰν χάριν ῾ my favor means 'for my sake', makes no difference for the sense, but does matter somewhat for the construction in what follows, which has been damaged in transmission and which even the insertion of τε and does not fully remedy. But if one writes φλογμόν τ᾽ ὀμματοστερῆ and the eye-destroying flame, then one can easily attach τό τε μὴ φλογμὸν περᾶν ὅρον and that the flame not pass its boundary to τὰν ἐμὰν χάριν my favor (substantive) as a further elaboration. Ὀφθαλμός eye of the eye of plants is a common metaphor (Theophrastus and others); on τόπων of places cf. ἐν τόποισι τοῖς ἐμοῖς in my places 858 (292, 706, 1023); (ἄκαρπος fruitless) αἰανὴς νόσος grievous disease repetition of 479 (ἄφερτος unbearable) αἰανὴς νόσος grievous disease. The imperative is simply synonymous with the optative, cf. in the suppliants' blessing song ἔστω let it be 669, 687, ἐπελθέτω let it come upon 679. – The blessing of the herds is wished for Hik. 691 as follows: πρόνομα δὲ βοτὰ τὼς πολύγονα τελέθοι may the grazing flocks be prolific; similarly here ξὺν διπλοῖσιν ἐμβρύοις with twin offspring. But the state of pregnancy must be followed by birth, and to this χρόνωι τεταγμένωι at the appointed time clearly points; therefore γόνος offspring, after which two syllables are missing, must be corrected in γόνον offspring with a missing infinitive, perhaps γόνον offspring (τελεῖν to bring to fulfillment). I do not doubt Dobree's εὐθενοῦντα γᾶ thriving land instead of εὐθενοῦντ᾽ ἄγαν thriving exceedingly: γᾶ τρέφει the earth nourishes Ch. 585; but ἄγαν exceedingly is always pejorative in Aeschylus. Now if because of πλουτόχθων rich in land γόνος offspring was wrongly written instead of γόνον offspring, then a following nominative has probably also been corrupted into the accusative: correctly πλουτόχθων rich in land (θ th) ἑρμαία δαιμόνων δόσις τίοι may the gods' Hermaic gift honor, for which the Athenians are the object. How else is γόνος πλουτόχθων ἑρμαίαν δόσιν τίοι may the land-rich offspring honor the Hermaic gift to be explained? The reference to Laureion is clear in πλουτόχθων rich in land and in ἑρμαία Hermaic, since Hermes is the god of lucky finds; ὡς ἐφάνη τὰ μέταλλα τὰ ἐν Μαρωνείαι as the mines in Maroneia appeared Aristotle Πολ Pol. 19. 22, 7. Cf. Pers. 238.

This second system, corresponding to the following ones, was first correctly written by Weil. In the anapaests one usually distributes dimeters and monometers so as to follow the divisions of sense as closely as possible; accordingly, in c (968 ff.) and d (989 ff.) a monometer is placed in second position, and then likewise in penultimate position, since the total number of metra is even (14). The same number also occurs in b, and after the third strong sense-division; therefore monometer οἷ᾽ ἐπικραίνει what things she brings to fulfillment, cf. 969 ἐπικραινομένων of things being brought to fulfillment. The rest also fits in smoothly and pleasingly. Athena, similarly as before, duly emphasizes the significance of this blessing in relation to the representation of the citizens, the Areopagus. On πόλεως φρούριον the city's fortress cf. 919, and φρούρημα γῆς the land's defense 706. The combination of two resolutions in ἀκούετε πόλεως you hear of the city is objectionable; but one can write ἀκούεις you hear, since the singular is so often used by the chorus.
Ἐπικραίνει She brings to fulfillment: the wish of these deities includes its fulfillment.

Ἀθανάτοις to the immortals as the opposite of τοῖς ὑπὸ γαῖαν to those beneath the earth is no more objectionable than 349 ἀθανάτων of the immortals used exclusively of the Olympians. Under the earth are the spirits of the departed; true immortality belongs only to the gods of heaven who dwell in eternal light.

Ὑπὸ γαῖαν under the earth as at ὑπὸ χθόνα under the ground 395; since Homer ὑπό under with accusative is also used for the question 'where'. I would also not take offense at φανερῶς openly (for those in the know) τελέως completely. Ἀμβλωπὸς βίος δακρύων a life dimmed by tears explains itself; πρὸς δ᾽ ὄμματ᾿ ἀχλὺς ἀμβλωπὸς ἐφίζει and a dimming mist settles upon their eyes Critias 2, 11 Bgk. Choral strophe β b, 956-967. Trochees at beginning and end; in the middle dactyls, a pentapody and three tripodies, of which the first is catalectic; before them and after the pentapody θεαί τ᾽ ὦ Μοῖραι ματροκασιγνῆται and you, goddesses Moirai, sisters from the same mother = δι᾽ ὀργὰν ποινᾶς ἀντιφόνους ἄτας through wrath, the ruin of reciprocal vengeance. That looks like a dochmiac dimeter; but dochmiacs are impossible here. Rossbach-Westphal take the second part as a catalectic-dactylic tripody like the following, but θεαί τ᾽ ὦ Μοῖραι and you, goddesses Moirai as 「「「「「, i.e. as iambic, which seems to me hardly less inadmissible than the dochmiacs. If, however, one reads θεαί goddesses and treats the antistrophe accordingly, one has a catalectic pentapody as at 534. The blessing of the first antistrophe refers to the preservation of youth and at length to happy marriages: as if the Erinyes now thought differently about this too than before (212 ff. 605). ᾿Ανδροκμής man-slaying 248; ἀώρους τύχας untimely fates as θανάτων ἀώρων of untimely deaths in the Attic skolion (2 Bgk.), ἀπεννέπω I forbid Sept. 1053 (also Soph. and Eurip.). So the Suppliants 678 ff.: μηδέ τις ἀνδροκμὴς λοιγὸς ἐπελθέτω τᾶνδε πόλιν δαΐζων and let no man-slaying destruction come upon this city, laying it waste. – Κύρι᾽ ἔχοντες holding authority 960 the marriage gods, besides Aphrodite Hera τελεία perfect and Zeus τέλειος perfect (214 f.), to whom the Moirai now are added, cf. Pollux 3, 38 (above on 835), εὐνὴ ἀνδρὶ καὶ γυναικὶ μόρσιμος a marriage fated for man and wife 217. Ματροκασιγνῆται sisters from the same mother sisters on the mother's side, according to Hesiod Theog. 217; all these children of Night have no father according to Hesiod. Μετάκοινος sharing in 354, Hik. 1038; ἐπιβριθεῖς weighing heavily (only here) ruling mightily at all times with their just intervention (ὁμιλία company 57 etc.).
Athena expresses her great satisfaction at the reconciliation achieved through good words.

Ἐπικραίνω I bring to fulfillment is otherwise always active without middle, and therefore some construe: γάνυμαι τάδε I rejoice in these things, ἐπικραινομένων being fulfilled (pass.) αὐτῶν of them, which cannot please. Either, then, the middle is to be recognized here after all (they grant from their power, and cf. (ἀπ from)αξιοῦσθαι to be deemed worthy 367. 425; αὐδᾶσθαι to be spoken 379; Paley on Prom. 43), or ἐπικραινουσῶν of those fulfilling is to be written. The epic γάνυμαι I rejoice A. has only here.

Στέργω I love 'love'; Πειθοῦς σέβας the majesty of Persuasion already at 885; on ὄμματα eyes (the friendly face) Il. Wecklein compares Soph. Frg. 743 Dd. δεινὸν τὸ τᾶς Πειθοῦς πρόσωπον terrible is the face of Persuasion. The present ἐπωπᾶι she watches over I do not understand here, since the speech is about the persuasion that has taken place, which finally succeeded (aor. ἐκράτησε it prevailed); therefore ἐπώπα she watched over imperfect.

Ζεὺς Ἀγοραῖος Zeus of the Assembly, worshipped in Athens (CIA I, 23; Aristoph. Ἱππ Knights. 410; Hesych. under ἀγοραίου of the assembly), Sparta, Thebes, Olympia, etc. (Preller-Robert Myth. 150), guides the assemblies of the citizens and the speaking and persuading in them: καί σε φυλάττοι Ζεὺς Ἀγοραῖος and may Zeus of the Assembly protect you is said to Ἱππ Knights. 500 to the sausage-seller going into the council. ᾿Αγαθῶν ἔρις ἡμετέρα our strife for good things is explained by 1012 εἴη δ᾽ ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθὴ διάνοια πολίταις may there be good intent for good things among the citizens, and this again (Wieseler) by Aristoph. Βάτρ. 1530 (imitation of A.) τῆι δὲ πόλει μεγάλων ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθὸς ἐπινοίας and to the city grant good thoughts for great goods (namely δότε grant); therefore ἀγαθῶν of good things is neuter. Our strife, always directed toward the good, prevails as now constantly. In ἡμετέρα our Athena probably includes herself with Zeus. Chorus antistr. β b, 976-987. No civil war; concord of the citizens. Cf. in the blessing song of the Suppliants 661: μηδ᾽ ἐπιχωρίοις nor with native ⟨στάσις strife⟩ πτώμασιν αἱματίσαι πέδον γᾶς to stain the ground of the land with bloodshed. With 980 compare also Sept. 736 καὶ χθονία κόνις πίηι μελαμπαγὲς αἷμα φοίνιον and the dust of the earth may drink the black-clotted blood of murder. Μέλαν αἷμα black blood is Homeric. Ἁρπαλίζειν to snatch still Sept. 243 μή νυν ἐὰν θνήισκοντας ἢ τετρωμένους πύθησθε do not, I pray, learn of men dying or wounded, κωκυτοῖσιν ἁρπαλίζετε you snatch with lamentations; Hesych. explains with ἀσμένως δέχομαι I gladly accept. If the rhythm of 981 is correctly determined as dactylic, then δι᾽ ὀργάν through anger must be changed, most simply to ὀργᾶι he is angry (Ag. 216) and then ποινὰς ἀντιφόνους requitals in return for blood ⟨τ t’⟩ ἄτας ruin, cf. ἀντικτόνοις ποιναῖσι with requitals for murder 464. Πόλεως of the city yet to ἄτας ruin.
983 χάρματα δ᾽ ἀντιδιδοῖεν may they give joys in return stands in contrast to the preceding; καὶ στυγεῖν and to hate contains a further object parallel to χάρματα joys.

Exhortation to the citizens to honor these deities now also accordingly. The slightly corrupted beginning must be emended so that the Erinyes are not addressed (which happens only in the next, in content entirely different system); therefore φρονοῦσι they think(ν n) (M f) . .

εὑρίσκειν to find: are they not intent on finding the way to blessings? So Homer φρόνεον they intended . . ἐρύειν to draw Ρ 286; ἀκοντίζειν οὐκ ἐφρόνουν they did not intend to throw Xenoph. Kyr. 3, 3, 66, and A. himself φρόνει μὲν ὡς ταρβοῦσα μὴ ἀμελεῖν θεῶν think, as one fearing, not to neglect the gods Hik. 773. —
V. 990 προσώπων faces refers to the, naturally retained, terrifying mask = face.

V. 902 εὔφρονας εὔφρονες kindly-minded to kindly-minded as at 998 φίλας φίλοι friendly to friends, 1012 ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθή good to good etc., μέγα τιμῶντες greatly honoring cf. 12; on ὀρθοδίκαιον upright in justice cf. εὐθυδίκαιοι straight in justice 312. Πρέπειν to be fitting with participle as at Ag. 30 ἐγγέλλων πρέπει it is fitting to announce, 1222 σπλάγχνα πρέπουσ᾽ ἔχοντες having entrails that are fitting. On the use of διάγειν to pass one's life cf. Isocr. 3, 41 τὰς πόλεις ἐν ὁμονοίᾱι διάγειν to keep the cities in concord.
Πάντως in every way (g; conjectured by Bothe) is better than the weak πάντες all (Paley).

Still dactyls and trochees; the trochees of the simplest structure, namely three times two connected catalectic dimeters (binding by word-community twice in the antistrophe). The dactylic verse is usually restored as a logaoedic one, against the usage of this kind of strophe; but one can just as well scan διπλοίζω I double in the antistrophe and write αἰσιμίαις with just portions⟨ιν in⟩ in the strophe. The chorus prepares to depart to the dwelling-places to be assigned to it; thus the exodos is already prepared from here on.

Αἰσιμία just portion occurs only in this passage; ἐναισιμία righteousness (for one can also join into one word) Hesychius has with the explanation διοσημία divine sign; as adjectives αἴσιμος fated like ἐναίσιμος righteous are found in Homer. The sense must be: 'in the (or at the, χαίρουσαν εὐεστοῖ πόλιν the city rejoicing in prosperity Ag. 647) wealth granted by fate'.

Ἴκταρ near = ἐγγύς near Ag. 116 (Frg. 58), proverb in Plat. Πολιτεία ΙΧ Republic IX 575 C οὐδ᾽ ἴκταρ βάλλει nor does he strike near. But one must not mix in the θεῶν ἀγχίσποροι near-born of the gods and Πρίαμον ἐγγὺς θεῶν γεγονότα Priam, who was born near the gods and the like, since it is not at all about descent, but only about the mighty protection of Pallas; so this is the pious belief of the Athenian, which Solon already expresses (4, 1 ff. Bgk): ἡμετέρα δὲ πόλις κατὰ μὲν Διὸς οὔποτ᾽ ὀλεῖται αἶσαν καὶ μακάρων θεῶν φρένας ἀθανάτων But our city will never perish by the decree of Zeus and the mind of the blessed immortal gods· τοίη γὰρ μεγάθυμος ἐπίσκοπος ὀβριμοπάτρη Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη χεῖρας ὕπερθεν ἔχει For such a great-hearted guardian, Pallas Athena, daughter of a mighty father, holds her hands over it (see also Pers. 347, above 918 f.). The here meaningless ἐν χρόνωι in time (in time, with time, 498 etc.) has been excellently emended by Weil into ἔμφρονος of sound mind: σωφρονοῦντες ἔμφρονος being of sound mind like φίλας φίλοι friendly to friends.

Σώφρονος of sound mind neither the verse nor the sense suffered. 'Ὑπὸ πτεροῖς under wings metaphorically under the protection', taken from birds; so (Blaydes) Eurip. Herakles 10; clearly Andr. 441 ἢ καὶ νεοσσὸν τόνδ or even this nestling', ὑπὸ πτερῶν σπάσας having drawn under wings, and Tro. 751.
Ἄζεται he reveres: cf. ἄζονται they revere . . ἵκτορας suppliants 651; similar to σέβων τὸν ἱκέτην revering the suppliant above 151.

Now Athena turns to the departing chorus, to whom she now wishes to assign seats along with her citizens. It is striking that here the προπομποί escorts are mentioned as already present (τῶνδε of these), and likewise the sacrificial victims as present (1006). However, the goddess can arrange whatever she wishes without saying so and without it being noticed; whether, moreover, reference is made to something already visible is questionable, cf. on 1025 f. Θαλάμους ὑπὸ γῆς chambers beneath the earth also Pers. 624. — 1007

σύμεναι going: see on 786; for what follows, in which what is prayed for from chthonic deities in general is stated, cf. Pers. 222 ff. (Δαρεῖον Darius) ἐσθλά σοι πέμπειν τέκνωι τε γῆς ἔνερθεν ἐς φάος to send good things to you and to your child from beneath the earth into the light, τἄμπαλιν δὲ τῶνδε γαίας κάτοχα μουροῦσθαι σκότωι but the opposite of these, to be allotted to the darkness beneath the earth. The genitive χώρας of the land, which is difficult to construe, Paley has emended to the dative; then πόλεως ἐπὶ νίκηι for victory of the city belongs together (ἐπὶ νίκηι for victory Ch. 478. 868 with reference to the single actual battle; different here, where one will compare 974 f.). In 1010 the Areopagites are undoubtedly addressed, as in 949; since Athena herself has declared that she will lead, it must read χὐμεῖς δ᾽ and you.

Πολισσοῦχος city-protecting 775. 883; the legendary Κραναός Cranaus, as eponymous hero of the ancient Κραναοί Cranai, who in turn are named from the κραναὰ πόλις rocky city, appears here for the first time. Hdt. 8, 44 says that the Athenians in Pelasgian times were Pelasgians, under the name Κραναοί Cranai; the Κραναὰ πόλις rocky city occurs in Aristoph. Ἱππ Hipp.. 75 (exclamation ὦ Κρ O Cr.. π p.), Lysistr. 480 τὴν Κραναάν the rocky city (the Acropolis), Ὄρν Orn.. 123 τῶν Κραναῶν of the Cranai (Athens), and is said (Schol. Ach.) to have occurred also in Aeschylus and Sophocles. With the last words, likewise addressed to the representatives of the citizenry, Athena recalls 985 (διανοίαι with thought); on the meaning see on 975. Chorus antistr. γ g, 1014–1020, another farewell. The χαίρετε χαίρετε δ farewell, farewell, but' αὖθις again must refer to 996, and likewise the † ἐπιδιπλοίζω I double, in which ἔπη διπλ words double. may lie (Weil; with a nevertheless striking plural), or ἐπεὶ διπλοίζω since I double (Wieseler); further afield are ἐπανδιπλοίζω I double again (Hermann, after Prom. 817 ἐπαναδίπλαζε double again) and ἔπος διπλοίζω I double the word (Ddf.). The simplex διπλοίζω I double stands at Ag. 835. For the sense, ἐπανα again- seems more essential than ἔπος word, and thus I have adopted ἐπανδιπλοίζω I double again. Εὐ σέβοντες revering well instead of εὐσεβοῦντες revering well not only removes the rarer construction εὐσεβεῖν τινα to revere someone (Eurip. Tro. 85, Phoen. 1321, cf. Ag. 338 ἀσεβεῖν τινα to act impiously toward someoneEum. 270), but it also strengthens the sense, since εὐσεβεῖν to revere is the same as σέβειν to revere. Aeschylus wrote EΥΣΕΒΟΝΤΕΣ revering well, which can be this or that. Cf. εὖ προτίων honoring well 645 and elsewhere.
Συμφοράς misfortunes: see on 897; οὐ μέμψεσθε you will not blame litotes equivalent to ἐπαινέσετε you will praise; cf. 596, Hik. 137. 774 etc.
1021 κατευγμάτων of prayers as κατεύχομαι I pray 922;

λαμπάδων σελασφόρων of torch-bearing lights as λ l. φαεσφόρων light-bearing Ag. 489. Κάτω χθονός below the earth is not said (nor is Ag. 871 f. to be construed thus), but κατὰ χθονός down under the earth, which I restore. That Athena sends her own temple attendants along is a special honor; they must, however, be identical with a part of those named at 1025 ff., whom Athena designates as ὄμμα πάσης χθονὸς Θησῆιδος eye of all the land of Theseus, i.e., as the flower, the most precious thing of the whole Attic land. Cf. ὄμμα δόμων eye of the house Pers. 169 ὀφθαλμὸν οἴκων eye of the houseCh. 934 στρατιᾶς ὀφθαλμὸν ἐμᾶς eye of my armyPind. Ol. 6, 16 (Amphiaraus), Σικελίας ὀφθαλμός eye of Sicily 2, 11. (Θησῆιδος of Theseus on 402. 689). There was a priestess of Athena and beside her a τραπεζοφόρος table-bearer and a κοσμώ I adorn (Harpocr. τραπεζοφόρος table-bearer, Wecklein).

Δικαίως justly duly (Blaydes). Ἐξικέσθαι to arrive means 'to reach the goal' (Ag. 280. 303, Prom. 792. 810), but the optative with ἄν then can be a request, as at Choeph. 105 λέγοις ἄν you might say; so Athena bids the προπομποί escorts (1005), already visible to her before, now come fully forward.
Λόχος company as at 46;
στόλος procession 856.
Παίδων of children will be feminine (69, Prom. 865);

παίδων γυναικῶν of children and women asyndetic, like παῖδας γυναῖκας children and women Pers. 404 ἀνδρῶν γυναικῶν of men and womenSoph. Ant. 1059. All these are chosen from the noblest families; hence ὄμμα χθονός eye of the land. Compare, moreover, how in the Frogs Aeschylus himself is escorted (1520 ff.): φαίνετε τοίνυν ὑμεῖς τούτωι λαμπάδας ἱεράς show then you for this man sacred torches, χἄμα προπέμπετε τοῖσιν τούτου τοῦτον μέλεσιν καὶ μολπαῖσιν κελαδοῦντες and escort him with his own limbs and songs, celebrating. With the following verses (1028 f.) the προπομποί escorts are addressed, and according to Robert (Hermes 38, 634 ff.) the purple garments (1028) are to be put on the Eumenides by them, which also involved a change of masks; for in their original costume and with their original face masks they could hardly enter their new abodes as deities worthy of veneration. Since the orchestra was so exceptionally full, the necessary concealment from the spectators could easily be effected. A pause, however, not filled by words, after 1031 has even less difficulty than after 234. But now the speech of Athena is commonly regarded as transmitted with a lacuna, because, so it seems, according to credible and definite testimony something formerly stood in the tragedy and now does not, which belonged at this point. See the hypothesis: (Athena) τὰς Ἐρινύας πραΰνασα προσηγόρευσεν Εὐμενίδας having appeased the Erinyes she addressed them as Eumenides. Harpocration Εὐμενίδες Eumenides: Αἰσχύλος ἐν Εὐμενίσιν Aeschylus in the Eumenides, εἰπὼν τὰ περὶ τὴν κρίσιν τὴν Ὀρέστου having spoken about the trial of Orestes, φησὶν ὡς ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ πραΰνασα τὰς Ἐρινύας he says that Athena, having appeased the Erinyes, ὥστε μὴ χαλεπῶς ἔχειν πρὸς τὸν Ὀρέστην so that they were not angry with Orestes, Εὐμενίδας ὠνόμασεν she named them Eumenides. Even if one wished to derive this passage from the hypothesis instead of from the play, the first testimony would still remain, and the matter speaks for it; for that the renaming which actually did occur took place only in the title does not seem exactly credible. G. Hermann therefore placed the lacuna after 1027, also because of the asyndeton, which, however, one could easily remove (Robert): φοινικοβάπτοις dyed with purple ⟨δ d'⟩; Robert, on the other hand, after 1031, and he also gathers further material besides the change of name: thus the forgiveness for Orestes mentioned by the Eumenides (see above, Harpocration), for which, to be sure, words of Athena without an answer from those granting forgiveness would not suffice. Consider, however: if sense and construction after 1027 indicate no lacuna, then after 1031 they indicate none at all; I therefore do not venture to set the signs of one. –
Ἐνδυτοῖς ἐσθήμασιν with garments put on 1028 Hermann compares with Eurip. I. A. 1073, Tro. 257 and with ἐνδυτῆρα one who puts on Soph. Trach. 674.
— 1030 ἦδ᾽ ὁμιλία χθονός this company of the land exactly as at 406, 711; but εὔφρων kindly and no longer βαρεῖα heavy as at 711.
Πρέπειν to be conspicuous with dative Ch. 12. 18. 24, 'to stand out with'; here now with what she gives, εὔανδροι συμφοραί blessings of good men (1020 etc.).

Two short strophes with antistrophes; the rhythms are dactylic, just as in the Frogs the exit-song imitated from Aeschylus (1524 ff.) consists of dactylic hexameters. Str. α alpha, 1 tetrapody ending in a spondee; 3 (like a refrain) likewise catalectic; V. 2 is either a pentapody or a catalectic tetrapody + dipody, – ⏑ ⏑ – ⏑ ⏑ –, – ⏑ ⏑ – –, cf. 534 f. — Str. β beta, 2 acatalectic tetrapody cf. α alpha, 1 (the rhythm of 1 must first be investigated, since εὐθύφρονες straight-minded can also be – ⏑ ⏑ –); 3 catalectic tetrapody cf. α alpha, 3; the refrain an anapestic paroemiac, in rhythm attaching itself to the preceding verse, but there is hiatus or syllaba anceps between them.

Βᾶτε δόμωι Go to the house (Wellauer) seems grammatically inadmissible in the tragedians (since πέδωι ῾ to the ground 'to the ground' is also emended); since now Soph. Frg. 724 (in trimeter) βᾶτ᾽ εἰς ὁδόν go on your way stands, and below here 1041f. δεῦρ᾽ ἴτε come here . . καθ᾽ ὁδόν along the road, so before δόμον house, δόμους houses and all the many other conjectures Meineke's ἐς ὁδόν to the road seems to deserve preference. Βᾶτε Go is present (to βάω I go), not aor. = βῆτε you went, Kühner-Blass II 382. — As φιλότιμοι honor-loving the Eumenides have shown themselves greatly, and this is no reproach. Dindorf, however, explains here venerabiles, and Hik. 656 (φιλότιμος εὐχά honor-loving prayer) venerabundus (I prefer 'gladly honoring').

Παῖδες ἄπαιδες children without children as ἄπολιν πόλιν city without a city 457, νᾶες ἄναες ships without ships Pers. 680 (ships that are no longer ships, but destroyed); so one probably understands here too: those who are no longer children (but old women). Simpler yet and more obvious is 'childless' (Ddf.), pointing to the isolation of the dread goddesses (69). I cannot take offense at εὐθύφρονι with right mind (εὔφρονι with kindly mind L. Dindorf, Burney), and this form of the verse is more recommended by the antistrophe. Εὐθεῖαν δίκην Straight Justice 433, exactly i.e. just; also εὔφρονι with kindly mind would have to be 'well-thinking' and not 'well-disposed'. V. 1035, which interrupts the connected construction 1032f., 1036f., and correspondingly the other closing verses of the strophes are assigned by Kirchhoff to a herald; there certainly was a difference in the speaker or speakers. Χωρεῖτε Go forth Kirchhoff takes as an explanatory addition that has displaced the genuine πανδαμὶ with all the people = 1039; however Hermann's χωρῖται countrymen is actually no change and is supported by χωρίτης δράκων countryman snake Frg. 121. This then goes to the rest of the people.

Ὠγύγιος Ogygian the poets use for 'ancient', 'venerable', Sept. 321, Pers. 37.974 (everywhere of cities), Pind. N. 6, 54 (Φλειοῦντος ὑπ᾿ ὠγυγίοις ὄρεσιν) (from Phlius under the Ogygian mountains)Soph. Phil. 142 (κράτος power). There is no doubt about περίσεπτος much-revered; however, for the rhythm a short syllable is missing, and the parallel passage 1006 σφαγίων τῶνδ᾽ ὑπὸ σεμνῶν under these august sacrificial victims recommends περισέπται much-revered(σι si), cf. εὔσεπτος well-revered = εὖ σεβόμενος well-revering Soph. OT. 864.
Τύχᾶι Fortune = τύχηι ἀγαθῆι with good fortune (εὐπόμπωι τύχηι with favorable fortune 93).
Πανδαμεί with all the people (f g h) is to be written, since the length of the ending Sept. 296 is present (there also M -εί ei).
Ἵλᾶος propitious as in Homer A 583 etc.; in Aeschylus only here; Sophocles has ἵλᾶος propitious, OC. 1480, like Hom. I 639 etc.

For εὐθύφρονες γᾶι right-minded toward the land Meineke would like εὔφρονες αἴαι kindly-minded lands, with somewhat too much violence; τὰ δίκαια φρονοῦσαι τῆι γῆι thinking just things toward the land is nevertheless not inappropriate and corresponds to the disposition shown by the Athenians, 1034.
At line 1039 the Attic cult name Σεμναί August Goddesses appears (see already 383).

At 1042 M first had λαμπαὶ torches, corresponding to the οὕτως thus of the antistrophe; πεύκᾶι pine torch Schömann well conjectures (Ag. 288); Paley keeps λάμπᾶι torch and seeks to connect it in meaning with 387. The admonition of the refrain to the ὀλολυγμός ritual cry (Ch. 386, Sept. 268, Ag. 28. 595) is surely again addressed to the people, and specifically to the women, whose business this always is. Ag. 595 ὀλολυγμὸν ritual cry. . εὐφημοῦντα uttering auspicious sounds; so this too is a kind of the εὐφημεῖν to speak auspiciously (1035).
Ἐπὶ Upon as at 325.

Ὡς μή τιν᾿ οἶκον εὐθετεῖν ἄνευ σέθεν So that no house may prosper without you: Athena said at 895, and at 897 τῶι γὰρ σέβοντι συμφορὰς ὀρθώσομεν for to the one who reveres you we will set right misfortunes; so οἴκων Παλλάδος ἀστοῖς for the citizens of the house of Pallas fits with that, and also σπονδαί libations; for even if wine was not poured to the Eumenides, they still received libations of water and μελίκρατον honey-mixture. Schol. Soph. OC. 100: οὐ γὰρ σπένδεται οἶνος αὐταῖς ἀλλ᾽ ὕδωρ for wine is not poured to them, but water, καὶ νηφάλιαι καλοῦνται αἱ σπονδαὶ αὐτῶν and their libations are called wineless (Phot. νηφάλιοι θυσίαι wineless sacrifices· ἐν αἷς οἶνος οὐ σπένδεται in which wine is not poured, ἀλλὰ ὕδωρ καὶ μελίκρατον but water and honey-mixture, Paley on line 107). Now we can connect line 1044 to 1042, with the refrain interrupting the construction just as at 1035, and write σπονδᾶι with libation or σπονδαῖς with libations, but for ἔνδαιδες torch-bearing

ἔνδαιτες feasting together: ἔνδαις feasting in contrast to ἄδαιτος without a feast Ag. 147, and the construction as in ἄχαλκος ἀσπίδων without bronze, without shields and the like. If this is correct, then it follows that in the strophe, as at 1034, εὐθύφρονες straight-minded is to be scanned, and the verse is no longer dactylic, but consists of κατὰ βακχεῖον according to the bacchius, like Hik. 42 Δῖον πόρτιν ὑπερπόντιον τι the divine heifer from across the sea (μάορ᾽ ἶνίν τ΄ blessed son). Even so, ἐς τὸ πᾶν to the whole still resists, instead of - ◡ ◡; but ἐς πρόπᾶν to the whole can be written (πρόπαντος of the whole 898), since Euripides also scans πρόπᾶν the whole (Phoen. 1504), as does Aristophanes ἅπᾶν the whole, Kühner-Blass I, 481. Παν Pan (τ t) όπτας roasted of Zeus Hik. 139, Soph. OC. 1086.

Συγκατέβα I have consented 'has consented': this meaning is admittedly first attested in Polybius, εἰς πᾶν to everything 3, 10, 1 etc. in connection with εἰς to, on account of which Wieseler also proposes ἐς τάδε to these things here for the sake of consistency.
